# Use POTLIB surfaces through the potlibc engine

Source: docs/orgmode/howto/potlibc-engine.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/potlibc-engine.html

`libpotlibc_engine.so` is an optional engine plugin.
It keeps potlibc behind the generic engine C ABI: applications load one shared
library and pass one versioned create message.
There is no potlibc potential type or potlibc feature in `librgpot` or
`rgpot-core`.

### Install potlibc

Build and install potlibc first, at the revision the plugin tests run against.
The reference energies in `engines/test_potlibc_engine.c` can change between
potlibc revisions, so do not build the branch tip.
Its [surface catalog](https://omnipotentrpc.github.io/potlibc/) lists the
canonical surface ids and says which surfaces need an atom count. potlibc needs
a Fortran compiler and a `lapack` pkg-config module.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/potlibc.git
git -C potlibc checkout 85e9896be0da2b7f95d9a281a6f30c2c8ca76d8c
meson setup potlibc/build potlibc --prefix="$HOME/.local" --libdir=lib
meson compile -C potlibc/build
meson install -C potlibc/build
```

`--libdir=lib` puts `potlibc.pc` in `$HOME/.local/lib/pkgconfig` on every host.
Without it, Debian and Ubuntu install into a multiarch directory such as
`lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`, and the search path below would miss the file.
Make the prefix visible to `pkg-config` when it is not on the system search
path.

```bash
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$HOME/.local/lib/pkgconfig:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH"
```

### Build the plugin

`with_potlibc` is a Meson `feature` option and defaults to `disabled`.
`enabled` requires the `potlibc` pkg-config dependency and builds
`libpotlibc_engine.so`.

```bash
meson setup bbdir -Dwith_potlibc=enabled
meson compile -C bbdir libpotlibc_engine.so
meson test -C bbdir --print-errorlogs potlibc_engine engine_abi_stamps potlibc_engine_rust_loader
```

`potlibc_engine` drives the C entry points and the lock-failure build.
`engine_abi_stamps` compares the plugin's ABI stamp with the header.
`potlibc_engine_rust_loader` loads the plugin with `EnginePotential::load`,
checks the `brh2leps` energy and forces, and drives the lock-failure build to
confirm that `EngineError::Lock` latches the handle.

The plugin is separate from `librgpot`.
No potlibc symbols or headers enter the core library.

### Create a surface

`include/rgpot/potlibc_engine.h` declares `RgpotPotlibcConfigV2`, the message
new callers write, and `RgpotPotlibcConfigV1`, the 144-byte message a client
built against the original layout still sends.
Set the version-2 magic, size and version, copy one canonical catalog id into
`surface_id`, and set `atom_count` to zero for a fixed-size surface or to the
exact count for a variable-size surface.
`reserved` must be zero.
Version 1 has no size field: `magic` is at offset 0, `version` at offset 4,
`atom_count` at offset 8 and `surface_id` at offset 16.
Because
`RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_VERSION` now names version 2, a version-1 source recompiled against the current header must use `RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_VERSION_V1` (and `RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_V1_SIZE`); setting `RgpotPotlibcConfigV1.version` to `RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_VERSION`
is refused.
The plugin calls `potlibc_create` in the first case and `potlibc_create_sized`
in the second; it does not retry with another constructor.

```c
#include <string.h>

#include "rgpot/engine_c_abi.h"
#include "rgpot/potlibc_engine.h"

int main(void) {
RgpotPotlibcConfigV2 cfg = {
    .magic = RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_MAGIC,
    .size = sizeof(RgpotPotlibcConfigV2),
    .version = RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_VERSION,
    .reserved = 0,
    .atom_count = 0,
};
strcpy(cfg.surface_id, "brh2leps");

char error[512];
RgpotEnginePot *pot =
    rgpot_engine_create(&cfg, sizeof cfg, error, sizeof error);

rgpot_engine_destroy(pot);
return pot == NULL;
}
```

A version-2 message with `size < RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_MIN_SIZE` is refused as a
typed size error.
A larger version-2 message is accepted only when every unknown trailing byte up
to `size` is zero.
A version other than `RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_VERSION_V1` or
`RGPOT_POTLIBC_CONFIG_VERSION` is refused with the plain error string
`potlibc config version is unknown`.
The 144-byte version-1 message is accepted unchanged.

The engine ABI takes Angstrom and returns eV and eV/Angstrom.
The plugin performs the conversion to potlibc's Bohr and Hartree units.
When potlibc metadata gives atomic number 0 for an atom, that position is
unspecified and the plugin accepts the caller's species.
A nonzero catalog atomic number must match exactly.

### Load it from Rust

Enable the generic loader, not a potlibc-specific feature.

```toml
[dependencies]
rgpot-core = { version = "3.8.0", features = ["engine"] }
```

`rgpot_core::engine::PotlibcConfig` is the typed create message.
It is
`#[non_exhaustive]`: start from `PotlibcConfig::default()` or call `PotlibcConfig::new(surface_id, atom_count)`,
which refuses an empty, over-long or NUL-containing surface id.
`as_bytes` is the message to pass to `EnginePotential::load` with the path to `libpotlibc_engine.so`.

```rust
let config = PotlibcConfig::default()
    .with_surface_id("vbo-beta1")?
    .with_atom_count(4);
let mut engine =
    unsafe { EnginePotential::load(path, config.as_bytes()) }?;
```

`EnginePotential::force` evaluates energy and forces.
`EnginePotential::force_batch` evaluates systems of the surface's atom count in one `potlibc_evaluate`
call; a failed batch writes nothing.
`EnginePotential::hvp` uses `rgpot_engine_hvp` only when the surface advertises
an analytic product, and `into_potential` exposes that same handle to in-process
and RPC callers.

The complete symbol contracts and units are in the
[engine ABI reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/engine_abi.html).

---

# Use the parameterized coupled well engine

Source: docs/orgmode/howto/coupled-well-engine.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/coupled-well-engine.html

`libcoupled_well_engine.so` is a small analytic engine plugin for a
two-coordinate model with a quartic barrier and a transverse spring that is
shifted by the barrier coordinate.
It needs no model file and no third-party library, evaluates one atom, and has
exact energy, force and Hessian-vector product.
That makes it a reference for anything that consumes the generic engine C ABI: a
loader, a saddle-point or minimum search, a Hessian-vector method, or a batch
driver.
Nothing in it belongs to one method.

### The model

The engine acts on the x and y coordinates of one atom:

```
E(x, y) = V0 ((x / x0)^2 - 1)^2 + k / 2 (y - alpha x^2)^2
```

`V0` is the barrier energy in eV, `x0` the position of either minimum along x in
Angstrom, `k` the transverse spring in
eV/Angstrom^2 and `alpha` the coupling in 1/Angstrom.
The energy does not depend on z, so the z force is zero and the z row and column
of the Hessian are zero.
The cell is ignored: the model is not periodic.

With `u = x / x0` and `d = y - alpha x^2`, the gradient is

```
dE/dx = 4 V0 u (u^2 - 1) / x0 - 2 k alpha x d
dE/dy = k d
```

and the Hessian is

```
d2E/dx2  = 4 V0 (3 u^2 - 1) / x0^2 + k (4 alpha^2 x^2 - 2 alpha d)
d2E/dxdy = -2 k alpha x
d2E/dy2  = k
```

For `alpha = 0` the coordinates decouple into a double well in x and a harmonic
well in y.
The minima are at `(+/- x0, alpha x0^2)`, the barrier top at the origin has
energy `V0`, and the Hessian at a minimum is
`[[8 V0 / x0^2 + 4 k alpha^2 x0^2, -2 k alpha x0], [-2 k alpha x0, k]]`.

### Build the engine

On Unix-like builds, Meson builds `libcoupled_well_engine.so` without optional
dependencies.
Windows builds skip the engine plugin libraries, including this one.
When built for installation, it is installed with
`include/rgpot/coupled_well_engine.h`.

```bash
meson setup bbdir -Dwith_tests=true
meson compile -C bbdir
meson test -C bbdir --print-errorlogs coupled_well_engine
```

The test checks exact energies, forces and Hessian-vector products at the
minimum, the barrier top and a generic point against closed forms, the batch and
transform semantics, the compatibility rule of the ABI stamp, and concurrent use
of one handle.

### Create an instance

The create message new callers write is `RgpotCoupledWellConfigV2` from
`include/rgpot/coupled_well_engine.h`.
`RgpotCoupledWellConfigV1` is the 48-byte message a client built against the
original layout still sends: `magic` at offset 0, `version` at offset 4,
`atomic_number` at offset 8, `reserved` at offset 12 and the four parameters
from offset 16.
Because `RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_VERSION` now names version 2, a version-1
source recompiled against the current header must use
`RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_VERSION_V1` (and `RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_V1_SIZE`);
setting `RgpotCoupledWellConfigV1.version` to
`RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_VERSION` is refused.
Set the version-2 `magic`, `size` and `version`, the one `atomic_number` the
engine accepts, and the four parameters.
`reserved0` and `reserved1` must be zero.

```c
#include <string.h>

#include "rgpot/coupled_well_engine.h"
#include "rgpot/engine_c_abi.h"

int main(void) {
RgpotCoupledWellConfigV2 cfg;
memset(&cfg, 0, sizeof cfg);
cfg.magic = RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_MAGIC;
cfg.size = sizeof cfg;
cfg.version = RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_VERSION;
cfg.reserved0 = 0;
cfg.atomic_number = 1;
cfg.reserved1 = 0;
cfg.barrier_energy = 3.0;
cfg.well_position = 2.0;
cfg.transverse_spring = 4.0;
cfg.coupling = 0.25;

char error[256];
RgpotEnginePot *pot =
    rgpot_engine_create(&cfg, sizeof cfg, error, sizeof error);
if (pot == NULL) {
    return 1;
}
rgpot_engine_destroy(pot);
return 0;
}
```

`rgpot_engine_create` refuses, with a reason in `errbuf`, a version-2 message
with
`size < RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_MIN_SIZE`, a wrong magic or reserved field, a version other than `RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_VERSION_V1`
or `RGPOT_COUPLED_WELL_CONFIG_VERSION` (the plain error string
`coupled-well config version is unknown`), a non-positive
`atomic_number`, a `barrier_energy`, `well_position` or `transverse_spring` that
is not finite and positive, and a `coupling` that is not finite.
A negative `coupling` is valid.
A larger version-2 message is accepted only when every unknown trailing byte up
to `size` is zero.
The 48-byte version-1 message is accepted unchanged.

### Evaluate it

`rgpot_engine_force` takes exactly one atom of the configured species.
A different atom count or species is refused with code 1.
A position that is not finite after the optional transform is refused with code
1, and a position at which the energy or force overflows returns code 2.
Nothing is written to `forces`, `energy` or `variance` on an error, and the
reason is in `rgpot_engine_last_error`.
`rgpot_engine_hvp` follows the same rules, also refuses a direction that is not
finite, and refuses with code 1 when
`hv_out` overlaps `direction`, `positions`, `atomicNrs` or `box`, leaving `hv_out`
untouched.

`rgpot_engine_force_batch` evaluates `nSystems` systems of that one atom.
It applies the transform to every system and evaluates every system before it
writes anything, so a refused transform or an overflow leaves `forces`,
`energies` and `variances` unchanged.
It returns the first nonzero transform code, 1 for an invalid argument
(`invalid argument (batch)`), and 2 for a non-finite answer.

The library reports `RgpotEngineCaps` with `batched` and `analytic_hvp` set and
`reentrancy` 0.
The model is a pure function of the create message, so any number of threads may
call one handle at once, and `rgpot_engine_last_error` may run during an
evaluation.
When calls overlap, a successful call may clear a failure message from another
thread before it is read.

The library exports `rgpot_engine_available`, which returns 1, the ABI stamp and
`rgpot_engine_abi_compatible` with the rule of the [[file:../reference/engine_abi.org][engine
ABI reference]]: equal major and layout revision, and an engine minor no newer
than the host's.
It does not export the model digest, thread-setting or charge-and-spin symbols.

### Load it from Rust

Enable the generic loader, not an engine-specific feature.

```toml
[dependencies]
rgpot-core = { version = "3.8.0", features = ["engine"] }
```

`rgpot_core::engine::CoupledWellConfig` is the typed create message.
It is
`#[non_exhaustive]`, so start from `CoupledWellConfig::default()`, a valid unit well, and chain the `with_*`
builders.
`validate` applies the create-time checks of the engine before the library is
opened.
`as_bytes` is the message to pass to `EnginePotential::load`.

```rust
let config = CoupledWellConfig::default()
    .with_atomic_number(1)
    .with_barrier_energy(3.0)
    .with_well_position(2.0)
    .with_transverse_spring(4.0)
    .with_coupling(0.25);
config.validate()?;
let mut engine =
    unsafe { EnginePotential::load(path, config.as_bytes()) }?;
let request = EngineRequest {
    positions: &[1.0, 0.5, 0.0],
    atomic_numbers: &[1],
    box_matrix: &[10.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0],
};
let answer = engine.force(&request)?;
let product = engine.hvp(&request, &[1.0, 2.0, 0.0])?;
```

For the parameters of the example, the energy at (1, 0.5) is
29/16 eV, the force is (11/4, -1, 0)
eV/Angstrom, and the Hessian-vector product for the direction (1, 2, 0) is (-17/4,
6, 0).
`EnginePotential::force_batch` returns one `EngineEvaluation` per system.

---

# rgpot Potentials as eindir Objectives (and Minimizing Them with anneal)

Source: docs/orgmode/howto/eindir-anneal.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/eindir-anneal.html

## rgpot Potentials as eindir Objectives

This guide shows how an rgpot potential becomes an
[eindir](https://github.com/HaoZeke/eindir) objective and how
[anneal](https://github.com/HaoZeke/anneal) then minimizes it.
The three projects share one contract, eindir's `Objective`. rgpot produces
objectives and anneal consumes them, with no direct dependency between the two.

### The shared contract: `eindir_objective_t` and `Objective<f64>`

eindir defines the objective contract twice, with a bridge between the two
halves:

- A C ABI struct, `eindir_objective_t` (`#[repr(C)]`): `dim`, bounds `low` and
  `high`, and `eval_fn` and `grad_fn` callbacks over DLPack tensors.
- A Rust trait, `Objective<f64>` (plus `Gradient<f64>`).
- `EindirObjectiveWrapper` (in
  `eindir_core::ffi`), which borrows an `eindir_objective_t` and presents it as
  a Rust `Objective<f64>`.

Any language that can write the C struct produces an objective.
Any Rust code that takes `Objective<f64>` consumes one.

### rgpot side: `rgpot_potential_t` is an `eindir_objective_t`

`rgpot_potential_t` embeds `eindir_objective_t` as its first member, `base`.
A `rgpot_potential_t*` cast to `eindir_objective_t*` is therefore valid at the C
ABI with no conversion.
The embedded `eval_fn` and `grad_fn` call the rgpot force and energy callback
directly, so there is one evaluation path.
The gradient is the negative of the forces.

```rust
let pot = unsafe {
    rgpot_potential_new_eindir(
        callback,        // rgpot force/energy callback (LJ, CuH2, NWChem dlopen, ...)
        user_data, free_fn,
        n_atoms, atomic_numbers, box_matrix,
        bounds_low, bounds_high, // n_atoms * 3 values each, or null
    )
};
let objective = pot as *mut eindir_objective_t; // first-member cast
```

`rgpot_potential_new_eindir` copies the atomic numbers, the nine box values and
the bounds.
A null bound gives -50 or 50 in every dimension.
A null `atomic_numbers` gives zeros and a null `box_matrix` gives a zero box.
It returns null and sets `rgpot_last_error()` when `n_atoms * 3` overflows.
Free the result with
`rgpot_potential_free_eindir` or `rgpot_potential_free`, never with `eindir_objective_free`
on the embedded base.

Check the embedded base against the eindir-core of the loaded library before the
cast is read as an objective:

```rust
let stamp = rgpot_eindir_abi_stamp();
assert_eq!(unsafe { rgpot_eindir_abi_compatible(&stamp) }, 1);
```

`rgpot_eindir_abi_compatible` forwards to `eindir_core_abi_compatible` in the
eindir-core that rgpot was built with, so the check needs no second link to
eindir-core.
A null stamp is not compatible and returns 0.

A callback that returns
`RGPOT_SUCCESS` must set a non-null f64 CPU forces tensor with exactly `n_atoms * 3`
finite elements, and a finite energy.
Anything else makes `eindir_objective_eval` and `eindir_objective_grad` return
`EINDIR_INVALID_PARAMETER` and set the message read by `rgpot_last_error()`.
The same status and a message come back for an input tensor of the wrong shape,
dtype or device.
A callback that returns any other status makes them return
`EINDIR_INTERNAL_ERROR`; rgpot adds no message of its own in that case.
On every failure the output value or gradient is left untouched.

Charged-evaluation accounting reads the per-handle counters:

```c
rgpot_eval_counts_t c;
rgpot_potential_eval_counts(pot, &c);  // c.computed: callback invocations
                                       // c.served: gradients answered from the
                                       //           fused energy+gradient result
rgpot_potential_reset_eval_counts(pot);
```

A gradient is served without a callback when it is requested at the same
positions, bit for bit, as the evaluation just before it.
`rgpot_potential_eval_counts` returns `RGPOT_INVALID_PARAMETER` when `pot` or
the output pointer is null.

rgpot-core depends on eindir-core as a normal Cargo crate
(`features = ["capi"]`), not on a prebuilt `libeindir_core.a`.
A downstream Rust binary that links rgpot-core and anneal-core (both depending
on eindir-core) gets one compilation of eindir-core.
That avoids the duplicate symbols and the second Rust runtime a static library
would bring.

### anneal side: minimize any `Objective<f64>`

anneal's drivers are generic over `O: eindir_core::Objective<f64>`.
Wrap the rgpot objective and hand it to a variant:

```rust
let wrapper = unsafe { EindirObjectiveWrapper::new(&*objective) }; // impl Objective<f64>
let variant = boltzmann(wrapper, /*t_init*/ 3.0, /*sigma*/ 0.15)?;
let history = run_rs_qmc_variant(variant, /*n_starts*/ 24, /*n_epochs*/ 300, /*steps_per_epoch*/ 200, seed);
// history.best.pos / history.best.val hold the minimizer found by SA.
```

A runnable end-to-end demonstration lives in the anneal repository at
`examples/rgpot_minimize.rs` (`cargo run --features capi --example rgpot_minimize`).
It builds a 9-dimensional quadratic rgpot potential (three atoms) with bounds
`[-5, 5]` in every dimension, wraps it, and anneals it.
The example asserts that the best energy is below 0.1, the minimum being 0.

### Dependency shape

```
                 eindir-core  (Objective<f64>, eindir_objective_t, EindirObjectiveWrapper)
                  /        \
       rgpot-core           anneal-core
   (rgpot_potential_t        (run_rs_variant<O: Objective>,
    IS-A eindir_objective_t)  boltzmann / fast / gsa / QMC multistart)
                  \        /
              demo: examples/rgpot_minimize.rs
```

rgpot-core and anneal-core never depend on each other; eindir-core is the only
shared vocabulary.
Pin all three to the same eindir-core (and `dlpk`) version so the one shared
compilation lines up.

# eOn Potentials Over rgpot

Source: docs/orgmode/howto/eon-rgpot.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/eon-rgpot.html

The **eOn ↔ rgpot** integration gives eOn access to rgpot's quantum-chemistry
backends (**NWChem** via `nwchemc`, **CPMD** e.g. BLYP via `cpmdc`) through two
independent roles:

- **In-process (shipped in eOn):** eOn's `RgpotPot` (`-Dwith_rgpot=true`) links
rgpot's `NWChemPot` / `CPMDPot` frontends as a Meson subproject and
`dlopen=s the engine libraries directly. No sockets, no potserv. Configured through the eOn =[RgpotPot]`
INI section (`backend`, `basis`, `theory`,
`scf_type`, `functional`, `charge`, `multiplicity`, `engine_library`, ...).
- **Out-of-process RPC (this repo):** `potserv <port> NWChem|CPMD` serves the
Cap'n Proto `Potential` interface for any client; eOn can also act as an RPC
*server* via `eonclient --serve` (`-Dwith_serve=true`).

Engine builds live in `nwchemc` / `cpmdc`; rgpot frontends `dlopen` them at
runtime in both roles.

Why the integration is shaped this way is in
[The RPC Model](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/rpc-model.html), under eOn over rgpot.

## Landed Work Items

1. **eOn potential class** (eOn tree): `client/potentials/Rgpot/` —
`RgpotPot` (eOn `Potential` subclass) over an opaque `RGPotEngine` TU that
isolates rgpot / Cap'n Proto headers from eOn's own `Potential` type.
2. **CPMD BLYP example** (eOn tree): `examples/rgpot_cpmd_blyp/` with the
in-process `[RgpotPot]` configuration.
3. **NWChem comparison** (eOn tree): `scripts/bench_rgpot_vs_socket_forces.sh`
and `scripts/rgpot_nwchem_vs_socket.sh` compare `RgpotPot` against eOn's
`SocketNWChem` on a fixed deck class.
4. **rgpot ergonomics** (this repo): typed
   NWChem/CPMD arms and the metatomic outputs surface in `Potentials.capnp` (from the potentials-schema v1.12.0 pin), the schema-sync tests (Meson suite `schema`), and the in-process CPMD timing harness (`scripts/cpmd_inprocess_vs_subprocess_timing.sh`).
`subprojects/potentials-schema.wrap` now pins potentials-schema at commit
`190fee6`.

## Operator Cheatsheet (rgpot side)

`potserv <port> <PotentialType>` selects the backend.
Every build accepts `LJ`, `LJCluster`, `Morse`, `ZBL`, `Composite`, `D2`,
`D2Cpmd`, `NWChem`, `NWChem:basis[:theory[:xc]]` and `CPMD`.
A Fortran build also accepts `CuH2`.
The remaining names are present only when that backend was compiled in:
`IPI:unix:<path>` and `IPI:tcp:<host>:<port>`; `XTB` (GFN2-xTB), `GFNFF`,
`GFN0xTB` and `GFN1xTB`; `TBLite` (the same backend as `TBLiteGFN2`),
`TBLiteGFN1` and `TBLiteIPEA1`; `D3` and `D4`;
`Metatomic:<model_path>[:<device>]`; `Uma:<model_path>` and
`Uma:<model_path>:<task>`, with a task of `omol`, `omat`, `oc20`, `oc22`,
`oc25`, `odac` or `omc`; `Skala` and `Skala:<basis>`; and `CP2K`.
A missing type prints that list for the binary that is running.
The `configure` arms are a separate list, on
[PotentialConfig arms](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/potential_config.html).
The fake engines and `potserv` are built with
`-Dwith_rpc=true -Dwith_tests=true`.
`tests/test_rpc_e2e_c_abi.py` needs `RGPOT_POTSERV` and one engine variable per
backend.
Both `pixi run -e rpctest rpctest` and `potctl ci rpc-integ` export them.
The two end to end tests run there.
Outside those tasks, a run skips when `potserv` or an engine library is absent.
It prints the reason.

```bash
# Real engines (built in OmniPotentRPC/nwchemc and OmniPotentRPC/cpmdc)
NWCHEMC_LIBRARY=/path/to/libnwchemc.so ./bbdir/CppCore/potserv 12345 NWChem
CPMDC_LIBRARY=/path/to/libcpmdc.so   ./bbdir/CppCore/potserv 12346 CPMD

# Fake engines (meson -Dwith_rpc=true -Dwith_tests=true)
export RGPOT_POTSERV=./bbdir/CppCore/potserv
export NWCHEMC_LIBRARY=./bbdir/CppCore/libnwchemc_fake_engine.so
export RGPOT_CPMD_ENGINE=./bbdir/CppCore/libcpmdc_fake_engine.so
pixi run -e rpctest -- python tests/test_rpc_e2e_c_abi.py
```

See `CppCore/rgpot/NWChemPot/README.md`, `CppCore/rgpot/CPMDPot/README.md`, and
`docs/orgmode/howto/integration.org`.

## Related

- `docs/orgmode/howto/eindir-anneal.org` — minimizers via embedded eindir
objective in `rgpot-core` (orthogonal to eOn's own optimizers, but shares the
potential energy API story).
- eOn user guide pages `rgpot_pot.md` / `rgpot_integration.md` (eOn tree) for
the consumer-side documentation.

# Pair and shifted potentials

Source: docs/orgmode/howto/potentials-pair.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/potentials-pair.html

This page covers the classical pair potentials of rgpot and the three host
wrappers around the shifted Lennard-Jones form.
`LJ`, `LJCluster`, `Morse`, `ZBL` and `SuttonChen` are C++ kernels in
`CppCore/rgpot/`.
`Lammps`, `Gromacs` and `OpenMM` are the shifted Lennard-Jones potential seen
through a molecular dynamics engine, in that engine's units where it has any.
Each section gives the functional form read from the kernel, every parameter
with its source, a program that runs against the library, and the literature.
Constructors, configuration structs and error cases are listed in
[C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html).
The names that
`pair_coeff`, PLUMED and `rgpot-eval` accept are in [[file:../reference/potential_names.org][Potential
names]].
Energies are eV, lengths are Angstrom, forces are
eV/Angstrom and stresses are eV/Angstrom^3 unless a section says otherwise.

### `LJ` Lennard-Jones pair potential

#### What it is and how to reach it

`LJ` is the 12-6 Lennard-Jones potential, cut and shifted at a cutoff, with the
minimum image convention in all three directions.
Use it for noble-gas style systems and as a stiff, cheap reference pair
potential in periodic cells.
In C++ it is `rgpot::LJPot`, built from `rgpot::LJConfig` (header
`CppCore/rgpot/LennardJones/LJPot.hpp`).
In Python it is `rgpot.LJPot(u0, cutoff, psi, switch_width)`.
`pair_coeff * * LJ`, the PLUMED action and `rgpot-eval LJ` take the options `u0`, `psi`, `cutoff` and `switch_width`.
`potserv <port> LJ` serves the default configuration.
The constructors and their errors are in the
[C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html) reference, the option
names in [Potential names](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/potential_names.html).

#### Functional form

With `r= the pair distance, the kernel in =CppCore/rgpot/LennardJones/LJPot.cc`
computes, for every pair with `r` up to the cutoff:

- the bare pair energy `v(r) = 4 u0 [(psi/r)^12 - (psi/r)^6]`, evaluated as
  `4 u0 a (a - 1)` with `a = (psi^2 / r^2)^3`;
- with `switch_width` 0, the pair energy `v(r) - v(cutoff)`, so the energy is
  zero at the cutoff and the force jumps there;
- with `switch_width` `w= above 0, the pair energy =v(r) S(t)` and no shift,
  where `t = clamp((r - (cutoff - w)) / w, 0, 1)` and
  `S(t) = 1 - 10 t^3 + 15 t^4 - 6 t^5` (the C^2 quintic of
  `CppCore/rgpot/PairSwitch.hpp`);
- the force on atom `i= along =d = r_i - r_j` is `fscale * d` with
  `fscale = 24 u0 a (2 a - 1) / r^2`; with the switch on, `fscale` is that value
  times `S(t)` minus `v(r) S'(r) / r`, where `S'` is the derivative of `S` with
  respect to `r`.

Pairs beyond the cutoff contribute nothing.
The cell must be given, since every pair uses its minimum image.
The call writes the stress.
Atomic numbers are not read.

#### Parameters

| Parameter      | Value | Unit     | Where it is set                 |
|----------------|-------|----------|---------------------------------|
| `u0`           |   1.0 | eV       | `LJConfig::u0`                  |
| `psi`          |   1.0 | Angstrom | `LJConfig::psi`                 |
| `cutoff`       |  15.0 | Angstrom | `LJConfig::cutoff`              |
| `switch_width` |   0.0 | Angstrom | `LJConfig::switch_width`        |

The values are the defaults of `LJConfig` in
`CppCore/rgpot/LennardJones/LJPot.hpp`.
Each field has an option of the same name in
`pair_coeff` and `rgpot-eval` (`engines/pot_spec.cpp`), where `cutoff` defaults
to the host's cutoff.
`u0` is the well depth, `psi` the zero crossing, so the unshifted minimum is at
`2^(1/6) psi` and has depth `u0`.
The defaults are reduced units, not a fitted material.
No paper supplies them: they are a convention of the code.
The program below passes its own values (`u0` 0.0104 eV, `psi` 3.40 Angstrom,
`cutoff` 8.5 Angstrom), which are the numbers of the LAMMPS input in
[LAMMPS](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-lammps.html) and are not a cited argon fit.

#### Example

The program evaluates one dimer at four separations with the shifted and the
switched kernel, next to the bare pair energy computed from the formula above.
The switch starts at 6.5 Angstrom, so the first two rows are unchanged by it and
the last row is almost zero.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/LennardJones/LJPot.hpp"

int main() {
  const double u0 = 0.0104;
  const double psi = 3.40;
  const double cutoff = 8.5;
  rgpot::LJPot shifted({.u0 = u0, .cutoff = cutoff, .psi = psi});
  rgpot::LJPot switched(
      {.u0 = u0, .cutoff = cutoff, .psi = psi, .switch_width = 2.0});

  const int z[2] = {18, 18};
  const double box[9] = {40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 40.0};
  const double rmin = std::pow(2.0, 1.0 / 6.0) * psi;
  const double rs[4] = {rmin, 6.0, 7.5, 8.4};

  std::printf("   r (A)   bare (eV)  shifted (eV)  switched (eV)\n");
  for (const double r : rs) {
    const double pos[6] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, r, 0.0, 0.0};
    double forces[6] = {};
    rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
    rgpot::ForceOut out{};
    out.F = forces;
    shifted.forceImpl(in, &out);
    const double e_shift = out.energy;
    switched.forceImpl(in, &out);
    const double s6 = std::pow(psi / r, 6.0);
    std::printf("%8.4f %11.6f %13.6f %14.6f\n", r, 4.0 * u0 * s6 * (s6 - 1.0),
                e_shift, out.energy);
  }
  return 0;
}
```

```
   r (A)   bare (eV)  shifted (eV)  switched (eV)
  3.8164   -0.010400     -0.010230      -0.010400
  6.0000   -0.001332     -0.001162      -0.001332
  7.5000   -0.000358     -0.000188      -0.000179
  8.4000   -0.000182     -0.000012      -0.000000
```

The shifted column is the bare column plus the constant 0.000170 eV, the
negative of `v(cutoff)` at 8.5 Angstrom.
The switched column equals the bare one up to 6.5 Angstrom and goes to zero
smoothly at the cutoff.

#### Literature

- Goswami papers: none of those read for this page uses this kernel, so none is
  listed.
- J. E. Jones, Proc.
  R. Soc.
  A 106, 463-477 (1924), doi:10.1098/rspa.1924.0082, the 12-6 form (the registry
  lists the single author as J. E. Jones).
- Parameters: the defaults and the argon-like values of the example have no
  paper.
  They are a convention of the code.

### `LJCluster` Lennard-Jones for free clusters

#### What it is and how to reach it

`LJCluster` is the `LJ` pair kernel with no minimum image and no periodic cell,
so a cluster in a box that is too small, or in no box at all, is not folded.
Use it for gas-phase clusters and global-optimization landscapes.
In C++ it is `rgpot::LJClusterPot`, built from `rgpot::LJClusterConfig` (header
`CppCore/rgpot/LennardJones/LJClusterPot.hpp`).
In Python it is `rgpot.LJClusterPot(u0, cutoff, psi, switch_width)`.
`potserv <port> LJCluster` serves the default configuration.
It has no `pair_coeff` or `rgpot-eval` name.
The class is documented in
[C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html).
The kernel is ported from eOn, as the header says.

#### Functional form

The pair energy, the shift, the switch and the force are those of `LJ` (see
above), computed from `CppCore/rgpot/LennardJones/LJClusterPot.cc`.
What differs:

- pair vectors come straight from the coordinates; the cell is never used to
  fold them, and `caps().periodic` is false;
- the call writes no stress;
- a box with a non-positive diagonal entry, or none, is replaced by a cube of
  1e6 Angstrom;
- when no switch is set and the whole cluster fits inside the cutoff, the kernel
  sums every pair directly; otherwise it walks the shared cell list.
  Both include the same pairs.

A `cutoff` of exactly 0 is not usable for the energy.
The shift is `4 u0 a (a - 1)` with `a = (psi / cutoff)^6`, which is infinite for
a zero cutoff, and the energy printed is `-inf` while the forces are finite.
Use a large positive cutoff to keep every pair of a small cluster.

#### Parameters

| Parameter      | Value | Unit     | Where it is set                 |
|----------------|-------|----------|---------------------------------|
| `u0`           |   1.0 | eV       | `LJClusterConfig::u0`           |
| `psi`          |   1.0 | Angstrom | `LJClusterConfig::psi`          |
| `cutoff`       |  15.0 | Angstrom | `LJClusterConfig::cutoff`       |
| `switch_width` |   0.0 | Angstrom | `LJClusterConfig::switch_width` |

The values are the defaults in `CppCore/rgpot/LennardJones/LJClusterPot.hpp`.
They are reduced units with no paper behind them, as for `LJ`.

#### Example

The first part puts a dimer 9 Angstrom apart in a 10 Angstrom box.
`LJPot` sees the neighbour image at 1 Angstrom and `LJClusterPot` sees the atoms
9 Angstrom apart, beyond the 4 Angstrom cutoff.
The second part builds the 13-atom icosahedron (a centre atom and the 12
vertices of `(0, +-1, +-phi)` and its cyclic permutations), finds the radius
with the lowest energy by ternary search, and removes the 78 pair shifts to
compare with the literature value.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/LennardJones/LJClusterPot.hpp"
#include "rgpot/LennardJones/LJPot.hpp"

int main() {
  const int z[2] = {18, 18};
  const double pos[6] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 9.0, 0.0, 0.0};
  const double box[9] = {10.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0};
  double forces[6] = {};
  rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces;

  rgpot::LJPot periodic({.u0 = 1.0, .cutoff = 4.0, .psi = 1.0});
  periodic.forceImpl(in, &out);
  std::printf("periodic: energy %.6f eV\n", out.energy);

  rgpot::LJClusterPot cluster({.u0 = 1.0, .cutoff = 4.0, .psi = 1.0});
  cluster.forceImpl(in, &out);
  std::printf("cluster:  energy %.6f eV\n", out.energy);

  const double phi = 0.5 * (1.0 + std::sqrt(5.0));
  const double raw[12][3] = {
      {0, 1, phi}, {0, -1, phi}, {0, 1, -phi}, {0, -1, -phi},
      {1, phi, 0}, {-1, phi, 0}, {1, -phi, 0}, {-1, -phi, 0},
      {phi, 0, 1}, {-phi, 0, 1}, {phi, 0, -1}, {-phi, 0, -1}};
  const double norm = std::sqrt(1.0 + phi * phi);
  const double cutoff = 15.0;
  rgpot::LJClusterPot lj13({.u0 = 1.0, .cutoff = cutoff, .psi = 1.0});
  const int z13[13] = {18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18};

  auto energy = [&](double r) {
    std::vector<double> p(39, 0.0);
    std::vector<double> f(39, 0.0);
    for (int i = 0; i < 12; ++i) {
      for (int d = 0; d < 3; ++d) {
        p[3 * (i + 1) + d] = r * raw[i][d] / norm;
      }
    }
    rgpot::ForceInput in13{13, p.data(), z13, box};
    rgpot::ForceOut out13{};
    out13.F = f.data();
    lj13.forceImpl(in13, &out13);
    return out13.energy;
  };

  double lo = 0.9;
  double hi = 1.3;
  for (int k = 0; k < 80; ++k) {
    const double m1 = lo + (hi - lo) / 3.0;
    const double m2 = hi - (hi - lo) / 3.0;
    if (energy(m1) < energy(m2)) {
      hi = m2;
    } else {
      lo = m1;
    }
  }
  const double r = 0.5 * (lo + hi);
  const double a = std::pow(1.0 / cutoff, 6.0);
  const double shift = 4.0 * a * (a - 1.0);
  std::printf("LJ13 icosahedron: centre-vertex %.5f, shifted %.6f eV\n", r,
              energy(r));
  std::printf("pair sum without the 78 shifts: %.6f eV\n",
              energy(r) + 78.0 * shift);
  return 0;
}
```

```
periodic: energy 0.000976 eV
cluster:  energy 0.000000 eV
LJ13 icosahedron: centre-vertex 1.08184, shifted -44.326774 eV
pair sum without the 78 shifts: -44.326801 eV
```

The periodic energy is the zero crossing at 1 Angstrom minus the shift, which is
-0.000976 eV, and the cluster energy is 0 because the pair lies beyond the
cutoff.
The last value is the 13-atom Ih entry, -44.326801, of the table of Wales and
Doye, to all six printed decimals.

#### Literature

- Goswami and coauthors, eOn v3.6.0, Zenodo (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18529495,
  the software release of eOn, from which the header of `LJClusterPot.hpp` says
  the kernel was ported.
  No Goswami paper read for this page uses the kernel by name.
- J. E. Jones, Proc.
  R. Soc.
  A 106, 463-477 (1924), doi:10.1098/rspa.1924.0082, the 12-6 form.
- Wales and Doye, J. Phys.
  Chem.
  A 101, 5111-5116 (1997), doi:10.1021/jp970984n, the Lennard-Jones potential in
  reduced units and the lowest energy clusters; its table lists -44.326801 for
  the 13-atom Ih cluster, the check above.
- Parameters: the defaults are reduced units and have no paper.

### `Morse` Morse pair potential with platinum parameters

#### What it is and how to reach it

`Morse` is the pairwise Morse potential, cut and shifted at 9.5 Angstrom, with
the platinum parameter set as its default.
Use it for fast metallic surface and cluster work, such as the Pt(111) heptamer
island benchmark, and as a smooth pair reference that is softer than
Lennard-Jones.
In C++ it is `rgpot::MorsePot`, built from `rgpot::MorseConfig` (header
`CppCore/rgpot/Morse/MorsePot.hpp`).
In Python it is `rgpot.MorsePot(De, a, re, cutoff, switch_width)`.
`pair_coeff * * Morse`, the PLUMED action and `rgpot-eval Morse` take the options `de`, `a=, =re`, `cutoff` and `switch_width`,
with 9.5 Angstrom as the cutoff when the host has none.
`potserv <port> Morse` loads the platinum defaults.
The class is documented in
[C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html) and the names in
[Potential names](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/potential_names.html).

#### Functional form

From `CppCore/rgpot/Morse/MorsePot.hpp` and `MorsePot.cc`, for every pair with
`r` up to the cutoff:

- the bare pair energy is `De [1 - exp(-a (r - re))]^2 - De`, so the well has
  depth `De` at `re` and the energy tends to 0 at large `r`;
- with `switch_width` 0, the pair energy is the bare one minus its value at the
  cutoff (the constructor stores it, and `MorsePot::energyShift()` returns it);
- with `switch_width` above 0 the shift is replaced by the same C^2 quintic
  switch as in `LJ`, applied to the bare energy;
- with `x = a (r - re)` the derivative of the bare energy is
  `2 De a (1 - e^-x) e^-x`, and the force on the pair is minus that along the
  pair.

The minimum image is used in every direction on an orthogonal or sheared cell.
The call writes the stress.
Atomic numbers are not read.

#### Parameters

| Parameter      | Value  | Unit       | Where it is set                  |
|----------------|--------|------------|----------------------------------|
| `De`           | 0.7102 | eV         | `MorseConfig::De`, option `de`   |
| `a=            | 1.6047 | 1/Angstrom | =MorseConfig::a`, option `a`     |
| `re`           | 2.8970 | Angstrom   | `MorseConfig::re`, option `re`   |
| `cutoff`       |    9.5 | Angstrom   | `MorseConfig::cutoff`            |
| `switch_width` |    0.0 | Angstrom   | `MorseConfig::switch_width`      |

The values are the defaults in `CppCore/rgpot/Morse/MorsePot.hpp`, where the
field comments call them the platinum set.
The same numbers are in the Python binding
(`python/bind/bind_module.cpp`), the Cap'n Proto schema default (`rgpot-core/schema/Potentials.capnp`) and the Rust test `rgpot-core/tests/potential_config.rs`.

*Origin of the numbers.* The source names no paper for them.
The comments in `MorsePot.hpp` say only "platinum", and the header says the
kernel is ported from eOn, whose original attribution names A. Pedersen or G.
Henkelman, revised by J.-C.
C. Berthet.
Two papers print the same three numbers.
Sheppard, Terrell and Henkelman use a pairwise Morse potential for a heptamer
island on an fcc(111) surface with `De` 0.7102 eV, `alpha` 1.6047 per Angstrom
and `r0` 2.8970 Angstrom, "parameters fit to Pt", cut and shifted to zero at 9.5
Angstrom, and cite Bassett and Webber for the Pt fit.
Chill and coauthors give C = 0.7102 eV, a = 1.6047 per Angstrom and r0 = 2.8970
Angstrom for the Morse systems of their benchmark, "chosen to describe Pt", with
the same citation.
Bassett and Webber was not consulted for this page.
The reference page [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html)
attributes the defaults to Sheppard and coauthors.
That matches the numbers in the paper, but the source does not say it.

#### Example

The program prints the stored parameters, the shift, and the shifted energy and
force of a platinum dimer at four separations, next to the bare Morse energy
computed from the formula.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/Morse/MorsePot.hpp"

int main() {
  rgpot::MorsePot pot;
  const rgpot::MorseConfig &cfg = pot.config();
  std::printf("De %.4f eV, a %.4f 1/A, re %.4f A, cutoff %.1f A\n", cfg.De,
              cfg.a, cfg.re, cfg.cutoff);
  std::printf("energy shift %.12f eV\n", pot.energyShift());

  const int z[2] = {78, 78};
  const double box[9] = {40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 40.0};
  const double rs[4] = {2.50, cfg.re, 3.30, 9.40};
  std::printf("   r (A)   bare (eV)  shifted (eV)  force on atom 1 (eV/A)\n");
  for (const double r : rs) {
    const double pos[6] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, r, 0.0, 0.0};
    double forces[6] = {};
    rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
    rgpot::ForceOut out{};
    out.F = forces;
    pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
    const double d = 1.0 - std::exp(-cfg.a * (r - cfg.re));
    std::printf("%8.4f %11.6f %13.6f %24.6f\n", r, cfg.De * d * d - cfg.De,
                out.energy, forces[3]);
  }
  return 0;
}
```

```
De 0.7102 eV, a 1.6047 1/A, re 2.8970 A, cutoff 9.5 A
energy shift -0.000035537997 eV
   r (A)   bare (eV)  shifted (eV)  force on atom 1 (eV/A)
  2.5000   -0.146481     -0.146446                 3.839898
  2.8970   -0.710200     -0.710164                 0.000000
  3.3000   -0.549133     -0.549098                -0.568541
  9.4000   -0.000042     -0.000006                -0.000067
```

At `re` the force is zero, and the shifted energy is the bare -0.7102 eV plus
the 3.5538e-05 eV that `energyShift()` reports with a negative sign.
Inside `re` the force on atom 1 is positive (repulsive) and outside it is
negative.

### `ZBL` Screened nuclear repulsion

#### What it is and how to reach it

`ZBL` is the universal Ziegler-Biersack-Littmark screened Coulomb repulsion
between nuclei, taken to zero at a cutoff with a polynomial switch.
Use it for short-range repulsion at small separations, for example under another
potential in radiation damage work.
In C++ it is `rgpot::ZBLPot`, built from `rgpot::ZBLConfig` (header
`CppCore/rgpot/ZBL/ZBLPot.hpp`).
Python has no ZBL class and `pair_coeff` has no ZBL name.
`potserv <port> ZBL` serves the default configuration.
The class is documented in
[C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html).
The kernel is ported from eOn, which adapts the LAMMPS `pair_zbl` code, as the
headers say.

#### Functional form

From `CppCore/rgpot/ZBL/ZBLPot.cc`, for a pair of atomic numbers `Zi` and `Zj`
(read from the atomic numbers of the call) and every pair with `r` up to
`cut_global`:

- the screening length is
  `a_ij = 0.46850 / (Zi^0.23 + Zj^0.23)` Angstrom and `x = r / a_ij`;
- the unswitched energy is
  `Zi Zj e2 / r * (0.18175 exp(-3.19980 x) + 0.50986 exp(-0.94229 x)`
  `+ 0.28022 exp(-0.40290 x) + 0.02817 exp(-0.20162 x))`, with `e2 = 14.399645`
  eV Angstrom;
- the pair energy adds a constant `sw5` everywhere, and above
  `cut_inner` the cubic and quartic terms `t^3 (sw3 + sw4 t)` with `t = r - cut_inner`;
- with `tc = cut_global - cut_inner` and `fc`, `fcp`, `fcpp` the unswitched
  energy and its first and second derivatives at `cut_global`:
  `swa = (-3 fcp + tc fcpp) / tc^2`, `swb = (2 fcp - tc fcpp) / tc^3`,
  `sw3 = swa / 3`, `sw4 = swb / 4` and
  `sw5 = -fc + (tc / 2) fcp - (tc^2 / 12) fcpp`.
  Energy and force are then both zero at `cut_global`;
- pairs beyond `cut_global` contribute nothing.

Boundaries are free: no minimum image is applied and `caps().periodic` is false.
The call writes the stress when the cell volume is positive.
The source comments that its screening exponents are those carried by the LAMMPS
source and differ from the published values in the last digits.

#### Parameters

| Parameter        | Value                | Unit        | Where it is set  |
|------------------|----------------------|-------------|------------------|
| `cut_inner`      | 2.0                  | Angstrom    | `ZBLConfig`      |
| `cut_global`     | 2.5                  | Angstrom    | `ZBLConfig`      |
| weight 1 (`c=)   | 0.18175              | none        | =kC4`            |
| weight 2         | 0.50986              | none        | `kC3`            |
| weight 3         | 0.28022              | none        | `kC2`            |
| weight 4         | 0.02817              | none        | `kC1`            |
| exponent 1 (`d=) | 3.19980              | none        | =kD1`            |
| exponent 2       | 0.94229              | none        | `kD2`            |
| exponent 3       | 0.40290              | none        | `kD3`            |
| exponent 4       | 0.20162              | none        | `kD4`            |
| power of `Z=     | 0.23                 | none        | =kPZBL`          |
| length prefactor | 0.46850              | Angstrom    | `kA0`            |
| `e2`             | 14.399645            | eV Angstrom | `kQQR2E`         |

The cutoffs are the defaults of `ZBLConfig` in `CppCore/rgpot/ZBL/ZBLPot.hpp`,
matching eOn's `[ZBLPot]` options (the comment in the header).
The constants are those of `ZBLPot.cc`, where the comments name them the
universal screening function coefficients (`pair_zbl_const.h` of LAMMPS) and the
LAMMPS metal-unit Coulomb conversion.
The four `c` weights sum to 1.
The book cited below was not consulted for this page, so the constants are given
as the source carries them.

#### Example

The program evaluates homonuclear dimers of H, Si and Pt at four separations,
two of them inside the switching region.
It reads the atomic numbers to build the coefficients, so a different `Z` needs
no setup.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/ZBL/ZBLPot.hpp"

int main() {
  rgpot::ZBLPot pot;
  const rgpot::ZBLConfig &cfg = pot.config();
  std::printf("cut_inner %.1f A, cut_global %.1f A\n", cfg.cut_inner,
              cfg.cut_global);

  const double box[9] = {40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 40.0};
  const int zs[3] = {1, 14, 78};
  const double rs[4] = {0.5, 1.0, 2.2, 2.49};
  std::printf("  Z-Z   r (A)   energy (eV)  force on atom 1 (eV/A)\n");
  for (const int zz : zs) {
    const int z[2] = {zz, zz};
    for (const double r : rs) {
      const double pos[6] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, r, 0.0, 0.0};
      double forces[6] = {};
      rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
      rgpot::ForceOut out{};
      out.F = forces;
      pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
      std::printf("%3d-%-3d %5.2f %14.6f %20.6f\n", zz, zz, r, out.energy,
                  forces[3]);
    }
  }
  return 0;
}
```

```
cut_inner 2.0 A, cut_global 2.5 A
  Z-Z   r (A)   energy (eV)  force on atom 1 (eV/A)
  1-1    0.50       5.851709            26.135385
  1-1    1.00       0.964123             2.944889
  1-1    2.20       0.010804             0.097809
  1-1    2.49       0.000001             0.000153
 14-14   0.50     469.268591          2615.591909
 14-14   1.00      49.749855           189.796219
 14-14   2.20       0.298981             2.761733
 14-14   2.49       0.000014             0.004082
 78-78   0.50    6614.171853         43013.531125
 78-78   1.00     458.722043          2089.530609
 78-78   2.20       1.707216            15.985966

```

An independent evaluation of the formula above in double precision gives
49.749855 eV for Si-Si at 1.0 Angstrom, 0.298981 eV at 2.2 Angstrom and
6614.171853 eV for Pt-Pt at 0.5 Angstrom, matching the rows printed here.
At 2.49 Angstrom, 0.01 Angstrom inside the cutoff, the energy is at most 7.6e-5
eV in the rows above.

  No Goswami paper read for this page uses the kernel by name.

### `SuttonChen` Sutton-Chen many-body potential

#### What it is and how to reach it

`SuttonChen` is the Sutton-Chen embedded-atom style potential: a repulsive pair
term and a square-root embedding of a pair density, with exponents 10 and 8 and
reduced units by default, plus the platinum and gold rows in eV and Angstrom.
Use it for fcc transition metal clusters and crystals.
In C++ it is `rgpot::SuttonChenPot`, built from `rgpot::SuttonChenConfig`
(header
`CppCore/rgpot/SuttonChen/SuttonChenPot.hpp`); the presets are `rgpot::sutton_chen_platinum()` and `rgpot::sutton_chen_gold()` (`CppCore/rgpot/SuttonChen/SuttonChenScales.hpp`).
There is also a C entry point, `rgpot_sutton_chen_energy_forces`.
Python has no class for it and `potserv` has no type for it.
`pair_coeff * * SuttonChen`, the PLUMED action and `rgpot-eval SuttonChen` take
`preset` (`platinum` or `gold`), `epsilon`, `c=, =a`, `n=, =m` and `cutoff`, and
build it periodic with the stress on.
The convention, the stress, the thread rules and the checks are in the
[Sutton-Chen reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/sutton_chen.html) and are not
repeated here.
A crystal run is in [the stress how-to](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/sutton-chen-stress.html), and the
LAMMPS route is in [LAMMPS](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-lammps.html).

#### Functional form

From the header of `CppCore/rgpot/SuttonChen/SuttonChenPot.cc` and the kernel:

- `E = epsilon * [ S_pair - c * sum_i sqrt(rho_i) ]` with `S_pair = sum over pairs i < j of (a / r_ij)^n`,
  so each unordered pair contributes `epsilon (a / r)^n` once;
- `rho_i = sum over j other than i of (a / r_ij)^m` (no factor 1/2);
- only pairs with
  `r_ij` up to `cutoff` enter, in the density and the pair term, with no energy shift; an atom with `rho_i`
  not above 0 has no embedding term;
- the force on atom `i= along =d = r_i - r_j` is `fscale * d` with
  `fscale = -(dE/dr) / r`, including the embedding weight
  `epsilon c / (2 sqrt(rho))` of both atoms;
- `epsilon` sets the energy unit and `a` the length unit, so a reduced result is
  rescaled by multiplying the energy by `epsilon` and the coordinates by `a`.

Periodic evaluation uses the minimum image and throws `std::invalid_argument`
for a cutoff that is not positive; otherwise no cell folding happens.

#### Parameters

| Parameter  | Default |    Pt row |    Au row | Unit             |
|------------|---------|-----------|-----------|------------------|
| `epsilon`  |     1.0 | 1.98330e-2 | 1.27930e-2 | eV (energy unit) |
| `a`        |     1.0 |      3.92 |      4.08 | Angstrom         |
| `c`        |  34.408 |    34.408 |    34.408 | none             |
| `n`        |      10 |        10 |        10 | none             |
| `m`        |       8 |         8 |         8 | none             |
| `cutoff`   |    40.0 |      40.0 |      40.0 | coordinate unit  |
| `periodic` |   false |     false |     false | none             |
| `stress`   |   false |     false |     false | none             |

The rows are the fields of `rgpot::SuttonChenConfig`, in that order.
`a` is the length unit and the cutoff is in the coordinate unit.

The defaults are in `CppCore/rgpot/SuttonChen/SuttonChenPot.hpp`.
The two rows are the functions `sutton_chen_platinum()` and `sutton_chen_gold()`
in `CppCore/rgpot/SuttonChen/SuttonChenScales.cc`, which set `c=, =n` and `m` to
the table values and take only `epsilon` and `a` from the row.
The
`pair_coeff` and `rgpot-eval` route sets `periodic` and `stress` true (`engines/pot_spec.cpp`).

The numbers agree with the literature.
Table I of Çağın, Dereli, Uludoğan and Tomak (arXiv:cond-mat/9709114) lists, as
`a=, =D` (in units of 1e-2 eV), `c=, =m`, `n`: Pt 3.92, 1.98330, 34.408, 8, 10
and Au 4.08, 1.27930, 34.408, 8, 10.
Doye and Wales write that for Au and Pt `n= is 10, =m` is 8 and `c` is 34.408,
that their tables are in reduced units with `epsilon` and `a` equal to 1, and
that the energy is rescaled by `epsilon` and the coordinates by `a`.
The first line of the deposited point file read by the example below carries the
same five numbers.
The header of `SuttonChenPot.hpp` also records that the cutoff 40 matches the
cutoff of the optbench globalopt Lennard-Jones problems, a convention of the
code and not a paper value.

#### Example

The program reads the deposited 38-atom Oh cluster from
`CppCore/tests/data/sc108/pt38`, evaluates it in reduced units, then scales it
to the platinum row, and prints the bulk scales of that row.
Run it from the repository root, since the file name is relative.

```cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <fstream>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/SuttonChen/SuttonChenPot.hpp"
#include "rgpot/SuttonChen/SuttonChenScales.hpp"

int main() {
  std::ifstream file("CppCore/tests/data/sc108/pt38");
  double header[5];
  for (double &h : header) {
    file >> h;
  }
  std::vector<double> pos;
  for (double x; file >> x;) {
    pos.push_back(x);
  }
  const std::size_t n = pos.size() / 3;
  const std::vector<int> z(n, 78);
  const double box[9] = {80.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 80.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 80.0};
  std::vector<double> forces(pos.size());

  rgpot::SuttonChenPot reduced;
  rgpot::ForceInput in{n, pos.data(), z.data(), box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces.data();
  reduced.forceImpl(in, &out);
  std::printf("file header: %g %g %g %g %g\n", header[0], header[1],
              header[2], header[3], header[4]);
  std::printf("Pt%zu, reduced 10-8: %.4f epsilon\n", n, out.energy);

  const rgpot::SuttonChenConfig pt = rgpot::sutton_chen_platinum();
  for (double &x : pos) {
    x *= pt.a;
  }
  rgpot::SuttonChenPot physical(pt);
  rgpot::ForceInput in_pt{n, pos.data(), z.data(), box};
  physical.forceImpl(in_pt, &out);
  std::printf("Pt%zu, platinum row: %.4f eV (epsilon %.5e eV, a %.2f A)\n", n,
              out.energy, pt.epsilon, pt.a);

  const rgpot::SuttonChenScales s = rgpot::sutton_chen_scales(pt);
  std::printf("bulk nearest neighbour %.4f A, well depth %.4f eV\n",
              s.nearest_neighbor, s.well_depth);
  return 0;
}
```

```
file header: 1 34.408 1 10 8
Pt38, reduced 10-8: -10117.2454 epsilon
Pt38, platinum row: -200.6553 eV (epsilon 1.98330e-02 eV, a 3.92 A)
bulk nearest neighbour 2.7719 A, well depth 5.8599 eV
```

The reduced energy is the -10117.2454 that Doye and Wales tabulate for the
38-atom Oh cluster of the 10-8 potential.
The platinum energy is that value times `epsilon` 1.98330e-2 eV.
The nearest-neighbour distance is `a / sqrt(2)` at the static fcc minimum, and
the well depth is minus the energy per atom there.

#### Literature

- Goswami papers: none of those read for this page uses this potential, so none
  is listed.
- Sutton and Chen, Philos.
  Mag.
  Lett. 61, 139-146 (1990), doi:10.1080/09500839008206493, the functional form.
- Çağın, Dereli, Uludoğan and Tomak,
  arXiv:cond-mat/9709114 (1997), doi:10.48550/arXiv.cond-mat/9709114, whose
  Table I gives the platinum and gold rows.
- Doye and Wales, New J. Chem. 22, 733-744 (1998), doi:10.1039/a709249k, the
  10-8 cluster minima and the reduced-unit convention, source of the Pt38 energy
  checked above.

### `Lammps` Shifted Lennard-Jones through the engine plugin

#### What it is and how to reach it

`Lammps` is the shifted 12-6 Lennard-Jones potential evaluated by a dynamically
loaded engine plugin, the route a LAMMPS-side or other external host uses.
Use it to exercise the engine ABI with a known, cheap potential and to compare a
host with the in-tree kernel.
In C++ it is `rgpot::LammpsPot`, made by `rgpot::rgpot_lammps_potential` from an
`rgpot::ExternalLjConfig` (header `CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp`).
In Python it is `rgpot.rgpot_lammps_potential(u0, cutoff, psi, engine_path)`
returning `rgpot.LammpsPot`.
The C ABI is `rgpot_lammps_potential` in
`CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/external_potentials.h`.
It has no `pair_coeff`, `rgpot-eval` or `potserv` name.
Inside LAMMPS, `pair_coeff * * u0 psi` under `pair_style rgpot` is the shifted
Lennard-Jones `LJ` kernel; see [LAMMPS](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-lammps.html).
The ABI is in [External ABI](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/external_abi.html).

#### Functional form

The constructor opens an engine library and keeps it as the backend.
The library is searched in this order, from
`lammps_paths` in `CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.cc`: `engine_path`
alone when it is set; otherwise `RGPOT_LAMMPS_ENGINE`,
`LAMMPS_ENGINE`, `liblammps_engine.so` and `liblj_engine.so` (with the
platform's suffix).
The in-tree `liblj_engine.so` (`engines/lj_engine.cpp`) passes the three
parameters to `rgpot_lj_eval`
(`engines/lj_eval.cpp`), which builds an `LJ` kernel with `switch_width` 0.
So the energy is that of `LJ` with the shift: for every pair with `r` up to the
cutoff, `4 u0 [(psi/r)^12 - (psi/r)^6]` minus the same at the cutoff, with the
minimum image in every direction.
The positions, cell, energy and forces cross the plugin boundary in Angstrom and
eV.
A call writes no stress (`has_stress` is 0), the potential reports
`caps().periodic` true, and every call is serialised by a mutex.

#### Parameters

| Parameter     | Value | Unit     | Where it is set                  |
|---------------|-------|----------|----------------------------------|
| `u0`          |   1.0 | eV       | `ExternalLjConfig::u0`           |
| `cutoff`      |   8.0 | Angstrom | `ExternalLjConfig::cutoff`       |
| `psi`         |   1.0 | Angstrom | `ExternalLjConfig::psi`          |
| `engine_path` | empty | none     | `ExternalLjConfig::engine_path`  |

The values are the defaults in
`CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp` and the Python stub `python/rgpot/_core.pyi`.
The constructor throws
`std::invalid_argument` unless `u0`, `cutoff` and `psi` are positive and finite, and `std::runtime_error`
when no engine library opens.
The defaults are a convention of the code and no paper supplies them.

#### Example

The program builds the potential with an empty engine path, so the search above
finds `liblj_engine.so`, and evaluates an argon-like dimer at the minimum.
It needs that library to be built and findable, which meson does by default for
the tests and the how-to pages.
The energy equals the shifted column of the `LJ` example at 3.8164 Angstrom
(-0.010230 eV) to the precision of the 3.816 Angstrom separation used here.

```cpp
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp"

int main() {
  rgpot::ExternalLjConfig cfg;
  cfg.u0 = 0.0104;
  cfg.cutoff = 8.5;
  cfg.psi = 3.40;
  auto pot = rgpot::rgpot_lammps_potential(cfg);

  const int z[2] = {18, 18};
  const double pos[6] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 3.816, 0.0, 0.0};
  const double box[9] = {40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 40.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 40.0};
  double forces[6] = {};
  rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces;
  pot->forceImpl(in, &out);
  std::printf("energy %.8f eV\n", out.energy);
  return 0;
}
```

```
energy -0.01023030 eV
```

To run a real LAMMPS engine, set `RGPOT_LAMMPS_ENGINE` or
`engine_path` to a library that exports `rgpot_engine_create`, `rgpot_engine_destroy` and `rgpot_engine_force` (`CppCore/rgpot/engine_c_abi.h`).
Building the `pair_style rgpot` plugin needs a LAMMPS source tree; see
[LAMMPS](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-lammps.html) and
[Engine plugins](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-plugins.html).

#### Literature

- Goswami papers: none of those read for this page uses this wrapper, so none is
  listed.
- J. E. Jones, Proc.
  R. Soc.
  A 106, 463-477 (1924), doi:10.1098/rspa.1924.0082, the 12-6 form.
- Thompson and coauthors, Comput.
  Phys.
  Commun. 271, 108171 (2022), doi:10.1016/j.cpc.2021.108171, LAMMPS, the host of
  `pair_style rgpot`.
- The parameters `u0` 1, `cutoff` 8 and `psi` 1 have no paper: they are a
  convention of the code.

### `Gromacs` Shifted Lennard-Jones in nanometres and kJ/mol

#### What it is and how to reach it

`Gromacs` is the same shifted Lennard-Jones potential, with the parameters
stored once in GROMACS units.
Use it to check a GROMACS-side evaluation in nanometres and
kJ/mol against the eV and Angstrom kernel. In C++ it is `rgpot::GromacsPot`, made by `rgpot::rgpot_gromacs_potential` from an `rgpot::ExternalLjConfig` (header `CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp`).
In Python it is
`rgpot.rgpot_gromacs_potential(u0, cutoff, psi, engine_path)` returning `rgpot.GromacsPot`, which also has `native_u0`,
`native_cutoff` and `native_psi`. The C ABI is `rgpot_gromacs_potential` in
`CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/external_potentials.h`. It has no `pair_coeff`, `rgpot-eval` or `potserv` name. The constructor, the units and the test with GROMACS itself are in [GROMACS](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-gromacs.html); the drop-in library is in [[file:../reference/gromacs_dropin.org][the
GROMACS drop-in reference]].

#### Functional form

The constructor multiplies `u0` by `rgpot_md_kj_per_ev()` (96.48533212331
kJ/mol per eV) and the two lengths by 0.1 nm per Angstrom (`CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/md_units.hpp`). With an empty `engine_path`
the call runs an `LJ` kernel with
`switch_width` 0 in Angstrom and eV, so the energy is the shifted `4 u0 [(psi/r)^12 - (psi/r)^6]` minus its value at the cutoff, with the minimum image, and the call writes the stress. With an `engine_path`
the library must export `rgpot_engine_create`, `rgpot_engine_destroy` and
`rgpot_md_native_force`; every call converts positions and cell to nanometres, passes them on, and converts the energy and forces back to eV and eV/Angstrom, and the stress is not written. The in-tree `engines/native_lj_engine.cpp`
is such a library.

#### Parameters

| Parameter     | Value | Unit     | Where it is set                  |
|---------------|-------|----------|----------------------------------|
| `u0`          |   1.0 | eV       | `ExternalLjConfig::u0`           |
| `cutoff`      |   8.0 | Angstrom | `ExternalLjConfig::cutoff`       |
| `psi`         |   1.0 | Angstrom | `ExternalLjConfig::psi`          |
| `engine_path` | empty | none     | `ExternalLjConfig::engine_path`  |

The stored forms are `nativeU0()` in kJ/mol, `nativeCutoff()` and `nativePsi()`
in nanometres.
The values are the defaults in `CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp`.
They are a convention of the code and no paper supplies them.

#### Example

The program stores the defaults in GROMACS units and evaluates a dimer at 1.5
Angstrom in process.
The energy is the value that `engine-gromacs.org` quotes for these parameters.

```cpp
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp"

int main() {
  rgpot::ExternalLjConfig cfg;
  cfg.u0 = 1.0;
  cfg.cutoff = 8.0;
  cfg.psi = 1.0;
  auto pot = rgpot::rgpot_gromacs_potential(cfg);
  std::printf("stored: %.11f kJ/mol, %.1f nm, %.1f nm\n", pot->nativeU0(),
              pot->nativeCutoff(), pot->nativePsi());

  const int z[2] = {1, 1};
  const double pos[6] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.5, 0.0, 0.0};
  const double box[9] = {20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0};
  double forces[6] = {};
  rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces;
  pot->forceImpl(in, &out);
  std::printf("energy %.10f eV, force on atom 1 %.10f eV/A\n", out.energy,
              forces[3]);
  std::printf("has_stress %d\n", out.has_stress);
  return 0;
}
```

```
stored: 96.48533212331 kJ/mol, 0.8 nm, 0.1 nm
energy -0.3203213355 eV, force on atom 1 -1.1580288310 eV/A
has_stress 1
```

Running GROMACS itself needs `gmx` and the PLUMED module, which are not required
for this program; the zero-step and Sutton-Chen runs are in
[GROMACS](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-gromacs.html).

#### Literature

- Goswami papers: none of those read for this page uses this wrapper, so none is
  listed.
- J. E. Jones, Proc.
  R. Soc.
  A 106, 463-477 (1924), doi:10.1098/rspa.1924.0082, the 12-6 form.
- Abraham and coauthors, SoftwareX 1-2, 19-25 (2015),
  doi:10.1016/j.softx.2015.06.001, GROMACS, whose units the factors follow.
- The parameters `u0` 1, `cutoff` 8 and `psi` 1 have no paper: they are a
  convention of the code.

### `OpenMM` Shifted Lennard-Jones through an OpenMM engine

#### What it is and how to reach it

`OpenMM` is the same shifted Lennard-Jones potential with the parameters stored
once in nanometres and kJ/mol, and an optional engine library that evaluates it
as an OpenMM `CustomNonbondedForce`.
Use it to compare an OpenMM context with the eV and Angstrom kernel.
In C++ it is `rgpot::OpenMMPot`, made by `rgpot::rgpot_openmm_potential` from an
`rgpot::ExternalLjConfig` (header `CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp`).
In Python it is
`rgpot.rgpot_openmm_potential(u0, cutoff, psi, engine_path)` returning `rgpot.OpenMMPot`, which also has `native_u0`,
`native_cutoff` and `native_psi`.
The C ABI is `rgpot_openmm_potential` in
`CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/external_potentials.h`.
It has no `pair_coeff`, `rgpot-eval` or `potserv` name.
The constructor, the engine library and its test are in
[OpenMM](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-openmm.html).

#### Functional form

The conversions and the in-process path are those of `Gromacs`: `u0` times
96.48533212331
kJ/mol per eV, lengths times 0.1 nm per Angstrom, and an empty `engine_path` runs the `LJ` kernel in Angstrom and eV with `switch_width` 0. With an `engine_path` the library has to export `rgpot_engine_create`, `rgpot_engine_destroy` and `rgpot_md_native_force`. The in-tree `engines/openmm/openmm_engine.cpp` builds a `CustomNonbondedForce` with the expression `4*sqrt(eps1*eps2)*((sqrt(sig1*sig2)/r)^12-(sqrt(sig1*sig2)/r)^6)` minus the same expression at `r = rc`, per-particle `eps` equal to `u0` in kJ/mol
and `sig` equal to `psi` in nanometres, a global `rc` equal to the cutoff in
nanometres, the `CutoffPeriodic` method and the CPU platform.
With equal parameters on every atom the geometric combination reduces to `u0`
and `psi`.

#### Parameters

| Parameter     | Value | Unit     | Where it is set                  |
|---------------|-------|----------|----------------------------------|
| `u0`          |   1.0 | eV       | `ExternalLjConfig::u0`           |
| `cutoff`      |   8.0 | Angstrom | `ExternalLjConfig::cutoff`       |
| `psi`         |   1.0 | Angstrom | `ExternalLjConfig::psi`          |
| `engine_path` | empty | none     | `ExternalLjConfig::engine_path`  |

The stored forms are `nativeU0()` in kJ/mol, `nativeCutoff()` and `nativePsi()`
in nanometres.
The values are the defaults in `CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp`.
They are a convention of the code and no paper supplies them.

#### Example

The first program is a trimer in a 14 Angstrom cell, where the third atom
reaches the first through the periodic boundary at 3.5 Angstrom.
It evaluates the potential in process and the `LJ` kernel with the same
parameters and prints both.
OpenMM itself is not involved, so it runs anywhere.

```cpp
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp"
#include "rgpot/LennardJones/LJPot.hpp"

int main() {
  rgpot::ExternalLjConfig cfg;
  cfg.u0 = 0.0104;
  cfg.cutoff = 8.5;
  cfg.psi = 3.40;
  auto omm = rgpot::rgpot_openmm_potential(cfg);
  rgpot::LJPot host({.u0 = cfg.u0, .cutoff = cfg.cutoff, .psi = cfg.psi});
  std::printf("stored: %.6f kJ/mol, %.2f nm, %.2f nm\n", omm->nativeU0(),
              omm->nativeCutoff(), omm->nativePsi());

  const int z[3] = {18, 18, 18};
  const double pos[9] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 3.8, 0.0, 0.0, 10.5, 0.0, 0.0};
  const double box[9] = {14.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 14.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 14.0};
  double f_omm[9] = {};
  double f_host[9] = {};
  rgpot::ForceInput in{3, pos, z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out_omm{};
  rgpot::ForceOut out_host{};
  out_omm.F = f_omm;
  out_host.F = f_host;
  omm->forceImpl(in, &out_omm);
  host.forceImpl(in, &out_host);
  std::printf("OpenMMPot energy %.10f eV, LJPot energy %.10f eV\n",
              out_omm.energy, out_host.energy);
  std::printf("force on atom 0, x: %.10f and %.10f eV/A\n", f_omm[0],
              f_host[0]);
  return 0;
}
```

```
stored: 1.003447 kJ/mol, 0.85 nm, 0.34 nm
OpenMMPot energy -0.0161629635 eV, LJPot energy -0.0161629635 eV
force on atom 0, x: 0.0399147328 and 0.0399147328 eV/A
```

The second program passes an engine path, so the evaluation goes through OpenMM.
This machine has no OpenMM, so it is only compiled.
Running it needs the `openmm` Python package or libraries, a build with
`-Dwith_openmm=enabled` that produces `libopenmm_engine.so`, and the library on
the path given (or in `RGPOT_OPENMM_ENGINE` for the meson test).

```cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <exception>

#include "rgpot/ExternalPot/ExternalPot.hpp"

int main() {
  rgpot::ExternalLjConfig cfg;
  cfg.u0 = 1.0;
  cfg.cutoff = 8.0;
  cfg.psi = 1.0;
  cfg.engine_path = "libopenmm_engine.so";
  try {
    auto pot = rgpot::rgpot_openmm_potential(cfg);
    const int z[2] = {1, 1};
    const double pos[6] = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.5, 0.0, 0.0};
    const double box[9] = {20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0};
    double forces[6] = {};
    rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
    rgpot::ForceOut out{};
    out.F = forces;
    pot->forceImpl(in, &out);
    std::printf("%.10f eV\n", out.energy);
  } catch (const std::exception &error) {
    std::fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", error.what());
    return 1;
  }
  return 0;
}
```

For these parameters `engine-openmm.org` quotes -0.3203213355 eV from
`rgpot-lj`, the value the engine has to reproduce.
