# Metal and embedded-atom potentials

Source: docs/orgmode/howto/potentials-metals.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/potentials-metals.html

Seven `PotType` enumerators evaluate metals with an embedded-atom or an
effective-medium energy: `CuH2`, `EAMAl`, `FeHe`, `EMT`, `EAMCell` and
`EAMTable`, plus the first- and second-neighbour modified embedded-atom method
`MEAM`.
Each section below says how to reach the potential, gives its functional form as
the kernel evaluates it, lists the parameters with where they are set, runs a
program, and cites the literature.
The names a host accepts (`rgpot-eval`,
`pair_coeff`, the PLUMED `POTENTIAL` keyword) are in [[file:../reference/potential_names.org][Potential
names]].
The class contracts are in
[C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html) and the Python classes
in [Python API](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/python_api.html).

Lengths are Angstrom, energies are eV and forces are eV/Angstrom.
All six read the cell as periodic in every direction.
None of the kernels writes a stress except `EAMTable`, and only when asked.

| Name       | C++ class                      | Python           |
|------------|--------------------------------|------------------|
| `CuH2`     | `rgpot::fortranpots::CuH2Pot`  | `rgpot.CuH2Pot`  |
| `EAMAl`    | `rgpot::fortranpots::EAMAlPot` | `rgpot.EAMAlPot` |
| `FeHe`     | `rgpot::fortranpots::FeHePot`  | `rgpot.FeHePot`  |
| `EMT`      | `rgpot::EMTPot`                | none             |
| `EAMCell`  | `rgpot::EAMPot`                | none             |
| `EAMTable` | `rgpot::EAMTablePot`           | none             |
| `MEAM`     | `rgpot::MEAMPot`               | none             |

`CuH2`, `EAMAl` and `FeHe` need a build with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`, and
`EAMTable` needs `-Dwith_eam_table=true`.
`EMT` and `EAMCell` are always built.
`MEAM` reads LAMMPS MEAM library and parameter files.

Every example evaluates the energy of a small geometry and prints it next to the
same energy computed by hand from the formulas in the section, using the
parameters in its table.
The two numbers agree, which is the check that the text states the kernel's
form.
The dimers sit in a cubic box of 20 Angstrom, so only the pair itself interacts.
Where an example prints a force, it prints a central difference of the energy
with step 1e-5 Angstrom beside it.

Three of the kernels share one form family.
The embedded-atom energy is

```
E = sum_{i<j} phi(r_ij) + sum_i F(rho_i)
rho_i = sum_{j /= i} rho(r_ij)
```

and `CuH2`, `EAMAl` and `EAMCell` take for `phi` a Morse function written as two
exponentials.
For `rho` they take the shape `r^6 (e^(-beta r) + 512 e^(-2 beta r))`.
That is the form of Voter and Chen, who also point out that `F -> F + g rho`
with `phi -> phi - 2 g rho` leaves the energy unchanged, and that scaling `rho`
by a constant while rescaling `F` does too.
The Fortran kernels evaluate it in gather form (see
[Fortran kernels](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/fortran-kernels.html)): densities first,
then `F= and =F'` for every atom, then the force.

### `CuH2` copper and hydrogen

#### What it is and how to reach it

An embedded-atom potential for copper (atomic number 29) and hydrogen (atomic
number 1) in any order, with a cutoff of 6.1 Angstrom.
It is the eOn `CuH2` potential.

- C++: `rgpot::fortranpots::CuH2Pot` in `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp`.
- Python: `rgpot.CuH2Pot`.
  It has an analytic Hessian-vector product.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `CuH2` (a build with the Fortran potentials), as in `pair_coeff * * CuH2 Cu H`.
- `potserv`: type `CuH2`, as in `potserv 12345 CuH2`.
- Reference: [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html),
  [Fortran potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/fortran_potentials.html) and
  [Python API](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/python_api.html).

Any other atomic number, or two atoms at the same position, is an error.

#### Functional form

The kernel is `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_cuh2.f90`.
The species of the two atoms of a pair pick the pair function, and the species
of a neighbour picks the density it gives.

- Pair term, once per pair with `r < rcut`, for the pairs `cucu`, `hcu` and
  `hh`: `da * e^(-alpha_a r) + db * e^(-alpha_b r) - phicut`, in eV.
- Density an atom of species `s= gives at distance =r`:
  `rho_s(r) = scale_s * r^neta_s * g_s(r) - rhocut_s` with `g_s(r) = e^(-beta_a_s r) + gamma_s * e^(-beta_b_s r)`.
  For copper `neta` is 6 and `gamma` is 512.
  For hydrogen `neta` and `gamma` are 0, so the density is
  `scale_h * e^(-beta_a_h r)`.
- Embedding energy:
  `F_cu(rho) = sum_{k=1..8} f_cu(k) rho^k` and `F_h(rho) = sum_{k=1..5} f_h(k) rho^k`,
  in eV.
  There is no constant term, so an isolated atom has no embedding energy.
- Total: `E = sum_{i<j} phi(r_ij) + sum_i F_{Z_i}(rho_i)`, with
  `rho_i` the sum over neighbours `j= of the density of the species of =j` at `r_ij`.
- Shifts: `phicut` and `rhocut` are the pair energy and the density at `rcut`
  before the shift.
  Subtracting them makes both vanish at the cutoff, and a pair at `r >` rcut= is
  skipped.
  The slopes do not vanish there.

#### Parameters

The values are the defaults of `cuh2_params_t` in
`CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_cuh2.f90`.
A caller of `CuH2Pot` has no way to change them.
Pair energies are in eV and decay rates in 1/Angstrom.

| Component      | Value    | Meaning                       |
|----------------|----------|-------------------------------|
| `da_cucu`      | 2862.3   | Cu-Cu pair amplitude (eV)     |
| `alpha_a_cucu` | 3.51236  | Cu-Cu pair decay (1/Angstrom) |
| `db_cucu`      | -109.107 | Cu-Cu pair amplitude (eV)     |
| `alpha_b_cucu` | 1.75618  | Cu-Cu pair decay (1/Angstrom) |
| `da_hcu`       | 86.1495  | H-Cu pair amplitude (eV)      |
| `alpha_a_hcu`  | 4.21154  | H-Cu pair decay (1/Angstrom)  |
| `db_hcu`       | 15355.5  | H-Cu pair amplitude (eV)      |
| `alpha_b_hcu`  | 6.07604  | H-Cu pair decay (1/Angstrom)  |
| `da_hh`        | 79.5013  | H-H pair amplitude (eV)       |
| `alpha_a_hh`   | 2.47961  | H-H pair decay (1/Angstrom)   |
| `db_hh`        | -107.555 | H-H pair amplitude (eV)       |
| `alpha_b_hh`   | 2.99918  | H-H pair decay (1/Angstrom)   |
| `scale_cu`     | 0.273072 | Cu density prefactor          |
| `beta_a_cu`    | 3.69051  | Cu density decay (1/Angstrom) |
| `beta_b_cu`    | 7.38101  | Cu density decay (1/Angstrom) |
| `gamma_cu`     | 512.0    | Cu density second-term weight |
| `neta_cu`      | 6        | Cu density power of r         |
| `scale_h`      | 2.14389  | H density prefactor           |
| `beta_a_h`     | 3.77701  | H density decay (1/Angstrom)  |
| `beta_b_h`     | 0.0      | H density second decay        |
| `gamma_h`      | 0.0      | H density second-term weight  |
| `neta_h`       | 0        | H density power of r          |
| `rcut`         | 6.1      | cutoff (Angstrom)             |

The embedding coefficients are `f_cu(1:8)` and `f_h(1:5)`, in eV per density to
the power `k`.

| k | `f_cu(k)`     | `f_h(k)` |
|---|---------------|----------|
| 1 | -112.945      | -81.7537 |
| 2 | 8510.04       | 838.668  |
| 3 | -261734.0     | -3952.35 |
| 4 | 4780090.0     | 8767.87  |
| 5 | -52341900.0   | -6599.37 |
| 6 | 339124000.0   |          |
| 7 | -1201500000.0 |          |
| 8 | 1796190000.0  |          |

The source names the kernel as eOn's `CuH2` and no paper for these numbers.

#### Example

This program needs a build with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.
It evaluates a copper dimer at 2.55 Angstrom and a copper-hydrogen dimer at 1.7
Angstrom.
For the copper dimer the embedding energy of each atom is `F_cu` at the shifted
density of its one neighbour.
For the copper-hydrogen pair the copper atom takes
`F_cu` at the shifted hydrogen density and the hydrogen atom takes `F_h` at the
shifted copper density.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp"

namespace {

const double rc = 6.1;

double phi_cucu(double r) {
  return 2862.3 * std::exp(-3.51236 * r) - 109.107 * std::exp(-1.75618 * r);
}
double phi_hcu(double r) {
  return 86.1495 * std::exp(-4.21154 * r) + 15355.5 * std::exp(-6.07604 * r);
}
double rho_cu(double r) {
  return 0.273072 * std::pow(r, 6) *
         (std::exp(-3.69051 * r) + 512.0 * std::exp(-7.38101 * r));
}
double rho_h(double r) { return 2.14389 * std::exp(-3.77701 * r); }

double embed_cu(double d) {
  const double c[8] = {-112.945,     8510.04,      -261734.0,    4780090.0,
                       -52341900.0, 339124000.0, -1201500000.0, 1796190000.0};
  double e = 0.0, p = d;
  for (double ck : c) {
    e += ck * p;
    p *= d;
  }
  return e;
}
double embed_h(double d) {
  const double c[5] = {-81.7537, 838.668, -3952.35, 8767.87, -6599.37};
  double e = 0.0, p = d;
  for (double ck : c) {
    e += ck * p;
    p *= d;
  }
  return e;
}

double energy(rgpot::fortranpots::CuH2Pot &pot, int z1, double r, double *fx) {
  const double pos[6] = {10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 + r, 10.0, 10.0};
  const int z[2] = {29, z1};
  const double box[9] = {20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0};
  double forces[6] = {};
  rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces;
  pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
  if (fx)
    *fx = forces[3];
  return out.energy;
}

double shifted(double (*f)(double), double r) { return f(r) - f(rc); }

} // namespace

int main() {
  rgpot::fortranpots::CuH2Pot pot;
  const double h = 1e-5;
  double fx = 0.0;

  // Cu-Cu dimer: one pair term and one embedding term per atom.
  const double r = 2.55;
  const double e = energy(pot, 29, r, &fx);
  const double by_hand = shifted(phi_cucu, r) +
                         2.0 * embed_cu(shifted(rho_cu, r));
  const double fd = -(energy(pot, 29, r + h, nullptr) -
                      energy(pot, 29, r - h, nullptr)) / (2 * h);
  std::printf("Cu-Cu at %.2f: kernel %.8f, by hand %.8f eV\n", r, e, by_hand);
  std::printf("force on atom 1, x: %.6f, central difference %.6f\n", fx, fd);

  // Cu-H dimer: the Cu atom sees the H density and the H atom the Cu density.
  const double s = 1.7;
  const double e_h = energy(pot, 1, s, &fx);
  const double by_hand_h = shifted(phi_hcu, s) +
                           embed_cu(shifted(rho_h, s)) +
                           embed_h(shifted(rho_cu, s));
  std::printf("Cu-H at %.2f: kernel %.8f, by hand %.8f eV\n", s, e_h,
              by_hand_h);
  return 0;
}
```

```
Cu-Cu at 2.55: kernel -1.73811469, by hand -1.73811469 eV
force on atom 1, x: -1.480595, central difference -1.480595
Cu-H at 1.70: kernel -1.28277140, by hand -1.28277140 eV
```

#### Literature

The source cites no paper for this potential.
The pair term as two exponentials and the `r^6` density with weight 512 are the
Morse and density forms of Voter and Chen; that paper treats nickel and
aluminium and has no hydrogen, and its numbers are not these.

- eOn, the software this kernel descends from: Goswami,
  TheochemUI/eOn: v3.6.0, Zenodo (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18529495.
- Voter and Chen, MRS Proceedings 82, 175 (1986), doi:10.1557/PROC-82-175.
- Daw and Baskes, Phys.
  Rev. B 29, 6443-6453 (1984), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.29.6443, for the
  embedded-atom energy.

### `EAMAl` double-exponential aluminium

#### What it is and how to reach it

An embedded-atom potential for aluminium with a cutoff of 7.1 Angstrom.
The kernel does not read the atomic numbers; every atom is aluminium.

- C++: `rgpot::fortranpots::EAMAlPot` in
  `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp`.
- Python: `rgpot.EAMAlPot`.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `EAMAl` (a build with the Fortran potentials), as in `pair_coeff * * EAMAl Al`.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html),
  [Fortran potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/fortran_potentials.html) and
  [Python API](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/python_api.html).

For the cell-list aluminium of the same family with a shorter cutoff, see
`EAMCell` below.

#### Functional form

The kernel is `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_eam_al.f90`.
With `s= for =density_scale`, `g= for =g_transform` and
`c_k` for `embed_coeff(k)`:

- Density: `rho(r) = s * (h(r) - h(rcut))` with
  `h(r) = r^6 * (e^(-beta_a r) + 512 e^(-beta_b r))`.
  Here `beta_a` and `beta_b` are `density_decay_a` and `density_decay_b`.
- Pair term, in eV: `phi(r) = p(r) - p(rcut) - 2 g rho(r)` with
  `p(r) = A e^(-a r) + B e^(-b r)`.
  Here `A=, =a`, `B= and =b` are `pair_amp_a`, `pair_decay_a`, `pair_amp_b` and
  `pair_decay_b`.
- Embedding: `F(rho) = g rho + sum_{k=1..8} c_k rho^k`, in eV.
- Total: `E = sum_{i<j} phi(r_ij) + sum_i F(rho_i)`.
- Cutoff: a pair with `r^2 > 0.9999 rcut^2`, that is `r > 7.09964` Angstrom,
  contributes nothing.
  The shifts make `phi` and `rho` vanish at `rcut`; the slopes do not, which is
  why the kernel drops the pair slightly inside the cutoff.
- The two exponentials of the pair term have decay rates in the ratio 2, so the
  pair term is a Morse function with `Dm = B^2 / (4 A)` = 4.0197 eV, `alpha = b`
  = 1.5103 1/Angstrom and `Rm = ln(-B / (2 Dm)) / alpha` = 2.1013 Angstrom,
  apart from the shift and the `g` term.
- The value of `g` does not change the energy: the sum of
  `g rho_i` over the atoms cancels the sum of `-2 g rho(r_ij)` over the pairs.
  `scripts/validation/eam_al.py` checks the density, pair, embedding and force
  expressions of the kernel symbolically.

#### Parameters

The values are the defaults of
`eam_al_params_t` in `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_eam_al.f90`.
A caller of `EAMAlPot` has no way to change them.
The source writes each as a default-real literal, so the kernel stores the
single-precision rounding of the digits shown.
The table gives the digits as written.

| Component          | Value             | Unit           |
|--------------------|-------------------|----------------|
| `g_transform`      | -0.60647886749203 | eV per density |
| `pair_amp_a`       | 2294.3609145535   | eV             |
| `pair_decay_a`     | 3.0205380362464   | 1/Angstrom     |
| `pair_amp_b`       | -192.06894637533  | eV             |
| `pair_decay_b`     | 1.5102690181232   | 1/Angstrom     |
| `density_scale`    | 0.87928364657088  | dimensionless  |
| `density_decay_a`  | 3.3068828537934   | 1/Angstrom     |
| `density_decay_b`  | 6.6137657075868   | 1/Angstrom     |
| `density_weight_b` | 512.0             | dimensionless  |
| `density_power`    | 6                 | power of r     |
| `rcut`             | 7.1               | Angstrom       |

| k | `embed_coeff(k)` |
|---|------------------|
| 1 | 4.4572157051836  |
| 2 | 193.21775368064  |
| 3 | -1173.6502684704 |
| 4 | 4203.3500116196  |
| 5 | -8785.1680280827 |
| 6 | 10632.994102532  |
| 7 | -6921.0410455328 |
| 8 | 1875.2698365752  |

The source names the numbers as the eOn aluminium parameters and no paper.

#### Example

This program needs a build with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.
It evaluates an aluminium dimer at 2.6 Angstrom.
The by-hand energy rounds every literal to single precision first, as the kernel
does.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp"

namespace {

// The kernel stores each literal of the eOn parameter file as a
// single-precision number, so the hand calculation does the same.
double f32(float x) { return static_cast<double>(x); }

const double g = f32(-0.60647886749203f);
const double pair_a = f32(2294.3609145535f), decay_a = f32(3.0205380362464f);
const double pair_b = f32(-192.06894637533f), decay_b = f32(1.5102690181232f);
const double scale = f32(0.87928364657088f);
const double beta_a = f32(3.3068828537934f), beta_b = f32(6.6137657075868f);
const double weight = f32(512.0f);
const double rcut = f32(7.1f);

double pair_shape(double r) {
  return pair_a * std::exp(-decay_a * r) + pair_b * std::exp(-decay_b * r);
}
double dens_shape(double r) {
  return std::pow(r, 6) *
         (std::exp(-beta_a * r) + weight * std::exp(-beta_b * r));
}
double rho(double r) { return scale * (dens_shape(r) - dens_shape(rcut)); }
double phi(double r) {
  return pair_shape(r) - pair_shape(rcut) - 2.0 * g * rho(r);
}
double embed(double d) {
  const double c[8] = {f32(4.4572157051836f),  f32(193.21775368064f),
                       f32(-1173.6502684704f), f32(4203.3500116196f),
                       f32(-8785.1680280827f), f32(10632.994102532f),
                       f32(-6921.0410455328f), f32(1875.2698365752f)};
  double e = g * d, p = d;
  for (double ck : c) {
    e += ck * p;
    p *= d;
  }
  return e;
}

double energy(rgpot::fortranpots::EAMAlPot &pot, double r, double *fx) {
  const double pos[6] = {10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 + r, 10.0, 10.0};
  const int z[2] = {13, 13};
  const double box[9] = {20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0};
  double forces[6] = {};
  rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces;
  pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
  if (fx)
    *fx = forces[3];
  return out.energy;
}

} // namespace

int main() {
  rgpot::fortranpots::EAMAlPot pot;
  const double r = 2.6, h = 1e-5;
  double fx = 0.0;
  const double e = energy(pot, r, &fx);
  const double by_hand = phi(r) + 2.0 * embed(rho(r));
  const double fd =
      -(energy(pot, r + h, nullptr) - energy(pot, r - h, nullptr)) / (2 * h);
  std::printf("kernel energy %.8f eV\n", e);
  std::printf("by hand       %.8f eV\n", by_hand);
  std::printf("force on atom 1, x: %.6f eV/Angstrom\n", fx);
  std::printf("central difference: %.6f eV/Angstrom\n", fd);
  return 0;
}
```

```
kernel energy -1.55821100 eV
by hand       -1.55821100 eV
force on atom 1, x: -0.563874 eV/Angstrom
central difference: -0.563874 eV/Angstrom
```

#### Literature

The source does not name a paper.
The functional form is that of Voter and Chen, including the Morse pair, the
`r^6` density with weight 512, and the two invariances of the energy that
`g_transform` and `density_scale` use.
Voter and Chen define `F` numerically from a universal binding curve, where this
kernel carries a polynomial.
Their Table II lists for aluminium `Dm` 3.7760 eV, `Rm` 2.1176 Angstrom, `alpha`
1.4859 1/Angstrom, `beta` 3.3232 1/Angstrom and `rcut` 5.5550 Angstrom.
The numbers of this kernel differ from those (see the Morse reading above and
`density_decay_a`), so the page does not call them that paper's fit.
No paper was found for the parameter set.

- eOn, the software this kernel descends from: Goswami,
  TheochemUI/eOn: v3.6.0, Zenodo (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18529495.
- Voter and Chen, MRS Proceedings 82, 175 (1986), doi:10.1557/PROC-82-175.
- Daw and Baskes, Phys.
  Rev. B 29, 6443-6453 (1984), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.29.6443, for the
  embedded-atom energy.

### `FeHe` iron and helium

#### What it is and how to reach it

An embedded-atom potential for iron (atomic number 26) and helium (atomic number 2)
with species-dependent pair terms and two embedding channels: a d-band density
fed by Fe-Fe pairs and embedded on iron, and an s-band density fed by Fe-He
pairs and embedded on both species.
Helium pairs feed neither density, so a pure helium configuration is the bare
He-He pair potential.
The neighbour table uses the largest of the five cutoffs, 5.4 Angstrom.

- C++: `rgpot::fortranpots::FeHePot` in `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp`.
- Python: `rgpot.FeHePot`.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `FeHe` (a build with the Fortran potentials), as in `pair_coeff * * FeHe Fe He`.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html),
  [Fortran potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/fortran_potentials.html) and
  [Python API](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/python_api.html).

Any other atomic number is an error.

#### Functional form

The kernel is `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_fehe.f90`.
Distances are in Angstrom and energies in eV.

- Total: `E = sum_{i<j} V_ab(r_ij) + sum_i (F_d(rho_d_i) + F_s(rho_s_i))`, where
  `F_d` acts on iron atoms only.
- Each pair term and each density is zero beyond its own cutoff.
  None of them is shifted.
- Fe-Fe pair, `r <` 5.3=: below 1.0 a screened Coulomb term
  `fe_zbl_scale / r * S(r)` with
  `S(r) = sum_{k=1..4} fe_zbl_weight(k) * e^(-fe_zbl_decay(k) r)`; from 1.0 to 2.05 the bridge `exp(c1 + c2 r + c3 r^2 + c4 r^3)` with `c1` to `c4` the `fe_bridge`
  entries; from 2.05 up the cubic knot sum
  `sum_k fe_pair_coeff(k) * max(fe_pair_knot(k) - r, 0)^3`.
- Fe-He pair, `r <` 3.9028=: a cubic knot sum with `fehe_knot` and `fehe_coeff`.
- He-He pair, `r <` 5.4=, in the reduced distance
  `x = r / he_rm`: `he_eps * (core(x) - D(x) * disp(x))` with
  `core(x) = he_aa * e^(-he_alpha x + he_beta x^2)` and `disp(x) = he_c6 / x^6 + he_c8 / x^8 + he_c10 / x^10`.
  The damping is `D(x) = e^(-(he_damp / x - 1)^2)` for `x < he_damp` and 1
  above.
- d-band density an iron neighbour gives, `r <` 4.2=: the cubic knot sum with
  `fe_rho_knot` and `fe_rho_coeff`.
- s-band density an unlike neighbour gives, `r <` 4.10=:
  `sband_amp * r^3 * e^(-2 sband_decay r)`.
- Embedding, for a density at or above 1e-35 and zero below:
  `F_d(rho) = -sqrt(rho) + fe_emb_quadratic * rho^2 + fe_emb_quartic * rho^4` and `F_s(rho) = a sqrt(rho) + b rho^2 + c rho^4`,
  with `a=, =b` and `c= the =sband_emb_sqrt`, `sband_emb_quadratic` and
  `sband_emb_quartic` entries.
  The s-band function is the same for both species.

#### Parameters

The values are the defaults of `fehe_params_t` in
`CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_fehe.f90`.
A caller of `FeHePot` has no way to change them.
The Fe-Fe and Fe-He knot positions and coefficients are the arrays
`fe_pair_knot`, `fe_pair_coeff`, `fe_rho_knot`, `fe_rho_coeff`,
`fehe_knot` and `fehe_coeff`; the example below carries every one of them,
copied from the source.

| Component             | Value                  | Meaning               |
|-----------------------|------------------------|-----------------------|
| `rcut_fe_pair`        | 5.3                    | Fe-Fe pair cutoff     |
| `rcut_fe_rho`         | 4.2                    | d-band density cutoff |
| `rcut_fehe_pair`      | 3.9028                 | Fe-He pair cutoff     |
| `rcut_fehe_rho`       | 4.10                   | s-band density cutoff |
| `rcut_he_pair`        | 5.4                    | He-He pair cutoff     |
| `fe_zbl_scale`        | 9.7342365892908e+03    | eV Angstrom           |
| `fe_zbl_weight(1:4)`  | 0.18180, 0.50990,      | dimensionless         |
|                       | 0.28020, 0.02817       |                       |
| `fe_zbl_decay(1)`     | 2.8616724320005e+01    | 1/Angstrom            |
| `fe_zbl_decay(2)`     | 8.4267310396064e+00    | 1/Angstrom            |
| `fe_zbl_decay(3)`     | 3.6030244464156e+00    | 1/Angstrom            |
| `fe_zbl_decay(4)`     | 1.8028536321603e+00    | 1/Angstrom            |
| `fe_bridge(1)`        | 7.4122709384068e+00    | dimensionless         |
| `fe_bridge(2)`        | -6.4180690713367e-01   | 1/Angstrom            |
| `fe_bridge(3)`        | -2.6043547961722e+00   | 1/Angstrom^2          |
| `fe_bridge(4)`        | 6.2625393931230e-01    | 1/Angstrom^3          |
| `fe_bridge_lo`        | 1.0000                 | Angstrom              |
| `fe_bridge_hi`        | 2.0500                 | Angstrom              |
| `fe_emb_quadratic`    | -6.7314115586063e-04   | d-band embedding      |
| `fe_emb_quartic`      | 7.6514905604792e-08    | d-band embedding      |
| `sband_amp`           | 20.0                   | s-band density        |
| `sband_decay`         | 1.5312426703208 / bohr | 1/Angstrom            |
| `sband_emb_sqrt`      | 0.220813420485         | s-band embedding      |
| `sband_emb_quadratic` | 1.367508764130         | s-band embedding      |
| `sband_emb_quartic`   | 3.382256025271         | s-band embedding      |
| `he_rm`               | 2.9683                 | Angstrom              |
| `he_c6`               | 1.35186623             | dimensionless         |
| `he_c8`               | 0.41495143             | dimensionless         |
| `he_c10`              | 0.17151143             | dimensionless         |
| `he_aa`               | 186924.404             | dimensionless         |
| `he_alpha`            | 10.5717543             | dimensionless         |
| `he_beta`             | -2.07758779            | dimensionless         |
| `he_damp`             | 1.438                  | reduced distance      |
| `he_eps`              | 10.956 k_B             | eV, 10.956 K          |

Here `bohr` is 0.529177210818181818 Angstrom, and `k_B` is converted with
1.380658e-23 J/K and 1.602177e-19 J/eV.
The knot arrays have 13 entries for the Fe-Fe pair, running from 2.2 to 5.3
Angstrom, 3 for the d-band density, and 8 for the Fe-He pair, running from
1.5440 to 3.9028 Angstrom.

#### Example

This program needs a build with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.
It evaluates three dimers, one for each pair of species, and compares each with
the formulas above.
The iron dimer at 2.5 Angstrom adds the d-band embedding energy of two atoms,
each at the density of one neighbour.
The iron-helium dimer at 2.0 Angstrom adds the s-band embedding energy of two
atoms, each at the s-band density of the pair.
The helium dimer at 3.2 Angstrom is the bare HFD-B pair.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp"

namespace {

// Sum of coeff[k] * (knot[k] - r)^3 over the knots beyond r.
double cubic_knots(const double *coeff, const double *knot, int n, double r) {
  double v = 0.0;
  for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k)
    if (knot[k] > r)
      v += coeff[k] * std::pow(knot[k] - r, 3);
  return v;
}

// Fe-Fe pair above 2.05 Angstrom and the d-band density, both cubic knots.
const double fe_knot[13] = {2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, 2.7, 2.8,
                            3.0, 3.3, 3.7, 4.2, 4.7, 5.3};
const double fe_coeff[13] = {
    -2.7444805994228e+01, 1.5738054058489e+01,  2.2077118733936e+00,
    -2.4989799053251e+00, 4.2099676494795e+00,  -7.7361294129713e-01,
    8.0656414937789e-01,  -2.3194358924605e+00, 2.6577406128280e+00,
    -1.0260416933564e+00, 3.5018615891957e-01,  -5.8531821042271e-02,
    -3.0458824556234e-03};
const double rho_knot[3] = {2.4, 3.2, 4.2};
const double rho_coeff[3] = {1.1686859407970e+01, -1.4710740098830e-02,
                             4.7193527075943e-01};

// Fe-He pair, cubic knots.
const double fehe_knot[8] = {1.5440, 1.6155, 1.6896, 1.8017,
                             2.0482, 2.3816, 3.5067, 3.9028};
const double fehe_coeff[8] = {559.804426025391, -45.916354995728,
                              35.550312671661,  164.319865173340,
                              -1.727464405060,  0.106771826237,
                              0.073715269849,   0.038235287677};

double dband_embed(double d) {
  return -std::sqrt(d) - 6.7314115586063e-04 * d * d +
         7.6514905604792e-08 * std::pow(d, 4);
}
double sband_embed(double d) {
  return 0.220813420485 * std::sqrt(d) + 1.367508764130 * d * d +
         3.382256025271 * std::pow(d, 4);
}
double sband_density(double r) {
  const double decay = 1.5312426703208 / 0.529177210818181818;
  return 20.0 * r * r * r * std::exp(-2.0 * decay * r);
}

// Helium dimer, HFD-B form in x = r / rm.
double he_he(double r) {
  const double eps = 10.956 * 1.380658e-23 / 1.602177e-19;
  const double x = r / 2.9683;
  const double disp = 1.35186623 / std::pow(x, 6) +
                      0.41495143 / std::pow(x, 8) +
                      0.17151143 / std::pow(x, 10);
  const double core =
      186924.404 * std::exp(-10.5717543 * x - 2.07758779 * x * x);
  const double damp = x < 1.438 ? std::exp(-std::pow(1.438 / x - 1.0, 2)) : 1.0;
  return eps * (core - damp * disp);
}

double dimer(int z0, int z1, double r, double *fx) {
  rgpot::fortranpots::FeHePot pot;
  const double pos[6] = {10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 + r, 10.0, 10.0};
  const int z[2] = {z0, z1};
  const double box[9] = {20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0};
  double forces[6] = {};
  rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces;
  pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
  *fx = forces[3];
  return out.energy;
}

} // namespace

int main() {
  double fx = 0.0;

  // Two Fe atoms: pair spline plus a d-band embedding on each atom.
  const double e_fefe = dimer(26, 26, 2.5, &fx);
  const double rho_d = cubic_knots(rho_coeff, rho_knot, 3, 2.5);
  const double h_fefe = cubic_knots(fe_coeff, fe_knot, 13, 2.5) +
                        2.0 * dband_embed(rho_d);
  std::printf("Fe-Fe at 2.5: kernel %.8f, by hand %.8f eV, Fx %.6f\n", e_fefe,
              h_fefe, fx);

  // Fe and He: pair spline plus an s-band embedding on both atoms.
  const double e_fehe = dimer(26, 2, 2.0, &fx);
  const double rho_s = sband_density(2.0);
  const double h_fehe = cubic_knots(fehe_coeff, fehe_knot, 8, 2.0) +
                        2.0 * sband_embed(rho_s);
  std::printf("Fe-He at 2.0: kernel %.8f, by hand %.8f eV, Fx %.6f\n", e_fehe,
              h_fehe, fx);

  // Two He atoms feed neither density: the bare HFD-B pair.
  const double e_hehe = dimer(2, 2, 3.2, &fx);
  std::printf("He-He at 3.2: kernel %.8f, by hand %.8f eV, Fx %.6f\n", e_hehe,
              he_he(3.2), fx);
  return 0;
}
```

```
Fe-Fe at 2.5: kernel -2.70130149, by hand -2.70130149 eV, Fx -1.404539
Fe-He at 2.0: kernel 0.53842992, by hand 0.53842992 eV, Fx 0.988719
He-He at 3.2: kernel -0.00081048, by hand -0.00081048 eV, Fx -0.000884
```

#### Literature

The source says the iron part is Ackland's 2004 many-body fit for alpha iron,
and that the helium part adds a second density channel.
Only some of the Fe-Fe constants of this source agree with the iron listing in
the Ackland paper below, so the page does not claim the Fe-Fe numbers are that
paper's table.
The Fe-He pair spline and the s-band parameters have no paper named in the
source, and none was found.

The He-He constants are those of the HFD-B3-FCII potential of Aziz, Janzen and
Moldover, Table I: `he_rm` 2.9683 Angstrom, `he_eps` 10.956 K, `he_c6`, `he_c8`,
`he_c10`, `he_aa`, `he_alpha`, `he_beta` and `he_damp` as in the table above.
The form is the HFD-B form of Aziz, McCourt and Wong, whose constants differ
slightly (its `he_eps` is 10.948 K).

- eOn, the software this kernel descends from: Goswami,
  TheochemUI/eOn: v3.6.0, Zenodo (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18529495.
- Ackland, Mendelev, Srolovitz, Han and Barashev, J. Phys.: Condens.
  Matter 16, S2629-S2642 (2004), doi:10.1088/0953-8984/16/27/003.
- Aziz, McCourt and Wong, Mol.
  Phys. 61, 1487-1511 (1987), doi:10.1080/00268978700101941, for the HFD-B form.
- Aziz, Janzen and Moldover, Phys.
  Rev. Lett. 74, 1586-1589 (1995), doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.1586, for the
  He-He constants.
- Daw and Baskes, Phys.
  Rev. B 29, 6443-6453 (1984), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.29.6443, for the
  embedded-atom energy.

### `EMT` effective medium theory

#### What it is and how to reach it

The Asap effective-medium potential of eOn's vendored tree, for H, Mg, Al, Ni,
Cu, Pd, Ag, Pt and Au with the default parameters, and for Al, Cu, Ag and Au
with the Rasmussen parameters.
The default configuration is the Asap provider, so a copper system takes the
copper row of the first table below.

- C++: `rgpot::EMTPot` in `CppCore/rgpot/EMT/EMTPot.hpp`, configured with
  `rgpot::EMTConfig{.rasmussen = true}` for the second table.
- Python: no class.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `EMT` with the option `parameters` set to `asap` (the default) or `rasmussen`, as in `pair_coeff * * EMT parameters rasmussen Cu`.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html) and
  [Potential names](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/potential_names.html).

An element the provider does not cover throws the Asap `Exception` class, which
does not derive from `std::exception`.
A periodic cell must be taller than twice the neighbour-list cutoff in every
direction, or the kernel throws the same class.
For copper in a cubic box the call throws at 10.85 Angstrom and runs at 11.0.
There is no stress.

#### Functional form

The kernel is the Asap code under `CppCore/rgpot/EMT/Asap`, in `EMT.cpp`,
`EMTParameterProvider.h` and the two parameter providers.
Lengths are in Angstrom; the provider tables below give the lengths in bohr and
the code converts them with 0.5291772.
With `beta = 1.809` and, for each atom `i= of element =e` with neighbours `j`:

- Fermi weight: `w(r) = 1 / (1 + exp(slope * (r - rc)))`.
  The cutoff is `rc = (beta * s0 / 2) * (sqrt(3) + sqrt(4))`, with `s0` the
  largest `seq` among the elements in use.
  The slope is `slope = ln(9999) / (r1 - rc)` with
  `r1 = rc * 2 * sqrt(4) / (sqrt(3) + sqrt(4))`.
  The weight is 1/10000 at `r1`, and the neighbour list reaches
  `1.04500185048 * rc`.
- Density sums over the neighbours `j= of atom =i`, with `chi = n0_b / n0_a` for
  a neighbour of element `b= and an atom of element =a`:
  `sigma1 = sum_j chi * w(r_ij) * exp(-eta2 * (r_ij - beta * s0_e))` and
  `sigma2 = sum_j w(r_ij) * exp(-(kappa / beta) * (r_ij - beta * s0_e))`.
  `sigma1` is floored at 1e-9.
- Neutral-sphere radius, with
  `dr = s - s0_e`: `s = s0_e - ln(sigma1 / (12 * gamma1)) / (beta * eta2)`.
- Cohesive term: `Ec = E0 * (1 + lambda * dr) * exp(-lambda * dr)`.
- Atomic-sphere term:
  `Eas = 6 * V0 * exp(-kappa * dr) - V0 * sigma2 / (2 * gamma2)`.
- Energy: `E = sum_i (Ec_i + Eas_i - E0_e)`.
  The kernel subtracts `E0` by default, so a perfect crystal at the equilibrium
  lattice constant has an energy near zero.
- The factors `gamma1` and `gamma2` come from the first three fcc shells (12, 6
  and 24 neighbours at
  `d_k = sqrt(k) * beta * s0`) with the weight `w=, normalised by the nearest-neighbour term: =gamma1 = sum_k w_k * pop_k * e^(-eta2 d_k) / (12 * e^(-beta s0 eta2))` and `gamma2 = sum_k w_k * pop_k * e^(-(kappa / beta) d_k) / (12 * e^(-kappa s0))`.

#### Parameters

The first table is the default (Asap) provider and the second the Rasmussen
provider, in the units of the source files: `E0`, `V0` in eV, `S0` in bohr
(`seq = S0 * 0.5291772` Angstrom), `eta2`, `kappa`, `lambda` in
1/bohr, and `n0` in 1/bohr^3.
The source also stores a mass and a length scale per element, which do not enter
the energy.
The rows are set in `EMTDefaultParameterProvider.cpp` and
`EMTRasmussenParameterProvider.cpp`.

| Element | Z  | E0     | S0   | V0    | eta2  | kappa | lambda | n0      |
|---------|----|--------|------|-------|-------|-------|--------|---------|
| Al      | 13 | -3.280 | 3.00 | 1.493 | 1.240 | 2.000 | 1.169  | 0.007   |
| Ni      | 28 | -4.44  | 2.60 | 3.673 | 1.669 | 2.757 | 1.948  | 0.0103  |
| Cu      | 29 | -3.510 | 2.67 | 2.476 | 1.652 | 2.74  | 1.906  | 0.0091  |
| Pd      | 46 | -3.90  | 2.87 | 2.773 | 1.818 | 3.107 | 2.155  | 0.00688 |
| Ag      | 47 | -2.96  | 3.01 | 2.132 | 1.652 | 2.790 | 1.892  | 0.00547 |
| Pt      | 78 | -5.85  | 2.90 | 4.067 | 1.812 | 3.145 | 2.192  | 0.00802 |
| Au      | 79 | -3.80  | 3.00 | 2.321 | 1.674 | 2.873 | 2.182  | 0.00703 |

and converted by the code: for H, `E0` 0.784035, `seq` 0.530015 Angstrom, `V0`
2.398292, `eta2` 4.401035, `kappa` 4.456708, `lambda` 2.108959 (all

|---------|----|--------|------|-------|-------|-------|--------|--------|
| Al      | 13 | -3.280 | 3.00 | 1.725 | 1.380 | 2.311 | 1.591  | 0.007  |

#### Example

The program evaluates copper in a cell of 4 x 4 x 4 conventional fcc cells, 256
atoms, which is tall enough for the cutoff.
It prints the energy per atom at three lattice constants next to the formulas
above for the perfect crystal, then moves one atom by 0.1 Angstrom and compares
the force on it with a central difference.
At 3.615 Angstrom, near the equilibrium lattice constant of copper, the energy
per atom is zero to the printed digits, because the kernel subtracts `E0`.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/EMT/EMTPot.hpp"

namespace {

// Default-provider copper row (energies eV, lengths bohr) of
// EMTDefaultParameterProvider.cpp.
const double bohr = 0.5291772, beta = 1.809;
const double E0 = -3.510, V0 = 2.476;
const double seq = 2.67 * bohr;
const double eta2 = 1.652 / bohr, kappa = 2.74 / bohr, lambda = 1.906 / bohr;

// Energy per atom of the perfect fcc crystal with lattice constant a.
// Three shells (12, 6 and 24 neighbours) lie inside the neighbour list.
double per_atom(double a) {
  const int pop[3] = {12, 6, 24};
  const double rf = 0.5 * seq * beta * (std::sqrt(3.0) + std::sqrt(4.0));
  const double r =
      rf * 2.0 * std::sqrt(4.0) / (std::sqrt(3.0) + std::sqrt(4.0));
  const double slope = std::log(9999.0) / (r - rf);
  double gamma1 = 0.0, gamma2 = 0.0, s1 = 0.0, s2 = 0.0;
  for (int k = 0; k < 3; ++k) {
    const double n = std::sqrt(k + 1.0);
    const double d0 = n * beta * seq, d = n * a / std::sqrt(2.0);
    const double w0 = 1.0 / (1.0 + std::exp(slope * (d0 - rf)));
    const double w = 1.0 / (1.0 + std::exp(slope * (d - rf)));
    gamma1 += w0 * pop[k] * std::exp(-eta2 * (d0 - beta * seq));
    gamma2 += w0 * pop[k] * std::exp(-kappa / beta * (d0 - beta * seq));
    s1 += w * pop[k] * std::exp(-eta2 * (d - beta * seq));
    s2 += w * pop[k] * std::exp(-kappa / beta * (d - beta * seq));
  }
  const double s = seq - std::log(s1 / gamma1) / (beta * eta2);
  const double ec =
      E0 * (1.0 + lambda * (s - seq)) * std::exp(-lambda * (s - seq));
  const double eas = 6.0 * V0 * std::exp(-kappa * (s - seq)) -
                     0.5 * V0 * 12.0 / gamma2 * s2;
  return ec + eas - E0;
}

// 4 x 4 x 4 conventional cells, 256 atoms. The cell must be taller than
// twice the Asap cutoff, which rules out 3 x 3 x 3 cells.
struct Crystal {
  std::vector<double> pos;
  std::vector<int> z;
  double box[9] = {};
  explicit Crystal(double a) {
    const double basis[4][3] = {
        {0.0, 0.0, 0.0}, {0.5, 0.5, 0.0}, {0.5, 0.0, 0.5}, {0.0, 0.5, 0.5}};
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
      for (int j = 0; j < 4; ++j)
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k)
          for (const auto &b : basis) {
            pos.push_back((i + b[0]) * a);
            pos.push_back((j + b[1]) * a);
            pos.push_back((k + b[2]) * a);
          }
    z.assign(pos.size() / 3, 29);
    box[0] = box[4] = box[8] = 4.0 * a;
  }
};

double evaluate(rgpot::EMTPot &pot, const Crystal &c, std::vector<double> &f) {
  f.assign(c.pos.size(), 0.0);
  rgpot::ForceInput in{c.z.size(), c.pos.data(), c.z.data(), c.box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = f.data();
  pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
  return out.energy;
}

} // namespace

int main() {
  rgpot::EMTPot pot;
  std::vector<double> f;
  for (double a : {3.615, 3.70, 3.80}) {
    const Crystal c(a);
    std::printf("a = %.3f: kernel %.6f eV/atom, by hand %.6f eV/atom\n", a,
                evaluate(pot, c, f) / static_cast<double>(c.z.size()),
                per_atom(a));
  }

  Crystal c(3.615);
  c.pos[0] += 0.1;
  const double e0 = evaluate(pot, c, f);
  const double fx = f[0];
  const double h = 1e-5;
  c.pos[0] += h;
  const double ep = evaluate(pot, c, f);
  c.pos[0] -= 2.0 * h;
  const double em = evaluate(pot, c, f);
  std::printf("atom 0 moved 0.1 Angstrom: energy %.6f eV\n", e0);
  std::printf("force x: %.6f eV/Angstrom, central difference %.6f\n", fx,
              -(ep - em) / (2.0 * h));
  return 0;
}
```

```
a = 3.615: kernel 0.000051 eV/atom, by hand 0.000051 eV/atom
a = 3.700: kernel 0.033910 eV/atom, by hand 0.033910 eV/atom
a = 3.800: kernel 0.120815 eV/atom, by hand 0.120815 eV/atom
atom 0 moved 0.1 Angstrom: energy 0.050128 eV
force x: -0.744357 eV/Angstrom, central difference -0.744357
```

#### Literature

The header `CppCore/rgpot/EMT/Asap/EMT.h` names the Jacobsen, Stoltze and
Norskov paper as the documentation of the method and no paper for the parameter
tables.
It does not name Rasmussen or any other paper for the second provider, so none
is cited for it.

- eOn, the software the vendored Asap tree comes from: Goswami,
  TheochemUI/eOn: v3.6.0, Zenodo (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18529495.
- Jacobsen, Stoltze and Norskov, Surf.
  Sci. 366, 394-402 (1996), doi:10.1016/0039-6028(96)00816-3.

### `EAMCell` cell-list aluminium, palladium and gold

#### What it is and how to reach it

The cell-list embedded-atom kernel from eOn, with a built-in table for aluminium
(13), palladium (46) and gold (79).
It has no options.
The neighbour list, the Verlet skin and the threading are described in
`docs/eam_cell.md`.

- C++: `rgpot::EAMPot` in `CppCore/rgpot/EAM/EAMPot.hpp`, with an empty
  `rgpot::EAMCellConfig`.
- Python: no class.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `EAMCell`, as in `pair_coeff * * EAMCell Al`.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html) and
  [Potential names](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/potential_names.html).

Only the diagonal of the box is read, and a diagonal entry that is not positive
throws `std::invalid_argument`.
An atomic number outside the table throws the same.
The minimum image is one half-box correction, so the box should be longer than
twice the cutoff in every direction.
There is no stress.

#### Functional form

The kernel is `CppCore/rgpot/EAM/EAM.cpp`.
For a pair at distance `r= with =r <` r_cut=:

- Density: `rho(r) = r^6 * (e^(-beta1 r) + 512 e^(-2 beta2 r))`.
- Pair term: `phi(r) = Dm * ((1 - e^(-alpha (r - Rm)))^2 - 1)`, in eV, once per
  pair.
- Embedding: `F(rho) = sum_{k=0..8} c_k rho^k`, in eV.
  The constant `c_0` is added for every atom, including one with no neighbour.
- Total: `E = sum_{i<j} phi(r_ij) + sum_i F(rho_i)`.
- Nothing is shifted: the pair term and the density keep their value at the
  cutoff.
- There are no cross-element terms.
  The density an atom receives and each pair with a higher-index partner use the
  parameters of the element of atom `i` alone, so the table is meant for one
  element at a time.

#### Parameters

The rows are the table `el_params` in `CppCore/rgpot/EAM/Parameters.h`.
Energies are in eV, lengths in Angstrom, and `alpha`, `beta1` and `beta2` in
1/Angstrom.

| Element | Z  | Dm       | alpha   | Rm      | beta1   | beta2   | r_cut  |
|---------|----|----------|---------|---------|---------|---------|--------|
| Al      | 13 | 3.63262  | 1.49303 | 2.12396 | 3.45762 | 3.54208 | 5.555  |
| Pd      | 46 | 1.6054   | 1.55083 | 2.35604 | 3.35148 | 3.34715 | 5.4120 |
| Au      | 79 | 0.669134 | 1.89707 | 2.57021 | 3.69785 | 3.69674 | 5.5155 |

The embedding coefficients `c_0` to `c_8`, in eV per density to the power `k`:

| k | Al         | Pd         | Au        |
|---|------------|------------|-----------|
| 0 | -0.0847305 | 0.0992627  | -0.198791 |
| 1 | 17.0887    | 4.8356     | -27.7663  |
| 2 | 60.7909    | -0.368647  | 224.068   |
| 3 | -75.8412   | 17.2739    | -594.101  |
| 4 | 39.9948    | -18.450    | 1316.31   |
| 5 | -6.21563   | 9.5018     | -2070.62  |
| 6 | -3.07993   | -2.69876   | 1973.14   |
| 7 | 1.51365    | 0.405341   | -1012.02  |
| 8 | -0.196034  | -0.0251768 | 214.373   |

#### Example

The program evaluates an aluminium dimer at 2.9 Angstrom, then perfect fcc
aluminium in a cell of 4 x 4 x 4 conventional cells at two lattice constants.
The by-hand dimer energy uses the formulas and the aluminium row above.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/EAM/EAMPot.hpp"

namespace {

// The aluminium row of CppCore/rgpot/EAM/Parameters.h.
const double Dm = 3.63262, alpha = 1.49303, Rm = 2.12396;
const double beta1 = 3.45762, beta2 = 3.54208;
const double c[9] = {-0.0847305, 17.0887,  60.7909, -75.8412, 39.9948,
                     -6.21563,   -3.07993, 1.51365, -0.196034};

double phi(double r) {
  const double d = 1.0 - std::exp(-alpha * (r - Rm));
  return Dm * d * d - Dm;
}
double rho(double r) {
  return std::pow(r, 6) *
         (std::exp(-beta1 * r) + 512.0 * std::exp(-2.0 * beta2 * r));
}
double embed(double d) {
  double e = 0.0, p = 1.0;
  for (double ck : c) {
    e += ck * p;
    p *= d;
  }
  return e;
}

double evaluate(rgpot::EAMPot &pot, const std::vector<double> &pos, double L,
                std::vector<double> &f) {
  const std::vector<int> z(pos.size() / 3, 13);
  const double box[9] = {L, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, L, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, L};
  f.assign(pos.size(), 0.0);
  rgpot::ForceInput in{z.size(), pos.data(), z.data(), box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = f.data();
  pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
  return out.energy;
}

} // namespace

int main() {
  rgpot::EAMPot pot;
  std::vector<double> f;

  const double r = 2.9, h = 1e-5;
  auto dimer = [&](double x) {
    return evaluate(pot, {10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 + x, 10.0, 10.0}, 20.0, f);
  };
  const double e = dimer(r);
  const double fx = f[3];
  std::printf("dimer at %.1f: kernel %.8f eV, by hand %.8f eV\n", r, e,
              phi(r) + 2.0 * embed(rho(r)));
  std::printf("force on atom 1, x: %.6f eV/Angstrom, central difference %.6f\n",
              fx, -(dimer(r + h) - dimer(r - h)) / (2.0 * h));

  const double basis[4][3] = {
      {0.0, 0.0, 0.0}, {0.5, 0.5, 0.0}, {0.5, 0.0, 0.5}, {0.0, 0.5, 0.5}};
  for (double a : {4.05, 4.40}) {
    std::vector<double> pos;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
      for (int j = 0; j < 4; ++j)
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k)
          for (const auto &b : basis) {
            pos.push_back((i + b[0]) * a);
            pos.push_back((j + b[1]) * a);
            pos.push_back((k + b[2]) * a);
          }
    const double ec = evaluate(pot, pos, 4.0 * a, f);
    std::printf("fcc a = %.2f, %zu atoms: %.6f eV/atom\n", a, pos.size() / 3,
                ec / static_cast<double>(pos.size() / 3));
  }
  return 0;
}
```

```
dimer at 2.9: kernel -1.09789446 eV, by hand -1.09789446 eV
force on atom 1, x: -0.790135 eV/Angstrom, central difference -0.790135
fcc a = 4.05, 256 atoms: -3.025594 eV/atom
fcc a = 4.40, 256 atoms: -3.315209 eV/atom
```

The energy per atom at 4.05 Angstrom, the experimental lattice constant of
aluminium, is still falling with the lattice constant, and the 4.40 Angstrom
value is lower.
This table with these formulas has its minimum near 4.4 Angstrom, so it is not a
description of aluminium at 4.05.
`EAMAl` above gives -3.356 eV per atom at 4.05 Angstrom.

#### Literature

The source cites no paper.
The form is that of Voter and Chen, with one change: this table has separate
`beta1` and `beta2`, where their density has one `beta`.
The aluminium row has the cutoff 5.555 Angstrom of their Table II, but its other
numbers differ from that table.
The palladium and gold rows are not in that paper.
No paper was found for the table.

- eOn, the software this kernel descends from: Goswami,
  TheochemUI/eOn: v3.6.0, Zenodo (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18529495.
- Voter and Chen, MRS Proceedings 82, 175 (1986), doi:10.1557/PROC-82-175.
- Daw and Baskes, Phys.
  Rev. B 29, 6443-6453 (1984), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.29.6443, for the
  embedded-atom energy.

### `EAMTable` tabulated EAM

#### What it is and how to reach it

An embedded-atom or Finnis-Sinclair potential read from a DYNAMO table, in the
three LAMMPS layouts `funcfl`, `setfl` and `fs`.
The energy, the interpolation and the agreement with LAMMPS are in
[the EAMTable reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/eam_table.html).
This section does not repeat them.

- C++: `rgpot::EAMTablePot` in `CppCore/rgpot/EAMTable/EAMTablePot.hpp`, built
  with `-Dwith_eam_table=true`.
- Python: no class.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `EAMTable` with the options `file`, `format` and `skin`, as in `pair_coeff * * EAMTable file Cu_u3.eam Cu`.
  The host builds it periodic and with the stress on.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [the EAMTable reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/eam_table.html) and
  [Potential names](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/potential_names.html).

An atom picks its element by atomic number, matched against the first field of
each element line of the file.

#### Functional form

The form is the one of the reference page,

```
E = sum_i F_a(rho_i) + sum_{i<j} phi_ab(r_ij)
rho_i = sum_{j /= i} rho_ab(r_ij)
```

with every function read from the file and interpolated by a seven-coefficient
cubic.
A `funcfl` file holds, for one element, `F(rho)`, an effective charge `Z(r)` and
`rho(r)`, and the pair term is `r * phi(r) = 27.2 * 0.529 * Z(r)^2` in eV
Angstrom.
Above the last density point the energy continues linearly with the slope at the
last point.

#### Parameters

There are no parameters in the code.
Everything comes from the file, and the configuration fields are:

| Field    | Default | Meaning                                 |
|----------|---------|-----------------------------------------|
| `path`   | none    | the table file                          |
| `format` | `Setfl` | `Funcfl`, `Setfl` or `FinnisSinclair`   |
| `skin`   | 1.0     | Verlet skin of the pair list (Angstrom) |
| `stress` | false   | write the Cauchy stress                 |

The repository ships two tables under `CppCore/tests/data/eam_table/`, a
`funcfl` copper file `Cu_u3.eam` and a `setfl` copper-nickel file
`CuNi.eam.alloy`.
The header of `Cu_u3.eam` gives the element line `29 63.550 3.6150 FCC`, that is
atomic number, mass, lattice constant in Angstrom and lattice type, and the grid
line
`500 5.0100200400801306e-04 500 1.0000000000000009e-02 4.9499999999999886e+00`,
that is the number of density points, the density step, the number of distance
points, the distance step in Angstrom and the cutoff in Angstrom.

#### Example

The first program writes a tiny `funcfl` table to the temporary directory, with
`F(rho) = -2 rho`, `Z(r) = 0.2 e^(-r)` and `rho(r) = e^(-r)`, on 101 density
points of step 0.02 and 201 distance points of step 0.025 Angstrom.
It reads the table back and evaluates a dimer at 2.0 Angstrom.
The by-hand energy is `phi(r) - 4 e^(-r)`: the pair term from `Z`, and the
embedding energy `-2 rho` of each atom at the density `e^(-r)` of its one
neighbour.
The file is removed once the potential has read it.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <filesystem>
#include <fstream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/EAMTable/EAMTablePot.hpp"

namespace {

// A funcfl file holds F(rho), Z(r) and rho(r), five numbers to a line.
// F(rho) = -2 rho, Z(r) = 0.2 exp(-r) and rho(r) = exp(-r).
void write_block(std::ofstream &f, const std::vector<double> &v) {
  for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)
    f << (i % 5 == 0 ? "" : " ") << v[i] << (i % 5 == 4 ? "\n" : "");
  f << "\n";
}

void write_table(const char *path) {
  const int nrho = 101, nr = 201;
  const double drho = 0.02, dr = 0.025;
  std::vector<double> F, Z, rho;
  for (int i = 0; i < nrho; ++i)
    F.push_back(-2.0 * i * drho);
  for (int i = 0; i < nr; ++i) {
    Z.push_back(0.2 * std::exp(-i * dr));
    rho.push_back(std::exp(-i * dr));
  }
  std::ofstream f(path);
  f.precision(17);
  f << "toy funcfl table\n";
  f << "29 63.55 3.615 FCC\n";
  f << nrho << " " << drho << " " << nr << " " << dr << " " << (nr - 1) * dr
    << "\n";
  write_block(f, F);
  write_block(f, Z);
  write_block(f, rho);
}

double energy(const rgpot::EAMTablePot &pot, double r, double *fx) {
  const double pos[6] = {10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 + r, 10.0, 10.0};
  const int z[2] = {29, 29};
  const double box[9] = {20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 20.0};
  double forces[6] = {};
  rgpot::ForceInput in{2, pos, z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces;
  pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
  if (fx)
    *fx = forces[3];
  return out.energy;
}

} // namespace

int main() {
  const std::string path =
      (std::filesystem::temp_directory_path() / "toy_funcfl.eam").string();
  write_table(path.c_str());
  const rgpot::EAMTablePot pot(
      {.path = path, .format = rgpot::EAMTableFormat::Funcfl});
  std::filesystem::remove(path);
  const double r = 2.0, h = 1e-5;
  double fx = 0.0;
  const double e = energy(pot, r, &fx);
  // r phi = 27.2 * 0.529 * Z^2, and each atom embeds -2 rho(r).
  const double phi = 27.2 * 0.529 * 0.04 * std::exp(-2.0 * r) / r;
  const double by_hand = phi - 4.0 * std::exp(-r);
  std::printf("kernel energy %.6f eV, by hand %.6f eV\n", e, by_hand);
  std::printf("force on atom 1, x: %.6f eV/Angstrom\n", fx);
  std::printf("central difference: %.6f eV/Angstrom\n",
              -(energy(pot, r + h, nullptr) - energy(pot, r - h, nullptr)) /
                  (2.0 * h));
  return 0;
}
```

```
kernel energy -0.536070 eV, by hand -0.536070 eV
force on atom 1, x: -0.528164 eV/Angstrom
central difference: -0.528164 eV/Angstrom
```

The second program reads the shipped `Cu_u3.eam`, with the stress on, and prints
the energy per atom and the pressure `-trace(sigma) / 3` of a cell of 3 x 3 x 3
conventional cells at three lattice constants.
The path is relative to the repository root, where the examples run.
At 3.615 Angstrom the pressure is zero to the printed digits and the energy is
the cohesive energy of the table, -3.54 eV.

```cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/EAMTable/EAMTablePot.hpp"

int main() {
  // Cu_u3.eam is the Foiles-Baskes-Daw copper table kept for the tests. The
  // path is relative to the repository root.
  const rgpot::EAMTablePot pot(
      {.path = "CppCore/tests/data/eam_table/Cu_u3.eam",
       .format = rgpot::EAMTableFormat::Funcfl,
       .stress = true});
  const double gpa = 160.2176634; // eV/Angstrom^3 to GPa
  const double basis[4][3] = {
      {0.0, 0.0, 0.0}, {0.5, 0.5, 0.0}, {0.5, 0.0, 0.5}, {0.0, 0.5, 0.5}};
  for (double a : {3.615, 3.55, 3.68}) {
    std::vector<double> pos;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i)
      for (int j = 0; j < 3; ++j)
        for (int k = 0; k < 3; ++k)
          for (const auto &b : basis) {
            pos.push_back((i + b[0]) * a);
            pos.push_back((j + b[1]) * a);
            pos.push_back((k + b[2]) * a);
          }
    const std::vector<int> z(pos.size() / 3, 29);
    const double L = 3.0 * a;
    const double box[9] = {L, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, L, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, L};
    std::vector<double> forces(pos.size());
    rgpot::ForceInput in{z.size(), pos.data(), z.data(), box};
    rgpot::ForceOut out{};
    out.F = forces.data();
    pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
    const double p =
        -(out.stress[0] + out.stress[4] + out.stress[8]) / 3.0 * gpa;
    std::printf("a = %.3f: %.5f eV/atom, pressure %.4f GPa\n", a,
                out.energy / static_cast<double>(z.size()), p);
  }
  return 0;
}
```

```
a = 3.615: -3.54000 eV/atom, pressure -0.0000 GPa
a = 3.550: -3.52423 eV/atom, pressure 8.4724 GPa
a = 3.680: -3.52600 eV/atom, pressure -6.5942 GPa
```

#### Literature

The tables are data files and carry their own citations in their headers.
`Cu_u3.eam` is from Foiles, Baskes and Daw.
The `fs` layout is the Finnis-Sinclair form and the embedded-atom energy is that
of Daw and Baskes.

- Foiles, Baskes and Daw, Phys.
  Rev. B 33, 7983-7991 (1986), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.33.7983.
- Daw and Baskes, Phys.
  Rev. B 29, 6443-6453 (1984), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.29.6443.
- Finnis and Sinclair, Philos.
  Mag.
  A 50, 45-55 (1984), doi:10.1080/01418618408244210.

### `MEAM` modified embedded-atom method

#### What it is and how to reach it

`rgpot::MEAMPot` evaluates the first-neighbour method of Baskes and the
second-neighbour extension of Lee and Baskes.
It reports `PotType::MEAM` and reads the library and parameter files accepted by
the LAMMPS `pair_style meam` implementation.
The configuration names the files, selects and orders their element records, and
optionally assigns an atomic number to each record.

#### Functional form, parameters and example

The energy, screening ellipses, reference lattices, mixing rules, file grammar,
errors and a complete aluminium example are in the
[MEAM reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/meam.html).
Lengths are Angstrom and energies are eV.
The model builds its pair tables once; one immutable `MEAMModel` can then serve
concurrent potential instances.

#### Literature

- Baskes, Phys.
  Rev. B 46, 2727-2742 (1992), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.46.2727.
- Lee and Baskes, Phys.
  Rev. B 62, 8564-8567 (2000), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.62.8564.

# Silicon potentials

Source: docs/orgmode/howto/potentials-silicon.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/potentials-silicon.html

Five `PotType` enumerators evaluate crystalline silicon in a periodic cell: the
Stillinger-Weber potential in two variants (`SWSi` and `SWSi1985`), the
environment-dependent interatomic potential (`EDIP`), the Lenosky potential
(`LenoskySi`) and the Tersoff potential (`TersoffSi`).
Each section below says how to reach the potential, gives its functional form as
the kernel evaluates it, lists the parameters with their source, runs a program,
and cites the literature.
The names a host accepts (`rgpot-eval`,
`pair_coeff`, the PLUMED `POTENTIAL` keyword) are in [[file:../reference/potential_names.org][Potential
names]].
The class contracts are in
[C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html).

Lengths are Angstrom, energies are eV, forces are
eV/Angstrom and the stress is eV/Angstrom^3.
All five potentials read the cell as periodic in every direction and ignore the
atomic numbers, except `TersoffSi`, which also accepts carbon.

The examples share one geometry: the conventional eight-atom diamond cell of
silicon with lattice constant 5.431 Angstrom, the usual value for silicon.
The 1985 Stillinger-Weber potential has a pressure of only -0.0028 GPa there.
The positions are the face-centred-cubic sites and the same sites shifted by a
quarter of the cell along each axis.
Each program prints the energy per atom of the perfect crystal, whether
`has_stress` is set, and, for a crystal with atom 0 moved by 0.1 Angstrom, the
analytic force on that atom next to a central difference of the energy with step
1e-4 Angstrom.

Energy per atom of the perfect crystal at 5.431 Angstrom, as the examples below
print it:

| Name        | Class               | eV/atom   | Stress |
|-------------|---------------------|-----------|--------|
| `SWSi1985`  | `StillingerWeberSi` | -4.334478 | yes    |
| `SWSi`      | `SWPot`             | -4.629989 | yes    |
| `EDIP`      | `EDIPPot`           | -4.649953 | no     |
| `LenoskySi` | `LenoskyPot`        | -4.612422 | no     |
| `TersoffSi` | `TersoffSiC`        | -4.629593 | yes    |

### `SWSi` Stillinger-Weber silicon with eOn's epsilon

#### What it is and how to reach it

This is the Stillinger-Weber (SW) silicon potential with the energy scale eOn
uses, 2.3149945 eV, which is 1.068176741337 times the published value.
Use it to reproduce eOn's silicon numbers; use `SWSi1985` below for the
published epsilon.

- C++: `rgpot::fortranpots::SWPot` in `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp`,
  built with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.
- Python: `rgpot.SWPot`.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `SWSi` (a build with the Fortran potentials), as in `pair_coeff * * SWSi Si`.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html) and
  [Stillinger-Weber silicon (1985)](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/sw_si.html), which
  explains why this class is not the 1985 kernel.

#### Functional form

The kernel is `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_sw.f90`.
With `rho = r / sigma` and `alpha` the reduced cutoff:

- Pair term, once per pair with `r < alpha * sigma`:
  `epsilon * A * (beta * rho^(-p) - 1) * exp(1 / (rho - alpha))`.
- Three-body term, for each centre atom `i` and each unordered pair of its
  neighbours `j= and =k` inside the cutoff:
  `epsilon * lambda * w_ij * w_ik * (cos(theta_jik) + 1/3)^2`, with `w_ij = exp(gamma / (rho_ij - alpha))`.
- The cutoff is `alpha * sigma` = 3.77118 Angstrom.
  Both terms go smoothly to zero there.
  An exponent below -300 is set to zero before `exp` is called.
- When `a0` is not zero, the pair energy gains `a0 * (cos(pi * r / s0) + 1)` for
  `r <` s0=.
  The default `a0` is 0, so the term is not used.

The class writes the Cauchy stress (`has_stress` 1) from the folded bond vectors
of its neighbour table.
`forceBatch` skips the virial.
Because both SW kernels are linear in `epsilon`, this class gives the energy,
forces and stress of `SWSi1985` multiplied by 1.068176741337.

#### Parameters

The values are the defaults of `sw_params_t` in
`CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_sw.f90`.
A caller of `SWPot` has no way to change them.

| Parameter           | Field     | Value        | Unit              |
|---------------------|-----------|--------------|-------------------|
| length scale        | `sigma`   | 2.0951       | Angstrom          |
| reduced cutoff      | `alpha`   | 1.8          | in units of sigma |
| energy scale        | `epsilon` | 2.3149945    | eV                |
| three-body strength | `lambda`  | 21.0         | dimensionless     |
| pair prefactor      | `a`       | 7.049556277  | dimensionless     |
| repulsion weight    | `beta`    | 0.6022245584 | dimensionless     |
| three-body decay    | `gamma`   | 1.2          | dimensionless     |
| repulsion exponent  | `p`       | 4            | dimensionless     |
| binary range        | `s0`      | 3.6          | Angstrom          |
| binary strength     | `a0`      | 0.0          | eV                |

The epsilon is the product `2.16826 * 1.06767385`, two literals copied from
eOn's `SWFortran.f90`; the source says the factor 1.06767385 is untraced.
The rows from `sigma` to `p= other than =epsilon` are the 1985 values (see
`SWSi1985`); lambda is 21 and is not rescaled.
`s0` and `a0` belong to the optional binary term and are not used by default.

#### Example

This program needs a build with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp"

int main() {
  const double a = 5.431;
  const double fcc[4][3] = {
      {0.0, 0.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 0.5, 0.5}, {0.5, 0.0, 0.5}, {0.5, 0.5, 0.0}};
  std::vector<double> pos;
  for (const auto &b : fcc)
    for (double shift : {0.0, 0.25})
      for (int k = 0; k < 3; ++k)
        pos.push_back((b[k] + shift) * a);
  const int z[8] = {14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14};
  const double box[9] = {a, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, a, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, a};
  std::vector<double> forces(pos.size());

  rgpot::fortranpots::SWPot pot;
  rgpot::ForceInput in{8, pos.data(), z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces.data();
  auto energy = [&] {
    pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
    return out.energy;
  };

  const double e0 = energy();
  double fmax = 0.0;
  for (double f : forces) fmax = std::max(fmax, std::fabs(f));
  std::printf("diamond, a = %.3f: %.6f eV/atom, forces vanish: %s\n", a,
              e0 / 8.0, fmax < 1e-9 ? "yes" : "no");
  std::printf("has_stress %d", out.has_stress);
  if (out.has_stress) {
    const double trace = out.stress[0] + out.stress[4] + out.stress[8];
    std::printf(", pressure %.4f GPa", -trace / 3.0 * 160.2176634);
  }
  std::printf("\n");

  pos[0] += 0.1;
  energy();
  const double fx = forces[0];
  const double h = 1e-4;
  pos[0] += h;
  const double e_plus = energy();
  pos[0] -= 2.0 * h;
  const double e_minus = energy();
  std::printf("atom 0 moved 0.1 A: Fx %.6f, -dE/dx %.6f eV/A\n", fx,
              -(e_plus - e_minus) / (2.0 * h));
  return 0;
}
```

```
diamond, a = 5.431: -4.629989 eV/atom, forces vanish: yes
has_stress 1, pressure -0.0030 GPa
atom 0 moved 0.1 A: Fx -1.886477, -dE/dx -1.886477 eV/A
```

The energy per atom is close to minus twice epsilon, 2 * 2.3149945 = 4.629989
eV, as the reference page derives for the diamond lattice.
The pressure is near zero because 5.431 Angstrom is close to the minimum of the
energy.
`has_stress` is 1, and the analytic force agrees with the difference.

#### Literature

- Goswami and coauthors, eOn v3.6.0, Zenodo (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18529495.
  eOn v3.6.0 builds its silicon Stillinger-Weber potential as
  `rgpot::fortranpots::SWPot`, the class of this section.
- Stillinger and Weber, Phys.
  Rev. B 31, 5262-5271 (1985), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.31.5262.
  The functional form, and the parameters apart from epsilon.
- The epsilon 2.3149945 eV has no paper: it is eOn's value, and its factor is
  untraced in the source.
- Thompson, Plimpton and Mattson, J. Chem.
  Phys. 131, 154107 (2009), doi:10.1063/1.3245303.
  The many-body virial behind the stress.

### `SWSi1985` Stillinger-Weber silicon with the published epsilon

#### What it is and how to reach it

This is the Stillinger-Weber silicon potential with the parameters of the 1985
paper.
Use it when you need the published energy scale, 2.16723920 eV.
It is a C++ kernel, so it needs no Fortran build.

- C++: `rgpot::StillingerWeberSi` in `CppCore/rgpot/StillingerWeber/SWSi.hpp`.
- Python: `rgpot.StillingerWeberSi`.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `SWSi1985`, which takes no options, as in `pair_coeff * * SWSi1985 Si`.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [Stillinger-Weber silicon (1985)](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/sw_si.html)
  and [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html).

#### Functional form

The kernel is `CppCore/rgpot/StillingerWeber/SWSi.cc`, with `u = r / kSigma` and
`kCut` the reduced cutoff:

- Pair term, once per pair with `u < kCut`:
  `kEpsilon * kA * (kB * u^(-kP) - 1) * exp(1 / (u - kCut))`.
- Three-body term, for each centre atom and each unordered pair of its
  neighbours:
  `kEpsilon * kLambda * w_ij * w_ik * (cos(theta_jik) + 1/3)^2`, with `w_ij = exp(kGamma / (u_ij - kCut))`.
- The cutoff is `kCut * kSigma` = 3.77118 Angstrom.
  A pair whose exponent `1 / (u - kCut)` is below -700 is dropped.
- Atomic numbers are not read.
  The force call writes the Cauchy stress.

#### Parameters

The values are the static members of `rgpot::StillingerWeberSi` in
`CppCore/rgpot/StillingerWeber/SWSi.hpp`.
The paper's Eq. (2.7) gives the dimensionless set and Eq. (2.9) gives sigma and
epsilon, as recorded in that header.

| Parameter           | Member     | Value        | Unit              |
|---------------------|------------|--------------|-------------------|
| energy scale        | `kEpsilon` | 2.16723920   | eV                |
| length scale        | `kSigma`   | 2.0951       | Angstrom          |
| pair prefactor      | `kA`       | 7.049556277  | dimensionless     |
| repulsion weight    | `kB`       | 0.6022245584 | dimensionless     |
| repulsion exponent  | `kP`       | 4.0          | dimensionless     |
| reduced cutoff      | `kCut`     | 1.80         | in units of sigma |
| three-body strength | `kLambda`  | 21.0         | dimensionless     |
| three-body decay    | `kGamma`   | 1.20         | dimensionless     |

`kEpsilon` is the paper's 3.4723e-12 erg, evaluated in the header as
`3.4723e-12 * 1.0e-7 / 1.602176634e-19` with 1 erg = 1e-7 J and the CODATA
electron-volt.
The members are compile-time constants, so this class has no configuration
struct.

#### Example

This program has no build requirement beyond `librgpot`.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/StillingerWeber/SWSi.hpp"

int main() {
  const double a = 5.431;
  const double fcc[4][3] = {
      {0.0, 0.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 0.5, 0.5}, {0.5, 0.0, 0.5}, {0.5, 0.5, 0.0}};
  std::vector<double> pos;
  for (const auto &b : fcc)
    for (double shift : {0.0, 0.25})
      for (int k = 0; k < 3; ++k)
        pos.push_back((b[k] + shift) * a);
  const int z[8] = {14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14};
  const double box[9] = {a, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, a, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, a};
  std::vector<double> forces(pos.size());

  rgpot::StillingerWeberSi pot;
  rgpot::ForceInput in{8, pos.data(), z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces.data();
  auto energy = [&] {
    pot.forceImpl(in, &out);
    return out.energy;
  };

  const double e0 = energy();
  double fmax = 0.0;
  for (double f : forces) fmax = std::max(fmax, std::fabs(f));
  std::printf("diamond, a = %.3f: %.6f eV/atom, forces vanish: %s\n", a,
              e0 / 8.0, fmax < 1e-9 ? "yes" : "no");
  std::printf("has_stress %d", out.has_stress);
  if (out.has_stress) {
    const double trace = out.stress[0] + out.stress[4] + out.stress[8];
    std::printf(", pressure %.4f GPa", -trace / 3.0 * 160.2176634);
  }
  std::printf("\n");

  pos[0] += 0.1;
  energy();
  const double fx = forces[0];
  const double h = 1e-4;
  pos[0] += h;
  const double e_plus = energy();
  pos[0] -= 2.0 * h;
  const double e_minus = energy();
  std::printf("atom 0 moved 0.1 A: Fx %.6f, -dE/dx %.6f eV/A\n", fx,
              -(e_plus - e_minus) / (2.0 * h));
  return 0;
}
```

```
diamond, a = 5.431: -4.334478 eV/atom, forces vanish: yes
has_stress 1, pressure -0.0028 GPa
atom 0 moved 0.1 A: Fx -1.766072, -dE/dx -1.766072 eV/A
```

The energy per atom is -2 epsilon, 2 * 2.16723920 = 4.334478 eV.
The ratio to the `SWSi` energy of the previous section is 1.068177.
The pressure is -0.0028 GPa, so 5.431 Angstrom is within a few thousandths of a
GPa of the minimum of this potential.

#### Literature

- Stillinger and Weber, Phys.
  Rev. B 31, 5262-5271 (1985), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.31.5262.
  The functional form and the parameters (Eqs. 2.7 and 2.9).
- Thompson, Plimpton and Mattson, J. Chem.
  Phys. 131, 154107 (2009), doi:10.1063/1.3245303.
  The many-body virial behind the stress.

### `EDIP` Environment-dependent interatomic potential for silicon

#### What it is and how to reach it

EDIP gives each silicon atom a pair sum and a three-body sum whose strengths
depend on an effective coordination number, so one parameter set covers the
diamond crystal, defects and disordered phases.
Use it for silicon defects and disordered phases, the cases its parameterization
paper targets.
The class does not write a stress.

- C++: `rgpot::fortranpots::EDIPPot` in `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp`,
  built with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.
- Python: `rgpot.EDIPPot`.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `EDIP` (a build with the Fortran potentials), as in `pair_coeff * * EDIP Si`.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html).

#### Functional form

The kernel is `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_edip.f90`.
The energy is `E = sum_i E_i` with

- `E_i = sum_j V2(r_ij, Z_i) + sum_(j<k) V3(r_ij, r_ik, theta_jik, Z_i)`.
- Coordination: `Z_i = sum_m f(r_im)`, where `f(r)` is 1 for `r < c`, 0 for
  `r >` b=, and `exp(alpha / (1 - x^(-3)))` between, with
  `x = (r - c) / (b - c)`.
- Pair term for `r < a`:
  `V2 = cap_a * ((cap_b / r)^rh - palp * exp(-bet * Z^2)) * exp(sig / (r - a))`.
- Three-body term, for neighbours inside `a`:
  `V3 = g(r_ij) * g(r_ik) * h(cos(theta), Z)` with `g(r) = exp(gam / (r - a))`.
- Angular function: `h = lam * (1 - exp(-x^2) + (delta / qo) * x^2)` with
  `x = (cos(theta) + tau(Z)) * sqrt(qo) * exp(-mu * Z / 2)`, and
  `tau(Z) = u1 + u2 * (u3 * exp(-u4 * Z) - exp(-2 * u4 * Z))`.
- The cutoff is the larger of `a= and =b`, 3.1213820 Angstrom.
  A triplet whose two ends are one atom reached through two periodic images is
  dropped, so the force is the exact gradient of the reported energy.
- The call throws `std::runtime_error` when the smallest perpendicular width of
  the cell is below the cutoff.
- The force call does not write a stress and leaves `has_stress` as set.

#### Parameters

The values are the defaults of `edip_params_t` in
`CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_edip.f90`, copied from the eOn kernel (Bazant's
routine as adapted by Goedecker).
The kernel splits the paper's `A= and =B` into `cap_a`, `cap_b` and `palp`; see
below the table.
A caller of `EDIPPot` has no way to change them.

| Field   | Paper symbol     | Value       | Unit          |
|---------|------------------|-------------|---------------|
| `cap_a` | see text         | 5.6714030   | eV            |
| `cap_b` | see text         | 2.0002804   | Angstrom      |
| `rh`    | rho              | 1.2085196   | dimensionless |
| `a`     | a                | 3.1213820   | Angstrom      |
| `sig`   | sigma            | 0.5774108   | Angstrom      |
| `lam`   | lambda           | 1.4533108   | eV            |
| `gam`   | gamma            | 1.1247945   | Angstrom      |
| `b`     | a (coordination) | 3.1213820   | Angstrom      |
| `c`     | c                | 2.5609104   | Angstrom      |
| `delta` | eta * Q0         | 78.7590539  | dimensionless |
| `mu`    | mu               | 0.6966326   | dimensionless |
| `qo`    | Q0               | 312.1341346 | dimensionless |
| `palp`  | see text         | 1.4074424   | dimensionless |
| `bet`   | beta             | 0.0070975   | dimensionless |
| `alp`   | alpha            | 3.1083847   | dimensionless |
| `u1`    | u1               | -0.165799   | dimensionless |
| `u2`    | u2               | 32.557      | dimensionless |
| `u3`    | u3               | 0.286198    | dimensionless |
| `u4`    | u4               | 0.66        | dimensionless |

The set is Table I of Justo and coauthors (1998), with the four `u` values from
the text after their Eq. (10).
Their table prints `A= = 7.9821730 eV, =B` = 1.5075463 Angstrom and `eta` =
0.2523244.
The kernel's `delta / qo` is 78.7590539 / 312.1341346 = 0.252324, and its
`cap_a * palp` is 7.98217305 eV.
The pair term `cap_a * (cap_b)^rh` is 13.1088543 eV Angstrom^rh against
`A * B^rho` = 13.1088539 from the table, a relative difference below 4e-8.
With `cap_a * palp` equal to `A`, the kernel's pair term is the paper's to the
digits the paper prints.
The paper uses one length `a` for the coordination cutoff, the pair cutoff and
the three-body cutoff; the kernel keeps `b= for the first and =a` for the other
two, and both are 3.1213820.

This program needs a build with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.


### `LenoskySi` Lenosky silicon, a spline MEAM model

#### What it is and how to reach it

The Lenosky potential has the modified-embedded-atom form: a pair term plus an
embedding energy of a local density that sums two-body and three-body pieces.
All five functions are cubic splines fitted by force matching.
The paper reports phonons, elastic constants, point defects, dislocation core
reconstructions and interstitial clusters.
The class does not write a stress.

- C++: `rgpot::fortranpots::LenoskyPot` in
  `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp`, built with
  `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.
- Python: `rgpot.LenoskyPot`.
- `rgpot-eval`, LAMMPS
  `pair_coeff` and PLUMED name: `LenoskySi` (a build with the Fortran potentials), as in `pair_coeff * * LenoskySi Si`.
- `potserv`: no type name.
- Reference: [C++ potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_potentials.html).

#### Functional form

The kernel is `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_lenosky.f90`.
For each atom `i`:

- Density:
  `dens_i = sum_j rho(r_ij) + sum_(j<k) f(r_ij) * f(r_ik) * g(cos(theta_jik))`.
- Energy: `E_i = sum_j phi(r_ij) / 2 + U(dens_i)`, and `E = sum_i E_i`.
- `phi`, `rho`, `f=, =U` and `g` are cubic splines on uniform knots.
  Outside the knot range each is continued linearly with the end slope.
- The neighbour cutoff is `lenosky_params_t%cutoff`, 4.5 Angstrom.
  `rho` and `f= end at 3.5 Angstrom with a last knot value of 0.0, and =phi`
  ends at 4.5 Angstrom with a last knot value of 0.0.
- The force call does not write a stress and leaves `has_stress` as set.

#### Parameters

The spline data are in
`CppCore/rgpot/fortran/rgpot_lenosky.f90` as the arrays `cof_<stem>` (knot
values) and `dof_<stem>` (the spline second derivatives at the knots), which
descend from eOn.
They are not copied here.
The five stems and their knot grids are:

| Stem | Role                 | Knots | Range                         |
|------|----------------------|-------|-------------------------------|
| phi  | pair energy, eV      | 10    | 1.5 to 4.5 Angstrom           |
| rho  | two-body density     | 11    | 1.5 to 3.5 Angstrom           |
| fff  | three-body radial    | 10    | 1.5 to 3.5 Angstrom           |
| uuu  | embedding energy, eV | 8     | -1.77093 to 7.90852 (density) |
| ggg  | three-body angular   | 8     | -1.0 to 0.80014 (cosine)      |

Anchor values read from the source, first and last knot of each `cof_*` array:

| Array     | First knot value | Last knot value |
|-----------|------------------|-----------------|
| `cof_phi` | 6.92994          | 0.0             |
| `cof_rho` | 0.13747          | 0.0             |
| `cof_fff` | 1.25031          | 0.0             |
| `cof_uuu` | -1.07493         | 2.39618         |
| `cof_ggg` | 5.25416          | 5.61799         |

I did not compare the arrays with the tables of the paper.
`lenosky_params_t` holds only the cutoff; the splines are fixed data.

#### Example

This program needs a build with `-Dwith_fortran_pots=enabled`.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

#include "rgpot/fortran/FortranPots.hpp"

  const double fcc[4][3] = {
      {0.0, 0.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 0.5, 0.5}, {0.5, 0.0, 0.5}, {0.5, 0.5, 0.0}};

  for (const auto &b : fcc)
    for (double shift : {0.0, 0.25})
      for (int k = 0; k < 3; ++k)
        pos.push_back((b[k] + shift) * a);
  const int z[8] = {14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14};
  const double box[9] = {a, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, a, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, a};
  std::vector<double> forces(pos.size());

  rgpot::fortranpots::LenoskyPot pot;
  rgpot::ForceInput in{8, pos.data(), z, box};
  rgpot::ForceOut out{};
  out.F = forces.data();

    return out.energy;
  };

  const double e0 = energy();

  std::printf("diamond, a = %.3f: %.6f eV/atom, forces vanish: %s\n", a,
              e0 / 8.0, fmax < 1e-9 ? "yes" : "no");
  std::printf("has_stress %d", out.has_stress);
  if (out.has_stress) {
    const double trace = out.stress[0] + out.stress[4] + out.stress[8];
    std::printf(", pressure %.4f GPa", -trace / 3.0 * 160.2176634);
  }
  std::printf("\n");

  energy();

  const double h = 1e-4;
  pos[0] += h;
  const double e_plus = energy();

  const double e_minus = energy();

              -(e_plus - e_minus) / (2.0 * h));

```

```
diamond, a = 5.431: -4.612422 eV/atom, forces vanish: yes
has_stress 0
atom 0 moved 0.1 A: Fx -1.363769, -dE/dx -1.363769 eV/A
```

`has_stress` stays 0.
The analytic force, which comes from a three-pass gather over the density
derivatives, matches the central difference of the energy.

  eOn v3.6.0 builds its Lenosky silicon potential as
