# Architecture

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/architecture.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/architecture.html

This page explains how the layers of `rgpot` fit together and why errors and
capabilities cross them the way they do.
Why the wire uses three carriers is in [The RPC Model](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/rpc-model.html).
The directory layout and the list of potentials are in
[Architecture reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/architecture.html).
The C entry points are in [C ABI of rgpot-core](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/c_abi.html),
and the C++ wrappers in [C++ API](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_api.html).

`rgpot` follows a /metatensor/-style layout.
A Rust crate, `rgpot-core`, defines the data exchange types and the RPC client
and server.
It exports them through a C ABI whose header `cbindgen` generates.
Hand-written C++ headers wrap that ABI in move-only handles.
The C++ potentials in `CppCore/rgpot/` plug into the Rust core through a
callback.

### Layer diagram

```
+------------------------------------------------+
|  C++ wrappers (move-only handles)              |
|  include/rgpot/*.hpp                           |
+------------------------------------------------+
|  C ABI (generated by cbindgen)                 |
|  rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h                    |
+------------------------------------------------+
|  Rust core                                     |
|  rgpot-core/src/                               |
|  - DLPack input and output structs             |
|  - callback dispatch (rgpot_potential_t)       |
|  - Hessian-vector products                     |
|  - status codes, thread-local message          |
|  - capability check (schema feature)           |
|  - profile loader (profile feature)            |
|  - Cap'n Proto RPC client and server (rpc)     |
+------------------------------------------------+
        | callbacks
+------------------------------------------------+
|  C++ potentials, CppCore/rgpot/<Name>/         |
|  classes derived from rgpot::Potential<Derived>|
+------------------------------------------------+
```

### Layers

#### Rust core (`rgpot-core/`)

The crate owns the public C types.
Every exported struct is `#[repr(C)]` and every exported function is
`extern "C"`.

- `rgpot_force_input_t` and `rgpot_force_out_t` :: the data exchange structs.
  The input holds three borrowed DLPack tensors: positions, atomic numbers and
  the box matrix.
  The output holds a forces tensor that the callback allocates and the caller
  frees with `rgpot_tensor_free`, plus the energy and the variance as plain
  doubles.
  DLPack keeps the structs independent of the device that holds the data.
- `rgpot_status_t` :: the status codes
  `RGPOT_SUCCESS`, `RGPOT_INVALID_PARAMETER`, `RGPOT_INTERNAL_ERROR`, `RGPOT_RPC_ERROR`, `RGPOT_BUFFER_SIZE_ERROR`,
  `RGPOT_NO_JET`, `RGPOT_JET_BRANCH` and `RGPOT_JET_DOMAIN`.
  Calls that can fail return one of them.
  Constructors such as `rgpot_potential_new_eindir` and `rgpot_rpc_client_new`
  return a pointer instead, and NULL on failure.
- `rgpot_potential_t` :: a `#[repr(C)]` struct whose first member is an
  `eindir_objective_t`, so a pointer to it is also a pointer to an eindir
  objective.
  It carries the callback, its `void*` user data and an optional destructor for
  that data.
  The core calls the callback without knowing the concrete C++ type behind it.
  Callers create it with `rgpot_potential_new` or
  `rgpot_potential_new_eindir` and release it with `rgpot_potential_free`.
- `rgpot_last_error` :: returns the thread-local message of the last failure.
  The pointer stays valid until the next `rgpot_*` call on the same thread.

##### Feature gates

`rgpot-core/Cargo.toml` keeps the default feature set empty.

- `schema` :: compiles `Potentials.capnp` with `capnpc` and adds the capability
  check and `rgpot_potential_set_peer_capabilities`.
- `profile` :: enables `schema` and adds the profile loader (`ProfileSession`),
  which opens a backend library with `libloading`.
- `rpc` :: enables `schema` and adds the Cap'n Proto RPC client and server, with
  `capnp-rpc`, `tokio`, `tokio-util` and `futures`.
- `cache` :: declared with no code behind it; the Meson option
  `-Dwith_cache=true` passes it to Cargo.
- `gen-header` :: regenerates `rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h` with `cbindgen`;
  `pixi r gen-header` runs `cargo build --features gen-header`.

The Meson build compiles the crate when `-Dwith_rust_core=true` is set.
It passes `rpc` when RPC is enabled and `cache` when `-Dwith_cache=true` is set.

##### The schema copy

The crate bundles `rgpot-core/schema/Potentials.capnp`, so a build from
crates.io has the schema.
`build.rs` prefers that copy and falls back to
`CppCore/rgpot/rpc/Potentials.capnp` when it is missing.
The Cap'n Proto wire format does not depend on the language, so a Rust client
can call a C++ server and the reverse.

#### C ABI (`rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h`)

The header is the contract between the Rust core and every C or C++ consumer.
`cbindgen` generates it from the Rust source, so nobody edits it by hand.
A change to the public API is made in the Rust source and the header is
regenerated.

The header holds the `#[repr(C)]` structs and enums, the function declarations,
and the Rust doc comments as Doxygen comments.
`rgpot_fused_cache_t` and `rgpot_rpc_client_t` are opaque; `rgpot_potential_t`
is a full struct.
Declarations that need the `rpc` feature sit inside
`#if defined(RGPOT_HAS_RPC)`.

#### C++ wrappers (`include/rgpot/`)

The headers give C++ callers handles that free themselves and exceptions in
place of status codes.

- `errors.hpp` :: `rgpot::Error`, a
  `std::runtime_error`, and `rgpot::detail::check_status`.
  `check_status` reads `rgpot_last_error` and throws `rgpot::Error` with a
  prefix that names the status category.
- `types.hpp` :: `rgpot::InputSpec` wraps caller buffers in non-owning DLPack
  tensors, and `rgpot::CalcResult` owns the forces tensor that a calculation
  returns.
  The names differ from `rgpot::ForceInput` and `rgpot::ForceOut` in
  `ForceStructs.hpp`, so both sets can appear in one translation unit.
- `potential.hpp` :: `rgpot::PotentialHandle`, a move-only owner of one
  `rgpot_potential_t`.
  `from_impl` wraps any object with a `forceImpl(const ForceInput&, ForceOut*)`
  method through a template trampoline.
  `from_callback` takes a C function pointer, its user data and an optional
  destructor.
  `calculate` runs the potential and returns a `CalcResult`.
- `rpc_client.hpp` :: `rgpot::RpcClient`, a move-only owner of one `rgpot_rpc_client_t`,
  with the same `calculate` interface.
  The constructor does not connect; the Rust client opens a connection for each
  `calculate`.
  The header compiles only when `RGPOT_HAS_RPC` is defined.
- `rgpot.hpp` :: includes the headers above, and
  `rpc_client.hpp` when `RGPOT_HAS_RPC` is defined.

#### C++ potentials (`CppCore/rgpot/`)

Each potential derives from the CRTP template `rgpot::Potential<Derived>` and
implements `forceImpl(const ForceInput&, ForceOut*) const`.
`rgpot::PotentialHandle::from_impl` turns such an object into an `rgpot_potential_t`
without copying it.
The caller keeps the object alive for as long as the handle exists.

A potential with a finite range can also declare how a domain-decomposed host
should evaluate it.
`locality()` returns the cutoff, whether the neighbour list is full, how many
cutoffs of ghost atoms the host must hold, and how many density values to
exchange.
`densityStage` and `forceStage` then run on the host's own atoms plus those
ghosts.
A pair potential and a density potential (EAM, Sutton-Chen) use a half list and
one cutoff of ghosts: the density exchange carries what the neighbours of the
neighbours contribute.
`StillingerWeberSi` and `TersoffSiC` declare a full list and a ghost reach of
twice the cutoff, because a three-body term on a local atom needs each
neighbour's list.
The host sums the energy of its owned atoms and adds the forces written on
ghosts back to their owners.
The kernels do not decompose the cell themselves.
Neighbour lists stay in the stack libraries (linkcell, vesin, minimage) and in
`nlist::build`.

### Error handling

Errors change form at each boundary, because each language has its own
convention and unwinding across a C boundary is not allowed.

1. *Inside Rust*, code uses `Result`, and the `extern "C"` entry points turn
   errors into status codes.
2. *Across the C ABI*, a call returns a status code, or NULL for a constructor,
   and stores a message that `rgpot_last_error` returns.
   No exception or panic crosses the boundary.
   `rgpot_potential_calculate`, `rgpot_potential_hvp`,
   `rgpot_potential_hvp_centre`, `rgpot_potential_set_taylor_jet`, `rgpot_potential_taylor_jet`,
   `rgpot_ch5_2008_taylor_jet`, `rgpot_rpc_calculate` and
   `rgpot_rpc_server_start` run their body inside `catch_unwind`, which turns a
   panic into `RGPOT_INTERNAL_ERROR` with the panic message.
   These are the entry points that run a user callback or the RPC runtime.
3. *Inside C++*, the wrappers pass every status to
   `rgpot::detail::check_status`, which throws `rgpot::Error`.
   In the other direction, the
   `from_impl` trampoline catches any exception from `forceImpl` and returns `RGPOT_INTERNAL_ERROR`.
   It does not store the exception text, so the message that `rgpot_last_error`
   returns afterwards does not describe that failure.

### Backend capability handshake

A backend can be incompatible with the host in ways a single call does not show:
another protocol, another schema, or another eindir bridge layout.
The capability handshake refuses such a backend before any work is dispatched.
It runs where a backend meets the host: when a library is loaded through the
potential profile, when an RPC client connects to a server, and when a callback
handle receives its peer's capabilities.
The fields it compares, the rules for unset metadata, and the error each path
returns are in [Architecture reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/architecture.html),
under Capability handshake.

---

# The RPC Model

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/rpc-model.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/rpc-model.html

A client needs an energy and forces for one geometry, from one backend.
The backends do not share a configuration language.
Lennard-Jones takes a few scalars, CPMD takes a deck, and a metatomic model
takes a file path.
The wire therefore splits the conversation into three carriers, all defined in
one Cap'n Proto schema (`Potentials.capnp`).

### Three carriers

- `ForceInput` carries the geometry for one evaluation: positions, atomic
  numbers, the cell, and the unit strings the caller wants back.
  It can also carry a per-step charge and spin multiplicity and a request for a
  neighbour list.
- `PotentialResult` carries the energy and the flat force array for that
  evaluation.
  Optional fields, such as a Hessian, a dipole or a stress tensor, are filled in
  by the backends that compute them.
- `PotentialConfig` carries backend setup, and only setup.
  A client sends it once through `configure`, then sends a new `ForceInput` for
  every geometry.

Geometry stays off the configuration message.
A change of method does not reshape the coordinates, and a change of coordinates
does not repeat the method.
The `libcpmdc` C ABI that `CPMDPot` loads uses the same split: a session takes
the Cap'n Proto `CPMDParams` once, and each step takes a `ForceInput`.

### One schema, many languages

The schema is the contract.
The C++ server, the Python tests, and the Rust core all read it.
The Rust crate vendors a copy so a crates.io build still has the schema.
The monorepo copy under `CppCore/rgpot/rpc/` is the fallback the build script
checks.
The Cap'n Proto wire format does not depend on the language, so a Rust client
can call a C++ server, and the reverse.

### Units

Inside the library the units are fixed: energy in eV, length in Angstrom, force
in eV/Angstrom.
A caller that works in Hartree or Bohr names those units on `ForceInput`.
`potserv` converts the inbound positions and cell to Angstrom before the
potential runs, and converts the energy and forces to the caller's units on the
way out.
The potentials themselves compute in eV and Angstrom.

### Engines stay outside the server

`NWChemPot` and `CPMDPot` are frontends.
They build whenever the RPC stack is on
(`-Dwith_rpc=true` or `-Dwith_rpc_client_only=true`).
At run time they `dlopen` `libnwchemc` and `libcpmdc` from the split projects.
rgpot does not embed those engines.
A test build can point the same frontends at the in-tree fake engines.
Method options travel in the matching `PotentialConfig` arm (`nwchem` or
`cpmd`).
The geometry still arrives on `ForceInput`.

### eOn over rgpot

eOn uses the same split, in process and over RPC; the setup is in
[eOn Potentials Over rgpot](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/eon-rgpot.html).

- `configure(PotentialConfig)` once per method (NWChemParams / CPMDParams).
- `calculate(ForceInput)` per geometry (positions, atomic numbers, cell, units).
- Units on the wire (`lengthUnit` / `energyUnit`); eOn's `RgpotPot` converts
Hartree → eV and Hartree/bohr → eV/Å at the boundary.
- Engines are optional at build time: CI uses fake `libnwchemc` / `libcpmdc`;
production sets `NWCHEMC_LIBRARY` / `CPMDC_LIBRARY` (or aliases).

### Where the layers sit

The schema is what a client sees.
Under it, a Rust core owns the public types and the C ABI, and hand-written C++
wrappers give move-only handles over that ABI.
The C++ potentials stay in `CppCore` and register back into the core through a
callback.
One `potserv` process hosts one backend, named by the selector it starts with.
A selector behind a meson option, such as `Skala`, only exists in a `potserv`
built with that option.

[../../orgmode/explanation/figures/rpc_layers.svg](../../orgmode/explanation/figures/rpc_layers.svg)

The layers, the error conventions and the capability check are explained in
[Architecture](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/architecture.html).
The status codes and entry points are listed in
[C ABI of rgpot-core](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/c_abi.html), and the directory layout
in [Architecture reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/architecture.html).

---

# ABI stamps

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/abi-stamps.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/abi-stamps.html

rgpot carries compatibility numbers that are separate from its package version.
This page explains what each one covers and why it exists.
The functions and macros are listed in the
[C ABI reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/c_abi.html).
The steps to change each number are in
[Bump the ABI numbers](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/contributing/developer/abi-bump.html).

### The C ABI stamp

`rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h` carries two identities.
The package version (`RGPOT_VERSION` and its parts) follows the crate.
The ABI stamp (`RGPOT_ABI_VERSION_MAJOR`, `RGPOT_ABI_VERSION_MINOR`,
`RGPOT_ABI_LAYOUT_REVISION`) follows the layout of the exported structs and the
signatures of the exported functions.
A release that changes no exported symbol leaves the stamp where it is.

A consumer that loads the library at run time compares the stamp it compiled
against with `rgpot_abi_stamp()` of the library it loaded, or passes its own
stamp to `rgpot_abi_compatible()`.
The major number moves for a change an old caller cannot survive.
The minor number moves for an addition that leaves every old call valid, so a
library with a higher minor still serves an older caller.
The layout revision moves when an exported struct changes size, field order or
field type; callers and libraries with different layout revisions never match.

The stamp is not an ELF soversion.
In a Meson build with `with_rust_core` and the fast pair list off, `librgpot`
links the static archive `librgpot_core.a` and keeps only the archive members it
references.
The umbrella references none of that archive's C ABI, so the shared library
exports 73 `rgpot_*` symbols, all of them from the rest of the umbrella.
Two of those are `rgpot_builtin_muller_brown_new` and
`rgpot_muller_brown_config_default`, and 21 are the `rgpot_md_session_*` entry
points.
One more is `rgpot_lammpc_potential`.
The archive still holds the whole C ABI, and the Meson test `abi_core_symbols`
checks the archive rather than the shared library.
With the fast pair list on, the archive is `librgpot_bundle.a`.
It defines 54 `rgpot_*` symbols: the same C ABI, plus the four fast-list entry
points.
Every one of those names is public
(`scripts/abi_core_baseline.txt` and `scripts/abi_baseline_fast.txt`).
The umbrella links this archive with `--whole-archive`, or with
`-force_load` on Darwin, so those 54 symbols are exported as well and the shared library exports 127 `rgpot_*`
symbols.
A process that also loads a separate rgpot-core shared library then has two
definitions of those names.
The Meson test `rgpot_so_exports` pins both export counts.

### Scope

The C ABI stamp covers `rgpot.h` only.
Other interfaces carry their own numbers:

- the C++ classes that cross the `librgpot` boundary: the layout stamp below and
  the soversion `kCxxSoversion`;
- the eindir objective that `rgpot_potential_t` embeds:
  `rgpot_eindir_abi_stamp()` and `rgpot_eindir_abi_compatible()`, which report
  and check the stamp of the `eindir-core` compiled into the library;
- the neighbour query: `RGPOT_NLIST_ABI` in `CppCore/rgpot/nlist/rgpot_nlist.h`;
- the plugin interface: `RGPOT_PLUGIN_API_VERSION` in `include/rgpot/plugin.h`;
- the engine libraries:
  `RGPOT_ENGINE_ABI_VERSION` in `CppCore/rgpot/engine_c_abi.h`;
- `librgpot_mpi`: `RGPOT_MPI_ABI_VERSION` in
  `CppCore/rgpot/calculator_mpi_abi.h`, with its own soversion 3.

The engine plugins (for example
`libclassical_engine.so` and `libmopac_engine.so`) are built without a soversion
and opened by those unversioned names.
Each plugin reports `RgpotEngineAbiStamp`
(`RGPOT_ENGINE_ABI_VERSION`, `RGPOT_ENGINE_ABI_MINOR`,
`RGPOT_ENGINE_ABI_LAYOUT_REVISION`) through `rgpot_engine_abi_stamp`, or is
minor 0, layout 1 when that symbol is absent.
Because engine minor bumps add optional exports that the host probes with
`dlsym` (such as
`rgpot_engine_last_components` and `rgpot_engine_component_name` in minor 5,
`rgpot_engine_unload_policy` in minor 7, and `rgpot_engine_taylor_jet` in minor
11), the Rust loader's `RgpotEngineAbiStamp::serves(host)` accepts any plugin
with the same major and layout revision whose minor is at most the host's
(`ENGINE_ABI_MINOR`), resolving optional exports only when present and reporting
them as absent otherwise, while rejecting plugins whose minor is newer than the
host's.
Minor 8 adds the negative code `RGPOT_ENGINE_ERR_LOCK` (-2) for a failed engine
or handle lock.
It exports no new symbol and changes no struct, so the layout revision stays at 1.
The meson test `engine_abi_stamps` opens every standalone engine plugin of the
build, `libpotlibc_engine` included when `with_potlibc` is enabled, and compares
its stamp with the header.

### The C++ layout stamp

The header-only C++ classes are a second boundary.
A consumer compiles `Potential`, the force structures and the pair potentials
from the headers, and the library supplies their out-of-line members.
A library built from another revision of those headers, or with another value of
`RGPOT_HAS_CACHE`, has the same C stamp and still runs with the wrong member
offsets or the wrong vtable.
`CppCore/rgpot/abi/CxxLayout.hpp` stamps that boundary.
It needs neither `rgpot.h` nor the Rust core.

The stamp is the C struct `rgpot_cxx_layout_stamp_t` with `revision`
(`kCxxLayoutRevision`), `features` and a 64-bit `hash`.
`rgpot::abi::header_stamp()` is a `constexpr` of the header: the stamp the
consumer compiled against.
`rgpot::abi::library_stamp()` calls the exported `rgpot_cxx_layout_stamp()`: the
stamp of the loaded library.
`rgpot::abi::layout_compatible()` is true when revision, feature bits and hash are equal; `rgpot_cxx_layout_compatible()`
is the same check for a caller that holds only the C struct, and returns 0 for
NULL.

```cpp
#include <cstdio>

#include "rgpot/abi/CxxLayout.hpp"

int main() {
  if (!rgpot::abi::layout_compatible()) {
    std::fprintf(stderr, "librgpot was built from other C++ layouts\n");
    return 1;
  }
  return 0;
}
```

The hash folds `kCxxLayoutRevision`, the feature bits, the sizes of `void *` and
`std::size_t`, and the `sizeof` and `alignof` of each covered type.
For the plain structures it also folds the `offsetof` of each field, and for the
enumerations the values consumers switch on.
For the polymorphic classes it folds the number of virtual functions, because a
vtable change does not show in `sizeof`.
Feature bit 0 is `RGPOT_HAS_CACHE`, which adds the virtual `setCache` to
`PotentialBase`.

Covered types:

- `ForceInput`, `ForceOut`, `ForceBatch`, `PotCaps`, `CalculatorGroup`
- `LJConfig`, `LJClusterConfig`, `MorseConfig`, `ZBLConfig`, `SuttonChenConfig`,
  `D2Config`, `D2CpmdConfig`, `D4Config`, `MullerBrownConfig`
- `Reentrancy` and `PotType`
- `PotentialBase`, `Potential<Derived>` (through one probe instantiation),
  `LJPot`, `LJClusterPot`, `MorsePot`, `ZBLPot`, `SuttonChenPot`, `SumPot`,
  `lr::SumPot`, `D2Pot`, `D2CpmdPot`, `MullerBrownPot`, `nlist::Builder`,
  `nlist::Walk`
- with the cache: `cache::EvalCounts` and `cache::PotentialCache`

The classes of the optional backends are not covered (xtb, tblite, dftd3, dftd4,
ExprPot, XcKernel, Metatomic, UMA, NWChem, CPMD, MOPAC, Skala, the Fortran
potentials).
`D4Config` is covered, because it sits in a header of its own that does not
include dftd4; `D4Pot` is not.
Their headers and features differ between builds, so a stamp over them would
refuse libraries that agree on everything a consumer uses.

The hash depends on the platform: operating system, architecture, standard
library and data model form the tag `kCxxPlatformTag`.
`kCxxSoversionTable` records the no-cache hash of each platform that CI builds,
and `CppCore/rgpot/abi/cxx_soversion_ledger.txt` records a platform-independent
fingerprint of the stamp's inputs for each soversion.
`kCxxSoversion` is the ELF soversion of `librgpot`, read by Meson and CMake; it
is not the hash.

### History

| Release | `rgpot.h` stamp | `librgpot` soversion |
|---------|-----------------|----------------------|
| 3.5.0   | 1, 0, 1         | 3                    |
| 3.5.1   | 1, 0, 1         | 4                    |
| 3.6.0   | 1, 1, 1         | 6                    |
| 3.7.0   | 1, 2, 1         | 6                    |
| 3.8.0   | 1, 10, 1        | 9                    |

3.6.0 raised the minor for `rgpot_eindir_abi_compatible`; a caller built against
minor 0 still matches it.
3.7.0 raised the minor to 2 for the Hessian-vector functions.
They are additions, and their state lives behind the
`fused_cache` pointer of the handle, so `rgpot_potential_t` keeps its layout and
the layout revision stays at 1.
A 3.7 library still serves a caller built against minor 0 or 1.
A caller built against minor 2 is refused by a 3.6 library.
3.8.0 raises the minor to 3 for
`RGPOT_SCC_NOT_CONVERGED`, `rgpot_set_last_error` and the fused-cache settings
and error kind.
They are additions, no old call changes, and the layout revision stays at 1.
It also raises the minor to 4 for the Taylor jet functions and the statuses
`RGPOT_NO_JET` (6), `RGPOT_JET_BRANCH` (7) and `RGPOT_JET_DOMAIN` (8).
The jet callback also lives behind `fused_cache`, so the layout revision stays
at 1.
It also raises the minor to 5 for the engine and RPC Hessian-vector interfaces.
It raises the minor to 6 for `rgpot_potential_new_eam_table` and the four
`RGPOT_EAM_TABLE_*` format codes.
They are additions that take no new struct, so the layout revision stays at 1.
It raises the minor to 8 for `rgpot_potential_hessian`,
`rgpot_potential_hvp_resolved`, the analytic and dual-number Hessian callbacks, the dual-number Hessian-vector callback, `rgpot_potential_derivative_caps`
and
`rgpot_potential_derivative_counts`, the new structs `rgpot_derivative_caps_t`
and `rgpot_derivative_counts_t`, the enum `rgpot_hessian_scheme_t`, and the
values `RGPOT_HVP_AD` (4) and `RGPOT_HVP_EXACT` (5).
The product takes its scheme as an `int`, so a library of minor 6 refuses the
new values with `RGPOT_INVALID_PARAMETER` instead of misreading them.
No existing struct changes and the new state lives behind `fused_cache`, so the
layout revision stays at 1.
It raises the minor to 9 for the `rgpot_mdi_server_start` export.
The symbol is present in every build, so a library that reports minor 9 has it.
A build without the Cargo feature `mdi` answers the call with `RGPOT_RPC_ERROR`
and a message that names the feature.
It raises the minor to 10 for `rgpot_rpc_client_select_orbitals`, which is an
additive export behind `RGPOT_HAS_RPC`, so the layout revision stays at 1.
The molecular-dynamics session entry points and their optional neighbour-query
and neighbour-setter slots are symbols of the C++ library, not of the core C
ABI, so this minor stays at 10.
The session operation table carries its byte size and the new slots follow
`destroy`, so an older table still loads.
The C++ layout revision stays 2 and `kCxxSoversion` stays 9, because the session
vtable is not one of the covered potential types.

The ledger notes that soversion 3 was the 3.4.0 layout, which 3.5.0 reused after
the layout changed, and that 4 is the 3.5.0 layout, shipped from 3.5.1.
Soversion 5 recorded `LJPot` and `MorsePot` gaining a neighbour list and a
cached pair table.
Soversion 6 drops the copied half-list from LJ and Morse and gives ZBL and the
open Lennard-Jones cluster a neighbour list.
A program linked against soversion 4 does not load `librgpot.so.6`.

Soversion 9 stamps `SumPot`, `lr::SumPot` and `PotType::LrSum`.
`lr::SumPot` derives from `SumPot` now, so it grows from 56 to 120 bytes and its
old constructor and `add` symbols leave the library.
It also stamps `D2Config`, `D2Pot` and `PotType::D2`.
It also stamps `D2CpmdConfig`, `D2CpmdPot` and `PotType::D2Cpmd`.
`D4Config` gains `periodic` in the padding after `atm`, so it keeps its size and
only the field offsets show it.
`D2CpmdConfig` gains `symmetry`.
`PotCaps` gains `analyticHessian`, `adHessian` and `adHvp`, and `PotentialBase`
gains the virtuals `hessianImpl`, `hessianAdImpl` and `hessianVectorAdImpl`
after `hessianVectorImpl`.
The vtable changed, so `kCxxLayoutRevision` is 2.
It also stamps `MullerBrownConfig` and `MullerBrownPot`.
The zero-argument `MullerBrownPot` constructor remains its own symbol.
It also stamps `nlist::Builder` and `nlist::Walk`, which move their state behind
a pointer so each is one pointer wide.
It also adds a process-unique generation id on `Neighbours`.
A program linked against soversion 8 does not load `librgpot.so.9`.

# Hessian-vector products

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/hessian-vector.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/hessian-vector.html

This page explains why a potential handle computes Hessian-vector products
itself and keeps a cached centre, how it reports the scheme that answered, and
when a caller should ask for the dense Hessian instead.
The functions, their arguments and their errors are in the
[C ABI reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/c_abi.html).

A minimum-mode search (Lanczos, dimer) applies the Hessian `H` of the energy to
many directions `v` at one geometry.
With only a force callback each product is a difference of two force
evaluations, and one of them is the centre the search has not moved from.
A potential handle answers `H v` itself and keeps the forces of that centre.

### Cost and error

| Scheme               | Force calls per product        | Error                 |
|----------------------|--------------------------------|-----------------------|
| `RGPOT_HVP_FORWARD`  | 1, plus 1 for each new centre  | `O(h)`                |
| `RGPOT_HVP_CENTRAL`  | 2                              | `O(h^2)`              |
| `RGPOT_HVP_ANALYTIC` | 0                              | the callback's        |
| `RGPOT_HVP_AD`       | 0                              | rounding of the duals |

The forward scheme reuses the forces of the centre.
`k= forward products at one centre therefore cost =k + 1` force calls instead of
`2k`.
No finite difference makes one call per product at `O(h^2)`.
The forward error is `(h/2) T(u, u) |v|`, with `T` the third derivative of the
energy and `u = v / |v|`, and cancelling it takes the second evaluation that the
central scheme makes.
A search that needs second-order products at no extra force call registers an
analytic product.

`h= is the displacement along the unit direction =u`, in the units of the
positions, and the difference is scaled back by `|v|`.
The forward product is therefore positively homogeneous in `v` but not odd: the
`O(h)` term keeps its sign when `v` changes sign.

### The cached centre

The handle keys its centre on the bits of the positions, the atomic numbers and
the cell.
Comparing bits rather than values keeps the forces computed at `0.0` from being
served at `-0.0`.
Moving one coordinate by one ulp, changing a species or changing the cell is a
new centre.

The centre is the entry of the handle's fused cache, which the eindir energy and
gradient share, and it stores the outcome of the force call: the forces, or the
failure.
A centre that failed, because the callback returned an error status or an SCC
did not converge, is returned again for the same bits and settings without
another call.
A failed energy is not retried at the same bits: a warm-start retry needs a
changed setting, installed with `rgpot_potential_set_fused_settings`, or a call
to `rgpot_potential_hvp_invalidate`.

The key does not see the state behind the callback's `user_data`, apart from the
settings the potential reports.
A potential whose other parameters change at a fixed geometry calls
`rgpot_potential_hvp_invalidate` to drop the centre.

A search usually needs the centre forces as well as the products.
`rgpot_potential_hvp_centre` returns them from the same cache, so the force call
that the search makes at the centre is the one the forward products reuse.
The handle holds one centre, which matches a search that stays at one geometry
for many products and then moves.

### Analytic and dual-number products

A potential that knows its Hessian registers the product with
`rgpot_potential_set_hvp_callback`.
`RGPOT_HVP_AUTO` then uses it and makes no force call.
A potential whose energy kernel is written over a scalar template can instead
evaluate it on second-order dual numbers, which carry a value, a first and a
second directional derivative through every operation.
The second derivative along `v` is exact up to the rounding of that arithmetic,
with no step to choose;
`rgpot_potential_set_ad_hvp_callback` registers that product, and `RGPOT_HVP_AD`
asks for it.
`RGPOT_HVP_AUTO` never takes the dual-number product, so a potential that has
both keeps its closed form.

In C++, `rgpot::PotentialHandle::from_impl` registers each hook a potential
advertises in `caps()`: `hessianVectorImpl` for `analyticHvp`,
`hessianVectorAdImpl` for `adHvp`, `hessianImpl` for `analyticHessian` and
`hessianAdImpl` for `adHessian`.
`MorsePot`, `LJPot` and the Fortran `CuH2Pot` have an analytic product,
`MorsePot` and `LJPot` an analytic Hessian, and `LJPot` both dual-number hooks.

### The scheme that ran

`RGPOT_HVP_AUTO` takes the analytic product when there is one and forward
differences otherwise.
That fallback is kept, but it is never silent:
`rgpot_potential_hvp_resolved` writes the scheme that ran, `rgpot::PotentialHandle::hvp` and the Python `hvp_resolved`
return it, and `rgpot_potential_derivative_counts` counts every product under
it.
A caller for which a finite-difference stand-in would be a wrong answer, rather
than a slower one, asks for `RGPOT_HVP_EXACT`: the analytic product, else the
dual-number one, and `RGPOT_INVALID_PARAMETER` before any call when the handle
has neither.
`RGPOT_HVP_ANALYTIC` and `RGPOT_HVP_AD` are refused the same way when their
callback is missing.

### Dense Hessians

`rgpot_potential_hessian` writes the `3N` square Hessian, row-major.
It has no automatic scheme, so a dense Hessian is differenced only when the
caller names `RGPOT_HESSIAN_CENTRAL`.

| Scheme                   | Force calls  | Error                 |
|--------------------------|--------------|-----------------------|
| `RGPOT_HESSIAN_ANALYTIC` | 0            | the callback's        |
| `RGPOT_HESSIAN_AD`       | 0            | rounding of the duals |
| `RGPOT_HESSIAN_EXACT`    | 0            | that of the one taken |
| `RGPOT_HESSIAN_CENTRAL`  | `6N`         | `O(h^2)`              |

The central scheme displaces each coordinate by `+-h`, so column `c` is
`(F(x - h e_c) - F(x + h e_c)) / (2 h)`, and it writes the symmetric part of the
differenced matrix.
Its calls bypass the cached centre and are counted apart from those of the
products.
`RGPOT_HESSIAN_EXACT` reports the scheme it took, like `RGPOT_HVP_EXACT`.

### Capabilities

`rgpot_potential_derivative_caps` reports, in one plain struct, which schemes a
handle has for the product and for the Hessian: an analytic and a dual-number
flag for each, set by the registered callbacks, and a finite-difference flag
that every handle sets.
It also gives the force calls the differenced schemes cost: one per forward
product at the cached centre, two per central product and six per atom for a
central Hessian.
The analytic and dual-number schemes make no force call, and their cost is that
of the potential, which the struct does not guess.

### Products or a dense Hessian

A caller that needs `k` products at one geometry pays
`t_hvp` for the first, which includes the centre or any other preparation, and `t_apply`
for each further one, against `t_dense` for the Hessian, after which every
product is a matrix-vector multiply.
The products are cheaper while `k < k*`, with
\[
k^* = \frac{t_\mathrm{dense} - t_\mathrm{hvp}}{t_\mathrm{apply}} + 1 .
\]
With finite differences only, counted in force calls,
`t_dense = 6N`, `t_hvp = 2` and `t_apply = 1`, so `k* = 6N - 1`: a dimer
rotation or a Lanczos search of a few tens of products stays on the products for
any but the smallest system.
With analytic or dual-number hooks the three times are those of the potential;
for a pair potential the product and the Hessian both cost a pass over the
pairs, so `k*` is small and a search that needs more than a handful of products
at one geometry, or the full spectrum, should take the Hessian.
The rule counts each multiply by the stored Hessian as free.
That multiply reads all `(3N)^2` entries, which for a pair potential with every
pair in range costs a large fraction of a product, so a caller near `k*` should
time it too: with
`t_mv` per multiply, the products are cheaper while `k < (t_dense - t_hvp + t_apply) / (t_apply - t_mv)`,
and always when `t_mv >` t_apply=.
No scheme is chosen for the caller: the handle reports the schemes and their
force-call costs, and the caller applies the rule to its own timings.

### Without the Rust core

`CppCore/rgpot/HessianVector.hpp` gives the same schemes, default step, centre
cache and counters to C++ potentials used without the Rust core.
`rgpot::HessianVectorCache::apply` returns the scheme that ran,
`rgpot::HessianVectorCache::hessian` takes an explicit `rgpot::HessianScheme`,
and `rgpot::derivativeCaps` reads the `caps()` bits of a potential.
The Python module uses it.

---

# Fortran kernels: port, not wrap

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/fortran-kernels.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/fortran-kernels.html

This page explains why the Fortran potentials in `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/` are
ports rather than wrappers, and why their force loops gather.
The rules a port follows, the module layout, the cell convention and the tests
are in
[Fortran potentials: porting rules](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/fortran_potentials.html).

### Why a port and not a wrapper

The Fortran kernels descend from eOn, as the header of each `rgpot_<pot>.f90`
module records.
The CuH2 routines that this repository carried before the port show what the
legacy code looked like.
They kept state across calls in COMMON blocks, used `goto`, and capped a system
at 500 atoms through a fixed array size.
Wrapping such code in `bind(c)` keeps all of that and adds a language boundary
on top.

Each kernel is instead rewritten as a Fortran 2018 module, and the Meson build
compiles it with `-std=f2018`.
The physics expressions carry over term by term; everything around them is
replaced.
Saved state is limited to the `_capi` module, which holds the neighbour table
and the parameter set.
`rgpot::fortranpots` gives each C++ instance its own workspace, so instances can
run on separate threads at once (`Reentrancy::PerInstance`).

### Gather, not scatter

A pair loop written as a scatter updates both atoms of a pair
(`f(i) += g; f(j) -= g`), so the atom loop carries dependencies and cannot be
parallelised as written.
Every port restates the sum as a *gather*: with a full neighbour list, atom `i`
accumulates the entire force acting on it and writes only `f(:, i)`.
Iterations then touch disjoint memory.
The Stillinger-Weber driver in `rgpot_sw.f90` is one example:

```fortran
do concurrent(i=1:natoms)
   call atom_contribution(par, table, i, e_atom(i), forces(:, i), &
                          w_atom(:, i))
end do

if (present(strain)) strain = sum(w_atom, dim=2)

energy = sum(e_atom)
```

Energy reduces through a per-atom array rather than a shared accumulator,
because `do concurrent` gained reduction clauses only in Fortran 2023.

#### What `do concurrent` buys

Compilers are not obliged to run these iterations in parallel. gfortran treats
the construct as an assertion about independence unless it is given
`-ftree-parallelize-loops`, and the Meson build does not pass that flag.
The assertion is still worth having.
It licenses vectorisation, and it documents the dependency structure for the
next reader.
It also enforces the discipline that made the port correct: every procedure the
loop body calls must be `pure`, and every write must land in memory no other
iteration touches.
Turning the construct into real parallelism later is then a compiler flag rather
than a rewrite.

#### Cost

A gather evaluates each pair term twice, once from each end.
For three-body terms an atom also walks its neighbours' neighbour lists to
collect the triplets in which it is an end atom rather than the centre.
In exchange the atom loop has no dependencies, and each iteration works on one
atom's neighbourhood.

#### When the gather does not close

Some terms have a force that cannot be attributed to one atom without
recomputing a large intermediate, such as a bond-order derivative that depends
on a full coordination sum.
EDIP closes its gather because the environment dependence collapses to one
scalar per atom, the coordination `Z_i` and `dE_i/dZ_i`, computed in a first
`do concurrent` pass.
Where restating a term would cost more than it saves, the design keeps a
structured scatter loop for that phase, runs the independent phases under
`do concurrent`, and names the dependency in a comment.
A scatter inside `do concurrent` breaks the independence the construct asserts,
so it is never placed there.

# GROMACS QM/MM through the CP2K interface

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/gromacs-qmmm.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/gromacs-qmmm.html

The steps are in
[GROMACS QM/MM drop-in](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/engine-gromacs-qmmm.html), and the input
keys and limits are in
[GROMACS QM/MM drop-in reference](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/gromacs_dropin.html).

GROMACS 2024 to 2026 has three in-process hooks for an external potential.

- QM/MM through libcp2k (`-DGMX_CP2K=ON`) calls a fixed C API, in double
  precision, every step, and passes the topology elements through a PDB file.
  Its energy is a GROMACS energy term.
  It carries no virial: `QMMMForceProvider` adds its forces without a virial
  contribution.
- NNPot (2025 and later) loads only TorchScript `.pt` models, converts positions
  to single precision, and also carries no virial.
- PLUMED applies a bias.
  It carries the virial but keeps the energy out of the GROMACS energy terms.

MiMiC serves CPMD only, and GROMACS has no i-PI client.
The libcp2k API is the one that takes any potential without a model format and
reports the energy as GROMACS' own, so the drop-in implements it.

# SIMD paths and dispatch

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/simd.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/simd.html

This page explains how the C++ core picks instruction sets at run time, and why
every path returns the same bits.

### Dispatch through Highway

`CppCore/rgpot/simd/` holds Lennard-Jones, Morse and analytical EAM pair kernels
and an orthorhombic minimum-image fold that pick an instruction set at run time
when the build links Google Highway (`-Dwith_highway`, `libhwy` 1.2 or newer).
The entry points are `rgpot::simd::lj_force`, `morse_force`,
`eam_force` and `fold_orthorhombic`; `lj_force_span` always runs the scalar
kernel.
`RGPOT_SIMD` names a target, and `rgpot::simd::chosen_target_name()` reports the
one in use.
`RGPOT_SIMD=scalar` selects the portable kernel.
A known target that the CPU cannot run, or an unknown name, leaves the choice to
Highway, and on x86-64 that choice is at least SSE2.
A build without Highway keeps the scalar kernels.

In this revision the potential classes do not call these entry points.
`LJPot`, `LJClusterPot`, `MorsePot` and `EAMPot` evaluate their pair terms
inside the shared neighbour walk in `CppCore/rgpot/nlist/`, with scalar code.
`CppCore/tests/IsaDispatchTest.cc` calls the dispatched kernels directly.

The ISA audit measures every function against x86-64 on x86-64 files and armv8-a
on aarch64 files.
A function that is not dispatched must stay inside that baseline.

### Fused multiply-add

A product-sum uses a hardware fused multiply-add only on a target that has the
instruction.
`rgpot::simd::detail::fma_hw_active()` decides that once per process.
On x86-64 under GCC or Clang it reads CPUID (FMA, OSXSAVE and AVX) and XCR0.
On glibc 2.33 and newer it also follows the glibc hwcaps mask, so
`GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.cpu.hwcaps=-FMA` turns the hardware path off.
`RGPOT_FMA=software` turns it off as well.
On other targets and compilers it returns false.

When the probe is true, callers enter `target("fma")` bodies that run the
instruction.
In the Highway kernels, the scalar kernel and the SSE2 and SSE4 kernels on
x86-64 do this, because those targets have no FMA of their own.
In the neighbour layer, `MinimumImage::fold` calls `fold_hardware`.
When the probe is false, `simd::exact_fma` computes the product with a Dekker
product and a round-to-odd sum, and falls back to `std::fma` for inputs outside
the range where that sequence is exact.
The hardware instruction and the software sequence return the same bits, so the
probe decides speed only.

`target("fma")` compiles the whole body with AVX encodings, including ordinary
moves, because the fused instruction is VEX-encoded.
`rgpot/isa-allow.toml` therefore names those bodies for `avx` and `fma`:
`accept_row_hw`, `eam_fma`, `eam_hw`, `exact_fma_hw`,
`exp2_hw`, `exp_hw_n`, `lj_hw`, `lj_hw_span`, `morse8_hw`, `morse_hw`,
`r2_hw` and `r2_hw_n`, and `fold_hardware` for `avx`, `fma` and `sse3`.
The baseline caller does not contain those instructions.

`target("fma")` is an x86 target name, so
`fold_hardware` carries it only on x86-64 under GCC or Clang, the one configuration where `fma_hw_active()`
can be true.
On aarch64 and under MSVC the fold always runs the portable path through
`simd::mul_add`, which returns the same bits.
`simd::mul_add` emits the instruction directly when the translation unit is
compiled with FMA, as on aarch64.

### The exponential

`MorsePot` computes `exp` with `simd::exp_fixed`, a fixed sequence of IEEE
additions, multiplications and bit operations.
That sequence has no table and no fused multiply-add, so the last bit does not
depend on the C library or the instruction set.
`exp_fixed_n` applies it to an array.
On x86-64 Linux, outside ThreadSanitizer builds, `exp_fixed_n` is a
`target_clones` function with baseline, AVX2 and AVX-512F clones.
The loader picks one clone from the CPU check in libgcc or compiler-rt, and each
clone returns the bits of the baseline one.

### Contraction

A compiler with contraction on may fuse a product and a sum into one fused
multiply-add, and the result can then move by an ulp.
Clang contracts by default and emits the instruction where the target has it,
which is every macOS arm64 build.
The Meson build compiles the core library, the `exp` and FMA helpers and
`MinimumImage.cpp` with `-ffp-contract=off`, or `/fp:precise` under MSVC, as
per-target arguments.
Meson places those after `cpp_args`, so a global `-ffp-contract=fast` does not
reach them.

### The Lennard-Jones cluster walk

`LJClusterPot` takes `lj_cluster_direct`, an all-pairs walk, when the
bounding-box diagonal of the cluster is within the cutoff.
It does so only without a switching function, outside stream mode and when no
per-atom output is requested.
Any other cluster goes through the shared neighbour walk.
On x86-64 `lj_cluster_direct` calls
`lj_avx2` only after `__builtin_cpu_supports("avx2")`; on aarch64 it calls `lj_neon`.
`lj_avx2`, `eval_quad` and `acc_quad` are `target("avx2")`.
The ISA audit proves from the linked library that they are reached only behind
that check, so the allowlist does not name them.
The same builtin's initializer, `__cpu_indicator_init`, is named for `xsave`
because it reads XCR0 with `xgetbv`.
`cpuid_fma_usable`, which `fma_hw_active()` calls, is named for `xsave` for the
same reason.

### The ISA gate

The static gate in `ci/isa-audit` stops a later `-march=native`, a stray
`-mavx2`, or an intrinsic outside a dispatched function from shipping.
An instruction above the baseline is allowed only when `rgpot/isa-allow.toml`
names the function and the feature, names the vendored file that contains a
third-party dispatcher, or the audit proves the function is a dispatched clone.
A dispatched clone is a local function entered only behind a libgcc CPU check or
from a `target_clones` resolver, for the features that check covers.
On a macOS arm64 slice, `lse` and `rcpc` are baseline: they are the platform
atomics, and no other CPU can load that binary.
The gate does not execute the instructions.
`IsaDispatchTest` lists the targets it exercised, and a target this machine
cannot run is absent from that list.
See `ci/isa-audit/README.org` for the allowlist format and for the reusable
workflow other repositories call by commit SHA.

### Same bits on every path

The design asks every path to return the same bits, whatever the instruction set
and the thread count.
The pair kernels in `rgpot::simd` reduce through eight partial sums combined in
a fixed order, the order of ndarray 0.17 `unrolled_dot`
(`CppCore/rgpot/simd/reduce.hpp`).
`tests/python/test_invariance.py` compares a SHA-256 of the raw float64 results
across Python and OpenMP thread counts.

`ci/isa-audit/README.org` names the cluster-pair layout of Páll and Hess,
Computer Physics Communications 184, 2641 (2013),
doi:10.1016/j.cpc.2013.06.003, as the layout the dispatched kernels follow. It leaves per-microarchitecture runs to real nodes through the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI), Dröge et al., Software: Practice and Experience 53, 176 (2023), doi:10.1002/spe.3075,
because the gate does not emulate.

---

# Thread safety

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/thread-safety.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/thread-safety.html

This page explains what the Python extension allows when several threads call it
at once.

The extension is built free-threaded when the interpreter is
(`Py_GIL_DISABLED`).
On that interpreter `import rgpot` and `import rgpot.ase` leave the GIL
disabled.
Sub-interpreters are not supported: nanobind declares the module unable to run
in more than one interpreter.

### One instance per calling thread

A potential object is not a session.
`LJClusterPot`, `MorsePot`, `ExprPot`, `D3Pot`, `D4Pot` and the Fortran
potentials wrap their kernel in a holder that keeps one kernel instance per
calling thread.
The constructing thread uses the instance built with the object.
Another thread's first call creates an instance for that thread, under a
per-object mutex that is taken only while the interpreter is detached.
Two threads may therefore call one such object at the same time.
A kernel that declares `Reentrancy::SharedInstance`, such as `LJPot`, keeps the
single instance for every thread instead.

The per-thread map keeps one instance for every caller thread id other than the
constructing thread.
A finished thread does not drop its entry.
The map grows with the number of distinct threads that have called the object,
and it is freed when the object is destroyed.
Fortran potentials keep one neighbour table per instance, so each thread also
has its own table.

`evaluate_batch` does not use that map.
It builds one instance per worker, and no more workers than there are
configurations.

The saved parameter block in each Fortran
`_capi` module is written once, from C++ `std::call_once`, and is read-only
after that.
The handle-free entry's legacy workspace is not used by Python.

Other classes, such as `StillingerWeberSi` and `TersoffSiC`, hold one kernel
instance and no per-thread map.
Do not call one such object from two threads at once.
One call may still use the library's own thread team.
`energyAndGradientBatch` spreads a configuration when that potential would not
open a team for it, across the threads `OMP_NUM_THREADS` requests, each on its
own neighbour list.

### What is not reentrant (F5)

The ASE `calculate` path writes `self.atoms` and `self.results`.
Do not call `get_potential_energy` or `get_forces` on one calculator from two
threads.
The pure protocol `__rg_evaluate__` does not mutate the calculator, and that
protocol is the reentrant path.
`calculate_many` builds one batch and does not mutate the input atoms.
An exception raised on the protocol path is the caller's; the calculator object
is left as it was.

### One connection at a time (F3)

The RPC calculator's connection is the exception to the per-thread workspace
rule.
It is in use by one thread at a time.
A second thread gets `RuntimeError` naming the calculator type, rather than
sharing the socket.

# Neighbour list design

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/neighbour-lists.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/neighbour-lists.html

This page says why the neighbour layers behave the way they do.
The tutorial is [Neighbour lists](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/tutorials/neighbour-list.html).
The C ABIs are in [Neighbour-list C ABI](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/nlist_abi.html) and
[Fast pair list C ABI](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/fast_nlist.html).

### All pairs below three bins

`rgpot_fast_pairs` answers with all pairs when a periodic axis is narrower than
three cutoffs; the table is in
[Fast pair list C ABI](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/fast_nlist.html).
Each linkcell bin is checked against itself and its 26 neighbours.
Below three bins on an axis, the bins on either side are the same bin.
Allen and Tildesley stop their cell-list codes below three bins,
/Computer Simulation of Liquids/, 2nd ed. (2017), section 5.3.2.

### Threads

Distinct `Table`, `Builder` and `Walk` objects may be used from different
threads.
One object is not shared.
`build` may start an OpenMP team when `OMP_NUM_THREADS` is set and the system
has at least 8192 atoms.
A smaller system stays on the calling thread.
The work is split into `OMP_NUM_THREADS` slices, and the threads the runtime
starts take all of them.
The stored index of the classical potentials is built on the same slices.
From 8192 atoms, with more than one thread requested, a stencil of at least 4096
candidates and more candidates than atoms is joined in atom order.
A shorter list stays on the calling thread.
Each row is sorted by partner index, so the list matches one thread.
An open axis whose nominal grid does not fit in reported memory is binned on the
atom span.
A periodic axis keeps the cell length.
A build inside another OpenMP region may get one thread and returns the same
list.
There is no mutable global.
`rgpot_nlist_strerror` returns a literal.

The thread rules of the potentials are in
[Thread safety](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/thread-safety.html).

### Where the design came from

`docs/neighbour_api_design.md` records the survey of vesin, JAX-MD, LAMMPS,
ArborX, matscipy, ASE, freud and torch-nl, and the passes that produced this
surface.
`docs/neighbour_layer.md` records the kernel the classical potentials still use.

---

# Calculator groups over MPI

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/mpi.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/mpi.html

This page explains how the MPI-parallel engines share one force call across the
ranks of a calculator.
The build option, the loader of `librgpot_mpi` and its C ABI are in
[MPI](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/mpi.html).
The C++ functions (`bindCalculators`, `shareFromCalculator`, `calculatorAgree`
and the rest) are in [C++ API](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/cpp_api.html).

### Collective force calls

`CPMDPot` and `CP2KPot` report `PotCaps::groupCollective`: every rank of a
calculator enters each of its force calls together, and the call's collectives
stay on that calculator's communicator.
A host may hand calculators an uneven batch, with some calculators making no
call at all, and then share results with `shareFromCalculator`.
A failure inside the call prints on every rank of the failing calculator, then
`MPI_Abort` on `MPI_COMM_WORLD` ends the run.

### The result cache

For such a potential the result cache decides hit or miss jointly, through
`calculatorAgree` (a logical AND over the calculator's communicator).
A geometry that any rank of the calculator misses is computed on all of its
ranks, so no rank waits alone inside the call.
Give each rank its own cache directory: RocksDB locks a directory to one
process.

### CP2K's communicator

`CP2KPot::bindCalculators` splits the world as `CPMDPot::bindCalculators` does
and hands the shim the calculator communicator through
`cp2kc_adopt_calculator_comm`.
It returns -1 without splitting when the shim does not load or lacks that
symbol.
Each force environment runs on that communicator, or on `MPI_COMM_WORLD` when no
split exists.
When MPI is initialised before the first session, the shim calls
`cp2k_init_without_mpi`; otherwise `cp2k_init` starts MPI and the shim finalises
CP2K and MPI at exit.

The CP2K tutorial is
[Evaluate diamond silicon with CP2K](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/tutorials/cp2k.html).

---

# Local and global minimization

Source: docs/orgmode/explanation/global-optimization.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/global-optimization.html

This page says when to reach for a local or a global minimizer, and why the
plots of the minimization tutorial need their own environment.
The tutorial is
[Find the Ground State of an EON Structure](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/tutorials/molecular-global-optimization.html).
How an rgpot potential becomes an `anneal` objective is in
[rgpot potentials as eindir objectives](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/eindir-anneal.html).

### Which minimizer for which job

- Local L-BFGS / FIRE / conjugate gradient (ASE or eOn): refine a structure
inside the basin you want -- an eOn saddle endpoint, a perturbed crystal, an MD
snapshot.
- `AnnealRunner`: search for the minimum when the basin is unknown -- cluster
  ground
states, conformer search, potential-parameter fitting.

Chain them: an `anneal` search to locate the basin, then a local polish.

Saddle searches on this stack are the enhanced climbing-image method of Goswami,
Gunde and Jónsson, Front.
Chem. 14, 1807063 (2026),
doi:10.3389/fchem.2026.1807063. How those searches are scored is Goswami, AIP Adv. 15, 085210 (2025), doi:10.1063/5.0283639.
eOn, which runs the bands, is the record doi:10.5281/zenodo.18529495.

### The eonviz environment

The ``eonviz`` environment is separate from the C++ build env: ``eon`` pins
``fmt>=12`` (clashing with rgpot's C++ ``fmt<12``), so it carries no default
feature and pulls ``eon``, ``ira``, ``jax``, and the released ``chemparseplot``
and ``rgpycrumbs`` (both pinned to 1.11.0, which carry the embedded-metadata
trajectory parser and ``plt-min``).
``pixi run check-eonviz-pins`` fails when ``chemparseplot`` or ``rgpycrumbs`` is
not an exact ``==`` pin, when a git dependency does not name a full commit, or
when an ``eonviz`` dependency has a path or url source or no version specifier.

# Architecture reference

Source: docs/orgmode/reference/architecture.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/architecture.html

The layers and why they exist are in
[Architecture](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/architecture.html).
To add a potential, see
[Add a potential to the Rust core](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/howto/add-potential.html).

### Potentials

Each potential lives under `CppCore/rgpot/<Name>/`.
`PotType` in `CppCore/rgpot/pot_types.hpp` names every type the library knows.
`CppCore/meson.build` decides which directories a build compiles.

#### Built-in Potentials

These are compiled in every build of the main library (every build except
`-Dwith_rpc_client_only=true`).

- `LJPot` (`PotType::LJ`) :: Standard 12-6 Lennard-Jones.
Configurable via `LJConfig` (`u0`, `cutoff`, `psi`, `switch_width`).
- `LJClusterPot` (`PotType::LJCluster`) :: 12-6 Lennard-Jones on free
  boundaries, for isolated clusters; the cell is ignored.
Configurable via `LJClusterConfig` (`u0`, `cutoff`, `psi`, `switch_width`).
- `MorsePot` (`PotType::Morse`) :: Pairwise Morse with a shifted cutoff,
  platinum parameters by default.
Configurable via `MorseConfig` (`De`, `a=, =re`, `cutoff`, `switch_width`).

With `switch_width` at 0 (the default) these three shift each pair energy to
zero at the cutoff, and the force jumps there.
A positive
`switch_width` multiplies the unshifted pair energy by the quintic switch $S(t) = 1 - 10t^3 + 15t^4 - 6t^5$, $t = (r - r_c +
w)/w$ clamped to $[0, 1]$, so energy, force and curvature reach zero at the
cutoff (`PairSwitch.hpp`).
The constructors throw `std::invalid_argument` unless $0 < w \le r_c$.
`scripts/validation/pair_kernels.py` checks the kernels and the switch with sympy, and `scripts/validation/quintic_switch.sollya`
bounds the switch's first-order binary64 rounding error at $28u$ for $S$ and
$12u$ for $S'$ ($u = 2^{-53}$).

These pair potentials take their pairs from the shared neighbour layer,
`nlist::updateCells` in `CppCore/rgpot/nlist/Neighbours.hpp`.
`nlist::Mode` selects a stored Verlet list (`Stored`), a walk over the cells
that stores no pair list (`Stream`), or `Auto`, which stores when the candidate
index array fits in the memory the OS reports as available.
The Verlet skin is 1 Angstrom for `LJPot` and one fifth of the cutoff for
`LJClusterPot` and `MorsePot`; a stream uses no skin.
A stored list is reused while every atom has moved by at most half the skin and
the cell, the atom count and the settings are unchanged.
That is the rule of `nlist::Neighbours`.
`nlist::Builder`, behind the C ABI and the long-range `DualList`, also keeps its
table across a cell change whose image moves fit in the skin.

- `StillingerWeberSi` (`PotType::SWSi1985`) :: Stillinger-Weber silicon with the
  1985 parameters (Phys. Rev. B 31, 5262).
Epsilon is 3.4723e-12 erg, 2.16723920 eV, the value of equation (2.9).
`energyAndGradient` evaluates one configuration, and `energyAndGradientBatch`
several configurations that share a cell and a species list.
A batch is spread across the threads `OMP_NUM_THREADS` requests when no
configuration would make `StillingerWeberSi` open a team.
`teamSize` uses `StillingerWeberSi::kTeamMinAtoms` and
`StillingerWeberSi::kTeamFrom`.
Each configuration is evaluated whole, on a neighbour list of its own.
See [Stillinger-Weber silicon (1985)](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/sw_si.html).
`locality` declares a full neighbour list and a ghost reach of twice the cutoff,
so a domain-decomposed host can evaluate owned atoms and reverse sum the forces
on the copies.
The Fortran `SWPot` kernel (`PotType::SWSi`) uses eOn's rescaled epsilon,
2.16826 × 1.06767385 = 2.3149945 eV.
The ratio of that epsilon to the published value is 1.068176741337.
The factor 1.06767385 is copied from eOn's `SWFortran.f90` and is untraced.
- `TersoffSiC` (`PotType::TersoffSi`) :: 1989 Tersoff kernel for silicon,
  carbon, and silicon carbide (Phys. Rev. B 39, 5566, and the 1990 erratum).
It accepts atomic numbers 14 and 6 and throws `std::invalid_argument` for any
other.
`TersoffSiC` always evaluates the 1989 form, including an all-silicon cell.
The Fortran `TersoffPot`, which also reports `PotType::TersoffSi` and is the
engine name `tersoff`, sends all-silicon calls and a null species pointer to its
Fortran gather and every other call to `TersoffSiC`.
`setHeldSkin` keeps one Verlet list for `forceImpl`.
`locality` declares a full neighbour list and a ghost reach of twice the silicon
outer cutoff, so a domain-decomposed host can evaluate owned atoms and reverse
sum the forces on the copies.
`energyAndGradientBatch` spreads configurations the same way as
`StillingerWeberSi`, from `TersoffSiC::kTeamMinAtoms` and
`TersoffSiC::kTeamFrom`.
See [Tersoff silicon-carbon (1989)](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/tersoff_sic.html).
- `ZBLPot` (`PotType::ZBL`) :: Screened nuclear repulsion
  (Ziegler-Biersack-Littmark) with the LAMMPS switching function, on free
  boundaries.
Configurable via `ZBLConfig` (`cut_inner`, `cut_global`); the constructor throws
`std::invalid_argument` unless `0 < cut_inner < cut_global`.
- `SuttonChenPot` (`PotType::SuttonChen`) :: Sutton-Chen 10-8 many-body
  potential, in reduced units by default.
See [Sutton-Chen potential](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/sutton_chen.html).
- `EMTPot` (`PotType::EMT`, `CppCore/rgpot/EMT/`) :: Effective medium theory
  from Asap.
`EMTConfig::rasmussen` selects the Rasmussen parameters; the default is the Asap
copper set.
- `EAMPot` (`PotType::EAMCell`, `CppCore/rgpot/EAM/`) :: Cell-list embedded-atom
  potential.
- `MOPACPot` (`PotType::MOPAC`, `CppCore/rgpot/MOPACPot/`) :: Frontend that
  loads the split `mopacc` engine at run time.
- `ORCAPot` (`PotType::ORCA`, `CppCore/rgpot/ORCAPot/`, `-Dwith_orca=true`) ::
  Frontend that runs the `orca` executable as a child process for each energy
  and gradient and reads the `.engrad` file.
  See `docs/orgmode/howto/orca.org`.
- `LammpsPot`, `GromacsPot`, `OpenMMPot` :: Shifted Lennard-Jones in
  `CppCore/rgpot/ExternalPot/`, as `PotType::Lammps`, `PotType::Gromacs` and `PotType::OpenMM`; `GromacsPot` and `OpenMMPot` store nm and kJ/mol
  parameters.
- Gupta and reduced cluster pairs :: C kernels
  (`rgpot_gupta`, `rgpot_cluster_lj`, `rgpot_cambridge_morse`, `rgpot_lj_gradient`, `rgpot_morse_gradient`) in `CppCore/rgpot/Gupta/`, `CppCore/rgpot/Morse/cambridge_morse.h`
  and `CppCore/rgpot/ReducedPair/`, not `Potential` classes.
  [Gupta and reduced cluster kernels](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/gupta.html) records the parameters
  and the checked energies.

#### Fortran Potentials

`-Dwith_fortran_pots` (a feature option, `auto` by default) builds the Fortran
2018 kernels under `CppCore/rgpot/fortran/` when a Fortran compiler is found.
The C++ classes are in `FortranPots.hpp`, in the namespace `rgpot::fortranpots`:

| Class        | `PotType`   | Potential                                                     |
|--------------|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| `CuH2Pot`    | `CuH2`      | Copper-hydrogen EAM                                           |
| `EDIPPot`    | `EDIP`      | Environment-dependent interatomic potential for silicon       |
| `LenoskyPot` | `LenoskySi` | Cubic-spline MEAM silicon force-matched to LDA                |
| `EAMAlPot`   | `EAMAl`     | EAM aluminium                                                 |
| `FeHePot`    | `FeHe`      | Fe-He embedded atom                                           |
| `WaterHPot`  | `WaterH`    | Andersson's `potH-H2O` surface for one H among water molecules |
| `SWPot`      | `SWSi`      | Stillinger-Weber silicon with eOn's epsilon                   |
| `TersoffPot` | `TersoffSi` | Tersoff silicon: Fortran gather, or `TersoffSiC` for other Z |

The porting rules are in
[Fortran potentials: porting rules](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/fortran_potentials.html).

#### Feature-gated Potentials

- `IPIPot` (`-Dwith_ipi`) :: Listens for one i-PI driver on a UNIX or TCP
  socket.
`-Dwith_ipi` is a feature option, `auto` by default; it needs POSIX sockets and
is off on Windows.
The driver connects and returns energy, forces and a virial in atomic units.
rgpot converts those to eV, eV/Angstrom and the Cauchy stress.
The same option builds `IPIDriver` and `rgpot-ipi-driver`, the client side.
They answer an i-PI server with any `engines/pot_spec.hpp` potential.
See `docs/orgmode/howto/ipi.org`.

- `EAMTablePot` (`-Dwith_eam_table=true`) :: EAM and Finnis-Sinclair potentials
  read from LAMMPS tables.
See [Tabulated EAM and Finnis-Sinclair potentials](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/eam_table.html).

- `MEAMPot` (`PotType::MEAM`, `CppCore/rgpot/MEAM/`) :: Modified embedded-atom
  method with first and second neighbours, driven by LAMMPS meam library and
  parameter files.
See [Modified embedded-atom method](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/meam.html).

- `TIP4PPot`, `SPCEPot`, `TIP4PPtPot` (`-Dwith_water=true`) :: Flexible TIP4P,
  SPC/E and SPC/E on platinum, in `CppCore/rgpot/Water/`.

- `XTBPot` (`-Dwith_xtb=true`) :: GFN tight-binding methods (GFN-FF, GFN0-xTB,
  GFN1-xTB, GFN2-xTB) via the [xtb](https://github.com/grimme-lab/xtb) C API.
`XTBConfig` holds the method, accuracy, electronic temperature (K), iteration
limit, charge, unpaired electrons (`uhf`) and `warm_move`, the largest atom move
in Angstrom that still reuses the previous wavefunction.
Do not share one instance across threads; create separate instances for parallel
use.
The `XTBDlopen` frontend, which loads xtb at run time, is built in every build
of the main library.

- `TBLitePot` (`-Dwith_tblite=true`) :: GFN tight-binding methods (GFN1, GFN2,
  IPEA1) via the [tblite](https://github.com/tblite/tblite) C API.
`TBLiteConfig` has the fields of `XTBConfig` except `warm_move`.

- `D3Pot` (`-Dwith_dftd3=true`) :: Grimme DFT-D3 via the
  [s-dftd3](https://github.com/dftd3/simple-dftd3) ISO C API.
`D3Config` selects BJ or zero damping, the functional key for the C6 parameters
(default `pbe`), and an `atm` flag for the Axilrod-Teller-Muto E(3) term
(default on).
It is an in-process `Potential` summand: it takes a `ForceInput` and returns
energy and forces.
It is not an XC kernel term.
The schema has `PotentialConfig.d3` @12, and its `D3Params` mirror `D3Config`.
Nothing applies that arm yet.
The `potserv` `D3` backend runs the default `D3Config`.
`configure()` refuses the `d3` arm by name on every `potserv` backend.

- `D4Pot` (`-Dwith_dftd4=true`) :: Grimme DFT-D4 via the
  [dftd4](https://github.com/dftd4/dftd4) ISO C API.
`D4Config` selects the functional key (default `pbe`), the total charge
forwarded to `dftd4_new_structure` (default 0), an `atm` flag for the many-body
(`mdb`) term (default on), and a `periodic` flag (default off) that passes the
box to dftd4 as a 3D lattice and returns the stress from its virial.
It is an in-process `Potential` summand: it takes a `ForceInput` and returns
energy and forces, plus stress when `periodic` is set.
It is not an XC kernel term.
The schema has `PotentialConfig.d4` @13, and its `D4Params` (with `periodic`
from `d4-periodic.diff`) mirror `D4Config`.
On a build with dftd4, `potserv <port> D4` starts with the default `D4Config`
and `configure()` applies `PotentialConfig.d4` to rebuild its `D4Pot` (refusing
unknown functionals with dftd4's message and other arms by name); `d4` is also a
builtin term in `PotentialConfig.composite` and `libcomposite_engine`.
Other `potserv` backends refuse the `d4` arm by name.

- `ExprPot` (`-Dwith_expr=true`) :: Energy as an expression over named child
  potentials.
The vendored OpenMM Lepton (`third_party/lepton`) compiles the expression.
The constructor takes an energy string and a list of names with
`unique_ptr<PotentialBase>` children.
It throws `std::invalid_argument` for an empty expression, no terms, a null
term, a name that is not a Lepton identifier (including an empty name), a
duplicate name, a name the expression does not use, an identifier in the
expression that is not a term, and an expression Lepton cannot parse or
differentiate.
Forces are the chain rule, with the weights from
`ParsedExpression::differentiate(name)`.
`D3Pot` and `D4Pot` can be children.
`PotentialConfig.expr` is in the schema as `ExprParams` (with `PotSpec`
children), but `potserv` does not apply it; `configure` refuses it by name.
`PotentialHandle::from_impl` and `rgpot_potential_new_eindir` wrap one `ExprPot`
as one eindir objective.

- `lr::CoulombPot`, `lr::DispersionPot`, `lr::NlhPot`, `lr::SumPot` :: Ewald,
  smooth PME or damped shifted force electrostatics, dispersion, SO3LR NLH
  repulsion, and a sum of summands, built with `-Dwith_long_range=true` from
  `CppCore/rgpot/LongRange/`.
`-Dwith_cuda=true` compiles the CUDA path with nvcc.

- `XcKernel` (`-Dwith_xckernel=true`) :: In-process libxckernel XC kernel.
It is not a `Potential`.

- `MetatomicPot` (`-Dwith_metatomic=true`) :: Pre-trained ML atomistic models
  via [metatomic](https://github.com/metatensor/metatomic) and PyTorch, loaded
  as TorchScript (`.pt`) in C++ with no Python at evaluation time.
Neighbour lists come from [vesin](https://github.com/Luthaf/vesin); the source
builds against vesin 0.3 and 0.5 or newer (`vesin_compat.hpp`).
PyTorch autograd gives the forces.
With vesin 0.5 or newer, pass CPU as `VesinDevice{VesinCPU, 0}`
(`struct { VesinDeviceKind type; int device_id; }`); `VesinCPU` alone is only
the kind enum.
An internal mutex serialises the Torch session, so a shared instance is safe
across threads.
`MetatomicConfig` sets the model path, device, dtype override, length unit,
consistency checks, and `torch_determinism`.
`TorchDeterminismPolicy::Fast` (default) does not touch process-global LibTorch
state.
`Strict` calls `apply_torch_determinism_policy`, which sets
`at::globalContext()` deterministic algorithms (no warn-only fallback), turns
off the flash, memory-efficient and cuDNN scaled-dot-product attention backends
and keeps the math backend, disables TF32 for cuBLAS and cuDNN, forces
deterministic cuDNN algorithms with benchmarking off, and fills uninitialized
memory deterministically.
Those flags are process-global: they affect every Torch user in the process, and
`Fast` does not restore a previous `Strict` setting.
CUDA host processes that need bit-stable cuBLAS must also export
`CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG`:4096:8= (or `:16:8`) before the first cuBLAS call;
that is process environment, not `at::globalContext()`.
On the RPC server pass `Metatomic:/path/to/model.pt`, optionally followed by
`:<device>`.
Build with the `metatomicbld` pixi environment (linux-64; it pulls torch,
metatomic-torch, and vesin `>=0.6.0,<0.7` from PyPI).
CI job `potentials_metatomic` is in `.github/workflows/ci-orchestrator.yml`.
`UmaPot` (`PotType::Uma`) builds with it when `with_python` is false.

The pip product (`rgpot` on PyPI) does not link Metatomic into the Python
extension.
It `dlopen=s a Metatomic engine library from =rgpot/lib/torch-X.Y/` that matches
the installed torch major.
Bundled engines start at torch 2.7.
See:

The remaining feature-gated potentials need the RPC stack
(`-Dwith_rpc=true` or `-Dwith_rpc_client_only=true`), because they read
parameters from the generated Cap'n Proto schema:

- `NWChemPot` (`PotType::NWChem`) and `CPMDPot` (`PotType::CPMD`) :: Frontends
  that load the split `nwchemc` and `cpmdc` engines at run time.
- `CP2KPot` (`PotType::CP2K`, `-Dwith_cp2k`, needs `with_rpc`) :: CP2K Quickstep
  through the `libcp2kc_rgpot` shim against libcp2k.
- `SkalaPot` (`PotType::Skala`, `-Dwith_skala=true`, needs `with_rpc`) :: Skala
  XC on NWChem DFT through `libnwchemc`.

Each feature-gated potential has its own Meson option.
External libraries are found with Meson `dependency()` (pkg-config or CMake),
some with a wrap fallback.

#### NWChemPot (`rgpot/NWChemPot/`)

`NWChemPot.cc` serializes `NWChemParams` and `dlopen=s =libnwchemc` (via
`DynLib.hpp`).
It is built whenever the RPC stack is on.
The consumer C ABI in `nwchem_c_abi.h` uses
`nwchemc_*` symbols and flat Cap'n Proto message bytes; `nwchem_c_abi_stub.c` is
a no-op ABI for tests. rgpot is a pure consumer: the engine implementation
(NWChem embed and Fortran) lives in the split
[nwchemc](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/nwchemc) project, not in rgpot.
The schema has `NWChemParams`, `PotentialConfig`, and `configure @1` on
`Potential`; start the server with `potserv <port> NWChem`.
Engine lookup tries `NWChemParams.enginePath`, then
`NWCHEMC_LIBRARY`, `RGPOT_NWCHEMC_ENGINE`, `RGPOT_NWCHEM_ENGINE`, and the
default library names.
A non-empty `nwchemRoot` is exported as `NWCHEM_TOP`.
Details: `CppCore/rgpot/NWChemPot/README.md`.

#### Units (`rgpot/units.hpp`)

rgpot's internal unit system is energy in eV, length in Angstrom, and force in
eV/Angstrom.

- Compile-time constants (CODATA 2018): `BOHR_TO_ANGSTROM`, `HARTREE_TO_EV`,
  `HARTREE_BOHR_TO_EV_ANGSTROM`,
  `NEG_GRAD_TO_FORCE`, `HARTREE_PER_BOHR3_TO_EV_PER_ANGSTROM3`, `KB_HARTREE` and
  `KB_EV`.
Backends that work in bohr and hartree, such as `XTBPot` and `TBLitePot`, use
them.
- Runtime expression parser (`unit_conversion_factor(from, to)`): a
  Shunting-Yard parser with SI dimensional analysis, derived from
  metatomic-torch (PR #173).
It accepts compound expressions such as `"kJ/mol"`, `"eV/angstrom^3"`, or
`"(eV*u)^(1/2)"`.
It throws `std::invalid_argument` on a dimension mismatch or an unknown token.
`validate_unit(quantity, unit)` checks a unit against a known quantity
(`length`, `energy`, `force`, `pressure`, `momentum`, `mass`, `velocity`,
`charge`).
- RPC negotiation: Cap'n Proto `ForceInput` carries `lengthUnit` and
  `energyUnit` (default `"angstrom"` and `"eV"`).
The server converts inbound positions and box into Angstrom before `forceImpl`,
then converts energy and forces into the caller's units on the response.

### Capability handshake

Why the handshake exists is in
[Architecture](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/architecture.html).

The current RPC identity is family `rgpot.potentials`, major 1, minor 2.
`ForceInput.neighbors` (@9) is present from minor 0 (v3.6.0).
Minor 2 adds only `hasOrbitalKey` and `orbitalKey`.
Clients that set an orbital-key field require a server that advertises minor 2.
They report the required and advertised minors instead of sending a request that
an older server would silently interpret without those fields.
That floor is the minor in which the fields appeared.
A later bump of the current minor does not raise it.
Requests that use only the pre-minor-2 `ForceInput` fields remain valid against
a minor-1 server.

A backend loaded through the potential profile reports a `Capabilities` message
through `<prefix>_capabilities_result`.
Before a session is created, `ProfileSession::load` (Rust) and
`rgpot::abi::checked_load` (C++) compare it with the host's expectation.
They refuse the backend with a message that names the first mismatch.
`ProfileSession::load` returns a `ProfileError`, and
`checked_load` throws `std::runtime_error`.

| Field                                                    | Refused when                                                                        |
|----------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `protocolFamily`                                         | the family differs from `rgpot.potentials`                                          |
| `protocolMajor`, `protocolMinor`                         | the major differs, or the minor is below the host's required minor                  |
| `schemaId`                                               | the identity differs from that of `Potentials.capnp`                                |
| `bridgeAbiMajor/Minor`, `bridgeLayout`, `bridgeFeatures` | another eindir ABI major, a newer minor, another layout, or feature bits not known  |
| `dlpackMajor/Minor`                                      | another DLPack major or a newer minor                                               |
| `operations`                                             | energy or forces is not served                                                      |

Metadata that a backend leaves unset is not a declaration and is not checked, so
backends that predate the fields keep loading.
An empty family skips the three protocol checks, an empty schema identity skips
the schema check, and a zero bridge or DLPack major skips that group.
`buildVersion` and `buildRevision` report the version and source revision of the
build that produced the message.
For a message that `rgpot-core` fills in, `rgpot_source_revision` returns the
same revision through the C ABI.

The same check guards RPC.
The rgpot servers implement `Potential.getCapabilities`, in `potserv` and in
`rgpot_rpc_server_start`.
The Rust client (`RpcClient`) asks for the capabilities on every connection, and
it opens one connection for each `calculate`.
The C bridge (`pot_calculate`) asks once, before its first `calculate`.
Both refuse a server whose capabilities are incompatible.
A server that does not implement the call answers UNIMPLEMENTED.
The client refuses it with a message that names `Potential.getCapabilities` and
asks for an rgpot release whose `Potentials.capnp` carries it.

A callback handle (`rgpot_potential_t`) takes the peer's message through
`rgpot_potential_set_peer_capabilities`, which exists only when the crate is
built with the `schema` feature.
When the peer is incompatible, `rgpot_potential_calculate`,
`eindir_objective_eval` and `eindir_objective_grad` fail before the callback
runs.
`rgpot_potential_calculate` returns `RGPOT_INVALID_PARAMETER`, and
`rgpot_last_error` holds `peer refused: <first mismatch>`.
A handle that never receives a message keeps the plain callback contract.
The C entry point is listed in [C ABI of rgpot-core](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/c_abi.html).

| Path                                   | Purpose                                                                                              |
|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `rgpot-core/Cargo.toml`                | Rust crate configuration.                                                                            |
