# Gupta and reduced cluster kernels

Source: docs/orgmode/reference/gupta.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/gupta.html

These are C kernels, not `rgpot::Potential` classes.
Lengths are the caller's length unit.
The Gupta arrays and the Sutton-Chen metal rows use Angstrom and eV.
The reduced Lennard-Jones and Morse kernels use the caller's reduced units,
where the well depth is 1.
The Morse equilibrium distance is 1.
The Lennard-Jones `sigma` is 1, so its pair energy is zero at `r = 1` and its
minimum is at `r = 2^(1/6)`, which is 1.1225 to four decimals.
None of them reads a cell.
A pair at zero separation is not differentiable.

### Gupta

`rgpot_gupta` (`CppCore/rgpot/Gupta/gupta.h`) is the second-moment form of
Gupta, Phys.
Rev. B 23, 6265 (1981),
doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.23.6265, with the parameters of Cleri and Rosato, Phys. Rev. B 48, 22 (1993), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.48.22.
There is no cutoff.
Every pair `i < j` is visited once, in that order.

For one ordered species pair the repulsive term added to the energy is
`2 A exp(-p (r/r0 - 1))` and each atom's density gains `xi^2 exp(-2 q (r/r0 - 1))`.
The energy is that repulsion minus the sum of the square roots of the densities.
`A=, =xi`, `p=, =q` and `r0` are row-major tables of `n_species * n_species`
entries.
`slot[i]` selects the species of atom `i`.

Cabrera-Trujillo et al., arXiv:1007.4009, Table 1, reprint the Cleri-Rosato gold
column: `p = 10.229`, `q = 4.036`, `A = 0.2061` eV, `xi = 1.790` eV and
`sqrt(2) r0 = 4.079` Angstrom, so `r0` is 2.884 Angstrom to three decimals.
Reference value: a dimer at `r = r0` has energy `2 A - 2 xi`.
For that gold row the value is -3.1678 eV.
`GuptaTest` checks the same identity to 1e-12.

The gradient is zeroed before any pair is visited.
The first pair with `r2 <= 0.0` sets the energy to positive infinity and
returns, so later pairs are not visited and the gradient stays zero.
Atoms 0 and 1 coincident and atom 2 `NaN` therefore give positive infinity and a
zero gradient.
For `n < 2` the pair loop does not run, so the energy is 0 and the gradient is
zero.
The call keeps thread local scratch and never shrinks it.
The density buffer is grown first.
It holds one double per atom (8 bytes) and is grown only when its capacity is
below `n`.
`realloc` asks for `n` doubles, and a successful return stores the new pointer
and that capacity before the pair buffer is considered.
A null return leaves the density buffer and its capacity unchanged and does not
allocate the pair buffer.
The pair buffer holds 6 doubles per pair (48 bytes).
The pair count is `n (n - 1) / 2` when `n >= 2`, and 0 otherwise, so `n < 2`
does not grow the pair buffer.
It is grown only when its capacity is below 6 doubles for each pair.
A null return from that `realloc` leaves the pair buffer and its capacity
unchanged.
The density buffer keeps the capacity already stored, which is the new one when
this call grew it.
On either failure the energy is positive infinity, the 3 n gradient entries are
zero, and the call returns before it reads a coordinate.
There is no status code, so the caller sees the same outputs as for a coincident
pair and cannot tell the two apart from the outputs alone.
A later call that fits the stored capacities still works, and a later call whose
pair capacity is still short tries that allocation again.
`NaN` is not `<= 0.0`.
A pair that is reached with a `NaN` coordinate is evaluated, and the energy and
the gradient become `NaN`.
Null pointers, `slot` entries at or above `n_species`, and `r0` entries that are
not positive are not checked.

### Reduced Lennard-Jones and Morse

`rgpot_cluster_lj` and `rgpot_cambridge_morse` (`cambridge_morse.h`) sum every
pair.
`rgpot_lj_gradient` and `rgpot_morse_gradient` (`ReducedPair.hpp`) are the same
physics with a cutoff: a cutoff of 0 or less keeps every pair, and a positive
cutoff keeps pairs with `r` strictly below it.
The gradient is `dE/dx`, not a force.

The 12-6 form is Lennard-Jones, Proc.
R. Soc.
A 106, 463 (1924),
doi:10.1098/rspa.1924.0082. Wales and Doye, J. Phys. Chem. A 101, 5111 (1997), doi:10.1021/jp970984n,
use it in reduced units for the cluster tables.
Reference value: `epsilon = 1`, `sigma = 1` and a dimer at `r = 2^(1/6)` have
energy -1.
`ReducedPairTest` checks that call to 1e-15, and the gradient to 1e-12.
The same dimer at `r = 1` has energy 0 and an `x` gradient of 24 and -24, which
that test checks exactly.
`rgpot_cluster_lj` checks the minimum to 1e-12.

The Morse form is Morse, Phys.
Rev. 34, 57 (1929), doi:10.1103/PhysRev.34.57.
The reduced cluster term is `epsilon exp(rho (1 - r/re)) (exp(...) - 2)`.
Reference value: `epsilon = 1`, `re = 1` and a dimer at `r = re` have energy -1
and a zero gradient.
`ReducedPairTest` checks both exactly, and `rgpot_cambridge_morse` checks the
unit dimer bit for bit.

`rgpot_tip4p_sites` is the rigid four-site water of Jorgensen et al., J. Chem.
Phys. 79, 926 (1983), doi:10.1063/1.445869, with the caller's oxygen
coefficients.
Sites are molecule-major O, H, H, M. Reference value: two oxygens 2 Angstrom
apart, charges off, `c6 = 2552.24` and `c12 = 2.5104e6`, give
`c12/r^12 - c6/r^6 = 573.011875` in the caller's energy unit.
`ReducedPairTest` requires a bit match to that expression.

### C entry points

#### `rgpot_gupta`

```c
void rgpot_gupta(const double *x, size_t n, const unsigned char *slot,
                 size_t n_species, const double *a, const double *xi,
                 const double *p, const double *q, const double *r0,
                 double *energy, double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: `x= (3 n coordinates), =n`, `slot` (one species index per atom),
  `n_species`, and the species-pair tables `a=, =xi`, `p=, =q` and `r0`.
- Units :: `x= and =r0` in the caller's length; `a= and =xi` in the caller's
  energy; `p= and =q` dimensionless.
  The gradient is energy per length.
- Outputs :: one energy and 3 n gradient components.
  For `n < 2` the pair loop does not run, so the energy is 0 and the gradient is
  zero.
- Errors :: no status code and no error message.
  The density scratch is grown first, and only when its capacity is below `n`.
  `realloc` asks for `n` doubles.
  On success the new pointer and capacity are stored before the pair buffer is
  considered.
  A null return leaves both buffers and both capacities unchanged, and the pair
  buffer is not allocated.
  The pair scratch is grown next, only when its capacity is below 6 doubles for
  each pair.
  The pair count is `n (n - 1) / 2` when `n >= 2`, and 0 otherwise.
  A null return from that `realloc` leaves the pair buffer and its capacity
  unchanged and keeps the density capacity already stored, including a growth
  from this call.
  Either failure sets `*energy` to `+INFINITY`, zeroes the 3 n entries of
  `gradient` and returns before a coordinate is read.
  The outputs are those of a coincident pair.
  The first pair with `r2 <= 0.0` sets `*energy` to `+INFINITY` and returns.
  The gradient is left at the zeros written before that pair, and later pairs
  are not visited.
  Atoms 0 and 1 coincident and atom 2 `NaN` therefore give `+INFINITY` and a
  zero gradient.
  `NaN` is not `<= 0.0`, so a pair that is reached with a `NaN` coordinate is
  evaluated and the energy and the gradient become `NaN`.
  Null pointers, `slot` entries at or above `n_species`, and `r0` entries that
  are not positive are not checked.

#### `rgpot_cambridge_morse`

```c
void rgpot_cambridge_morse(const double *x, size_t n, double rho,
                           double *energy, double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: `x= (3 n coordinates), =n` and `rho`.
  The well depth and the equilibrium distance are 1.
- Units :: `x= in the reduced length; =rho` is the dimensionless range; energy
  in the reduced energy; gradient in energy per length.
- Outputs :: one energy and 3 n gradient components.
  For `n < 2` the pair loop does not run, so the energy is 0 and the gradient is
  zero.
  For `n >= 2` a coincident pair (`r2 <= 0.0`) is skipped, and a `NaN`
  coordinate does not satisfy `r2 <= 0.0`, so `NaN` propagates into the energy
  and the gradient.
- Errors :: no status code and no error message.
  Null pointers are not checked.

#### `rgpot_cluster_lj`

```c
void rgpot_cluster_lj(const double *x, size_t n, double *energy,
                      double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: `x= (3 n coordinates) and =n`.
  `epsilon` and `sigma` are 1, and there is no cutoff.
- Units :: reduced length and reduced energy.
  The gradient is energy per length.
- Outputs :: one energy and 3 n gradient components.
  For `n < 2` the pair loop does not run, so the energy is 0 and the gradient is
  zero.
  For `n >= 2` a coincident pair (`r2 <= 0.0`) is skipped, and a `NaN`
  coordinate does not satisfy `r2 <= 0.0`, so `NaN` propagates into the energy
  and the gradient.
- Errors :: no status code and no error message.
  Null pointers are not checked.

#### `rgpot_lj_pair`

```c
int rgpot_lj_pair(double epsilon, double sigma, double r2, double *energy,
                  double *dvdr_over_r, double *d2vdr2);
```

- Inputs :: `epsilon`, `sigma`, the squared distance `r2`, and three output
  pointers.
- Units :: `epsilon` in the caller's energy, `sigma` and the distance in the
  caller's length.
  `dvdr_over_r` is `(dE/dr) / r`.
  `d2vdr2` is `d2E/dr2`.
- Outputs :: the pair energy and the two derivatives.
  When `!(r2 > 0.0)` or `r2` is not finite, writes zeros to all three outputs
  and returns 0.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `energy`, `dvdr_over_r` or `d2vdr2` is null, and 0
  otherwise, with no error message.

#### `rgpot_lj_curvature_pairs`

```c
int rgpot_lj_curvature_pairs(double epsilon, double sigma, int32_t npairs,
                             const double *r2, double *energy,
                             double *dvdr_over_r, double *d2vdr2);
```

- Inputs :: `epsilon`, `sigma`, `npairs` squared distances and three output
  arrays of that length.
- Units :: as `rgpot_lj_pair`, one entry per pair.
- Outputs :: energy, `(dE/dr) / r` and `d2E/dr2` for each pair; entries where
  `!(r2[i] > 0.0)` or `r2[i]` is not finite write zeros.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `npairs < 0`, or when `npairs > 0` and `r2`,
  `energy`, `dvdr_over_r` or `d2vdr2` is null, and 0 otherwise, with no error
  message.

#### `rgpot_lj_gradient`

```c
int rgpot_lj_gradient(double epsilon, double sigma, double cutoff,
                      int32_t natoms, const double *positions,
                      double *energy, double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: `epsilon`, `sigma`, `cutoff`, `natoms`, 3 `natoms` coordinates, and
  the energy and gradient pointers.
- Units :: `epsilon` in energy, `sigma` and `cutoff` and positions in length,
  gradient in energy per length.
  A cutoff of 0 or less keeps every pair.
- Outputs :: one energy and 3 `natoms` gradient components.
  A pair with `!(r2 > 0.0)` is skipped.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `natoms < 0`, `energy` is null, or `natoms > 0` and
  `positions` or `gradient` is null, and 0 otherwise, with no error message.

#### `rgpot_lj_atom_energies`

```c
int rgpot_lj_atom_energies(double epsilon, double sigma, int32_t natoms,
                           const double *positions, double *atom_energy);
```

- Inputs :: `epsilon`, `sigma`, `natoms`, positions and one energy per atom.
- Units :: as `rgpot_lj_gradient`, with no cutoff.
- Outputs :: each pair's energy added to both atoms.
  The total energy is half the sum of `atom_energy`.
  A pair with `!(r2 > 0.0)` is skipped.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `natoms < 0`, `atom_energy` is null, or `natoms > 0`
  and `positions` is null, and 0 otherwise, with no error message.

#### `rgpot_lj_partial_gradient`

```c
int rgpot_lj_partial_gradient(double epsilon, double sigma, int32_t natoms,
                              const double *positions, int32_t n_moved,
                              const int32_t *moved, double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: `epsilon`, `sigma`, `natoms`, positions, `n_moved` atom indices and
  a gradient of 3 `natoms` components.
- Units :: as `rgpot_lj_gradient`, with no cutoff.
- Outputs :: gradient rows of the atoms listed in `moved`.
  Every other row is zero, and pairs with `!(r2 > 0.0)` are skipped.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `gradient` is null, `natoms < 0`,
  `n_moved < 0`, `natoms > 0` and `positions` is null, `n_moved > 0` and `moved`
  is null, or `moved[m] < 0` or `moved[m] >= natoms`, and 0 otherwise, with no
  error message.
  An index outside `[0, natoms)` is checked after `gradient` is zeroed and after
  the earlier `moved` rows have been accumulated, so the gradient is partial on
  that error.
  The unit dimer at `r = 1` with `epsilon = 1`, `sigma = 1`, `natoms = 2` and
  `moved = {0, 5}` returns 1 and leaves `gradient[0] = 24`, with every other
  component still zero.

#### `rgpot_lj_arithmetic_gradient`

```c
int rgpot_lj_arithmetic_gradient(const double *sigma, double cutoff,
                                 int32_t natoms, const double *positions,
                                 double *energy, double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: one `sigma` per atom, `cutoff`, `natoms`, positions, energy and
  gradient.
  The pair diameter is the arithmetic mean.
- Units :: `sigma`, `cutoff` and positions in length.
  The energy is 4 times the sum of `(s^12 - s^6)` with
  `s = (sigma_i + sigma_j) / (2 r)`, and the well depth is 1.
- Outputs :: one energy and the gradient.
  A cutoff of 0 or less keeps every pair, and a pair with `!(r2 > 0.0)` is
  skipped.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `natoms < 0`, `energy` is null, or `natoms > 0` and
  `sigma`, `positions` or `gradient` is null, and 0 otherwise, with no error
  message.

#### `rgpot_morse_pair`

```c
int rgpot_morse_pair(double epsilon, double rho, double re, double r2,
                     double *energy, double *dvdr_over_r, double *d2vdr2);
```

- Inputs :: `epsilon`, `rho`, `re`, the squared distance and three output
  pointers.
- Units :: `epsilon` in energy, `re` and the distance in length, `rho`
  dimensionless.
  `dvdr_over_r` is `(dE/dr) / r`.
- Outputs :: the pair energy and the two derivatives.
  When `!(r2 > 0.0)` or `!(re > 0.0)` (zero, negative or `NaN`), writes zeros to
  all three outputs and returns 0.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `energy`, `dvdr_over_r` or `d2vdr2` is null, and 0
  otherwise, with no error message.

#### `rgpot_morse_gradient`

```c
int rgpot_morse_gradient(double epsilon, double rho, double re,
                         double cutoff, int32_t natoms,
                         const double *positions, double *energy,
                         double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: `epsilon`, `rho`, `re`, `cutoff`, `natoms`, positions, energy and
  gradient.
- Units :: `epsilon` in energy, `re`, `cutoff` and positions in length.
  A cutoff of 0 or less keeps every pair.
- Outputs :: one energy and the gradient.
  A pair with `!(r2 > 0.0)` is skipped.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `!(re > 0.0)` (`re` is zero, negative or `NaN`),
  `natoms < 0`, `energy` is null, or `natoms > 0` and `positions` or `gradient`
  is null, and 0 otherwise, with no error message.

#### `rgpot_binary_lj_gradient`

```c
int rgpot_binary_lj_gradient(int32_t n_a, const double *eps,
                             const double *sig, double cutoff,
                             int32_t natoms, const double *positions,
                             double *energy, double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: `n_a` (atoms of species A; the rest are B), `eps` and `sig` in the
  order AA, AB, BB, `cutoff`, `natoms`, positions, energy and gradient.
- Units :: `eps` in energy, `sig`, `cutoff` and positions in length.
- Outputs :: one energy and the gradient.
  A cutoff of 0 or less keeps every pair, and a pair with `!(r2 > 0.0)` is
  skipped.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `natoms < 0`, `n_a < 0` or `n_a > natoms`, `energy`,
  `eps` or `sig` is null, or `natoms > 0` and `positions` or `gradient` is null,
  and 0 otherwise, with no error message.

#### `rgpot_tip4p_sites_config`

- Inputs :: `c6`, `c12`, `epsilon`, `sigma`,
  `use_epsilon` (nonzero selects `epsilon` and `sigma`; zero selects `c6` and `c12`), `coulomb`, `q_h`
  and `q_m`.
- Units :: the caller chooses the energy unit through `c6`, `c12`, `epsilon` and
  `coulomb`.
  `sigma` and the site coordinates share one length.
  `q_h` and `q_m` are charges in the unit `coulomb` converts.
- Outputs :: the parameter block of `rgpot_tip4p_sites`.
- Errors :: none.
  The struct is not checked until the call.

#### `rgpot_tip4p_sites`

```c
int rgpot_tip4p_sites(const rgpot_tip4p_sites_config *cfg,
                      int32_t n_molecules, const double *sites,
                      double *energy, double *gradient);
```

- Inputs :: `cfg`, `n_molecules`, and `sites` laid out O, H, H, M per molecule
  (12 coordinates).
  The gradient has the same length.
- Units :: the length of `sites` and the energy unit of `cfg`.
- Outputs :: one energy and the gradient.
  Oxygen-oxygen is the Lennard-Jones term and every other site pair is
  `coulomb * q_i * q_j / r`.
- Errors :: returns 1 when `cfg` or `energy` is null,
  `n_molecules < 0`, or `n_molecules > 0` and `sites` or `gradient` is null, and
  0 otherwise, with no error message.

# Tabulated EAM and Finnis-Sinclair potentials

Source: docs/orgmode/reference/eam_table.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/eam_table.html

`EAMTablePot` reads an embedded atom method (EAM) potential from a DYNAMO table
and evaluates

```
E = sum_i F_a(rho_i) + sum_{i<j} phi_ab(r_ij)
rho_i = sum_{j != i} rho_ab(r_ij)
```

where a is the element of atom i, b is the element of atom j, and `rho_ab` is
the density a b neighbor puts at an a site.
The three layouts are those of the `pair_eam` page of the Large-scale
Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS),
https://docs.lammps.org/pair_eam.html.

| `EAMTableFormat` | LAMMPS style      | Suffix        | Arrays                                 |
|------------------|-------------------|---------------|----------------------------------------|
| `Funcfl`         | `eam`             | `.eam`        | F(rho), Z(r), rho(r), one element      |
| `Setfl`          | `eam/alloy`       | `.eam.alloy`  | F_a(rho), rho_b(r), r phi_ab(r)        |
| `FinnisSinclair` | `eam/fs`          | `.eam.fs`     | F_a(rho), rho_ab(r), r phi_ab(r)       |

A `Setfl` density depends only on the neighbor, so `rho_ab = rho_b`.
The `FinnisSinclair` layout carries a density for each ordered pair of elements.
It is the form of Finnis and Sinclair, Philosophical Magazine A 50, 45 (1984).
Section b of an `.eam.fs` file lists F_b and then `rho_1b` to `rho_Nb`, the
density b puts at a site of each element in turn.

The potential is opt-in.
Meson builds it with `-Dwith_eam_table=true` and CMake with
`-DRGPOT_WITH_EAM_TABLE=ON`.
Both define `RGPOT_HAS_EAM_TABLE`.
Without the option, no EAMTable code is compiled.

```cpp
#include "rgpot/EAMTable/EAMTablePot.hpp"

rgpot::EAMTablePot pot({.path = "CuNi.eam.alloy",
                        .format = rgpot::EAMTableFormat::Setfl,
                        .periodic = true,
                        .stress = true});
```

`read_eam_table` parses a stream into an `EAMTable`, and a second constructor
takes that table directly.

## From the C ABI, Rust and Python

A host that links `rgpot-core` and no C++ kernel builds the same potential with
`rgpot_potential_new_eam_table`, declared in `rgpot.h` since C ABI 1.6.
It takes the path, a format code and `periodic`, returns a handle of the usual
kind and reports a refusal as NULL with `rgpot_last_error`; the entry is in
[C ABI of rgpot-core](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/c_abi.html).
The format codes are
`RGPOT_EAM_TABLE_AUTO` (the suffix chooses), `RGPOT_EAM_TABLE_FUNCFL`,
`RGPOT_EAM_TABLE_SETFL` and `RGPOT_EAM_TABLE_FINNIS_SINCLAIR`, the rows of the
table above.
C++ calls `rgpot::PotentialHandle::eam_table`, which throws `rgpot::Error`
instead of returning NULL.

The Rust crate holds its own evaluation of the table, in
`rgpot_core::eam_table`, because `rgpot-core` links no C++ kernel and the handle
must work in a build that has none.
`EamTablePotential::open(path, format, periodic)` builds it and
`EamTablePotential::force` returns the energy and the forces.
It repeats the steps of the previous section, so the two implementations are
checked against the same LAMMPS data rather than against each other.
It differs from `EAMTablePot` in what it leaves out: no stress, no pair list and
no per-atom terms.
It visits every pair and takes the nearest image of the partner from rounded
fractional coordinates, so a periodic call needs every face spacing above twice
the cutoff, and the call fails with `RGPOT_INVALID_PARAMETER` for a smaller
cell.

Python builds the C++ potential, not the Rust one:
`rgpot.EAMTablePot(file, format)` is in [the Python API](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/python_api.html).

## Agreement with LAMMPS

The tables go through the steps of `src/MANYBODY/pair_eam.cpp`, so a file gives
the LAMMPS energy and forces to rounding.

- A `Funcfl` file is resampled by four-point Lagrange interpolation onto
  `lround((N - 1) d / d)` points, one fewer than the file lists, as
  `PairEAM::file2array` does for a single file.
- The pair term of a `Funcfl` file is `r phi = 27.2 * 0.529 * Z(r)^2` in eV
  Angstrom.
  27.2 is the Hartree in eV and 0.529 the Bohr radius in Angstrom, the rounded
  values LAMMPS uses.
- Each array becomes the seven-coefficient cubic of `PairEAM::interpolate`.
  Its slopes are five-point central differences inside the table, three-point
  central differences at the second and second-to-last points, and one-sided
  differences at the ends.
- Above `rhomax = (Nrho - 1) drho` of the file, the energy adds
  `F'(rho) (rho - rhomax)` with the slope at the last table point.
  Above the last distance point, both the value and the slope are those at the
  end of the table.
- A pair counts when r is below the cutoff on the grid line.

Two choices differ from LAMMPS.
An atom picks its element by atomic number, matched against the first field of
each element line, where LAMMPS maps types to the element names on line 4.
A file whose element lines do not carry atomic numbers cannot be used as it is.
Only one `Funcfl` file is read, so the LAMMPS mixing of several `.eam` files is
not available.
The `eam/he` and `eam/cd` layouts are not read.

Periodic evaluation sums every image of a pair that lies inside the cutoff.
When every face spacing is greater than twice the cutoff, that image is the
minimum image, and `forceImpl` walks the stored neighbour list.
When a face spacing is at most twice the cutoff, a pair can have several images
inside the cutoff, and an atom can see a translation of itself.
`forceImpl` then walks those images directly and does not build the stored list.
The walk refuses a cell whose image extent on one axis would pass 1024, and a
cell whose three axes together would visit more than 262144 lattice shifts for
one pair.
The constructor does not check the cutoff against a cell.
It throws `std::invalid_argument` for a file it cannot open or parse.
`forceImpl` throws `std::invalid_argument` when the image extent or the image
count is past that limit, for a periodic call without a cell, for an atomic
number that is in no element line, when a fractional separation is not finite,
and when the nearest integer to that separation plus the image extent does not
fit in an `int` lattice index.

## Stress

`EAMTableConfig::stress` is off by default.
When it is set, `forceImpl` writes the Cauchy stress `sigma = (1/V) dE/dstrain`
of `stress.hpp` and sets `has_stress`.
The force pass adds `-fscale * d d^T` for each pair, as `SuttonChenPot` does,
because the embedding term enters fscale through F'.
With the flag clear, the stress slots and `has_stress` are left as the caller
set them, and the energy and forces are the same bits.
Setting the flag changes `paramsKey()`.

## Pair list

The spline tables and the map from atomic numbers to elements are made once, in
the constructor.
The potential has no setter for them, so they change only with a new potential.
`forceImpl` and `forcePerAtom` keep one `nlist::Neighbours` list of the pairs
within the cutoff plus `EAMTableConfig::skin` (1 Angstrom by default), and reuse
it while every atom stays within half the skin of where it was at the last
build.
The image walk does not build or reuse that list.
The move is measured to the nearest periodic image, so atoms that the caller
wraps back into the cell keep the list.
A new cell, another atom count, or a move past half the skin rebuilds it.
Another element on a site does not, as the list holds positions only.
The pairs within the cutoff are visited in the same order with any skin, so the
skin changes how often the list is built, not the bits of the result, and it is
not part of `paramsKey()`.
`skin = 0` rebuilds the list whenever an atom moves.
`setNeighbourMode(nlist::Mode::Stream)` walks the cells on every call and keeps
no list.
`listReused()` tells whether the last call kept the list and `listBuilds()`
counts the builds.

The list is scratch that each call rewrites, so `caps().reentrancy` is
`Reentrancy::PerInstance`, as for the other potentials that keep one: give each
thread its own instance.
The two stages of `Staged.hpp` run on the host's list and do not touch it.

## Checks

`EAMTablePotTest` compares rgpot with LAMMPS version 22 Jul 2025.
`CppCore/tests/data/eam_table/make_lammps_ref.py` writes two references from
files in the LAMMPS `potentials` directory, copied unchanged.

- `Cu_u3.eam`, a `Funcfl` file for copper from Foiles, Baskes and Daw, Physical
  Review B 33, 7983 (1986).
  It has 500 points in rho and in r and a cutoff of 4.95 Angstrom.
- `CuNi.eam.alloy`, a `Setfl` file for copper and nickel from Onat and
  Durukanoglu, Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter 26, 035404 (2014).
  It has 500 points in rho and in r and a cutoff of 6.394332378 Angstrom.

The `Cu_u3` case is a jittered 108-atom fcc copper cell in a cubic box.
The `CuNi` case is a jittered 256-atom fcc cell in a sheared box, with nickel or
copper at random on each site.
A third case takes the Sutton-Chen platinum row as LAMMPS saw it.
`CppCore/tests/data/sutton_chen/make_lammps_ref.py` writes that row as a
50001-point `eam/fs` table, and the case compares with its cubic reference.

| Case           | LAMMPS style | energy gap (eV) | largest force gap (eV/Angstrom) | largest stress gap (eV/Angstrom^3) |
|----------------|--------------|-----------------|---------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `Cu_u3` cubic  | `eam`        |         2.3e-12 |                         8.1e-15 |                            7.3e-17 |
| `CuNi` sheared | `eam/alloy`  |         3.1e-12 |                         1.7e-14 |                            1.5e-16 |
| Pt cubic       | `eam/fs`     |         1.7e-12 |                         5.1e-12 |                            1.0e-14 |

The test asks for 1e-10 eV, 1e-10 eV/Angstrom and 1e-13 eV/Angstrom^3.
The test rebuilds the Sutton-Chen table in C++ from the formulas of that script
rather than reading a file.

`[skin]` follows the sheared `CuNi` cell through small moves, atoms shifted by
cell vectors and wrapped back, another element on some sites, one atom past half
the skin, a strained cell and one atom fewer.
After each step the potential with its 1 Angstrom skin gives the energy, the
forces, the stress and the per-atom energies and virials of a potential with
skin 0 to the bit, and `listReused()` and `listBuilds()` show a rebuild exactly
for the move past the skin, the strain and the atom count.
On a free `Cu_u3` cluster the kept list matches skin 0 to the bit and a stream
within 1e-10 eV and eV/Angstrom.

A two-element `eam/fs` table of constants checks the order of the density
blocks.
The A-A, A-B and B-B dimers give -2, -11 and -28 in the documented order.
Reading the sections or the blocks inside a section the other way round changes
at least one of them.

## The copper vacancy

`rgpot-core/tests/eam_table.rs`, `rgpot-core/tests/c/eam_table_capi.c` and `EAMTableHandleTest` evaluate 107 copper atoms around one vacancy through the Rust wrapper, the C ABI and the C++ handle, and compare with LAMMPS version 22 Jul 2025 (20250722), `pair_style eam`
with `pair_coeff * * Cu_u3.eam`.
`CppCore/tests/data/eam_table/make_vacancy_ref.py` writes `cu_u3_vacancy.ref`.
The script takes the 108 sites of a 3 x 3 x 3 fcc cell with a = 3.615 Angstrom,
moves every atom by a uniform random amount up to 0.12 Angstrom in each
coordinate (seed 23), removes the first atom, and runs LAMMPS with
`units metal`, `atom_style atomic`, `boundary p p p`, `neighbor 1.0 bin` and
`run 0`.
The cell is a 10.845 Angstrom cube, so every face spacing is 2.19 times the 4.95
Angstrom cutoff.
The file is
`Cu_u3.eam` with sha256 `3436c491a4c75ea8b7141adbc6ee382a118f5fdb47f609c2a660fc1eb772599f`, the copy in the LAMMPS `potentials` directory that `CppCore/tests/data/eam_table`
holds.
The energy is -371.54901154618921 eV.

| Case          | energy gap (eV) | largest force gap (eV/Angstrom) |
|---------------|-----------------|---------------------------------|
| Vacancy cell  |         4e-13   |                         6e-15   |

The tests ask for 1e-11 eV and 1e-12 eV/Angstrom.
The same suites read three refusals: a missing file, a file whose arrays end
early (`malformed_funcfl.eam`) and a NULL or empty path.

---

# Modified embedded-atom method

Source: docs/orgmode/reference/meam.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/meam.html

# Copyright 2023--present rgpot developers

## Modified embedded-atom method

`MEAMPot` is the modified embedded-atom method of Baskes, Physical Review B 46,
2727 (1992).
It carries the second-neighbour extension of Lee and Baskes, Physical Review B
62, 8564 (2000).
The class reports `PotType::MEAM` and lives in `CppCore/rgpot/MEAM/`.
It reads the library and parameter files of the LAMMPS `pair_style meam`, so a
parameter set that runs there runs here without conversion.
Lengths are Angstrom and energies are eV.

### Energy

The energy is

```
E = sum_i F_i(rhobar_i) + 1/2 sum_{i != j} phi_ij(r_ij) S_ij
F(rhobar) = A E_c rhobar ln(rhobar)
rhobar = rho0 G(Gamma) / rho_ref
Gamma = (t1 rho1 + t2 rho2 + t3 rho3) / rho0^2
```

rho_ref is the background density of the element's reference structure. rho0 to
rho3 are the partial densities of the paper, built from the radially screened
neighbours of atom i.
`ialloy` (0, 1 or 2) sets how the t weights average over species, and
`mixture_ref_t` and `bkgd_dyn` set the background.
G follows `ibar`.
Values 0 and 4 give sqrt(1 + Gamma) with the `gsmooth_factor` smoothing, 1 gives
exp(Gamma / 2), 3 a logistic form and -5 a signed square root.
`ibar` 2 is not defined and the constructor of `MEAMModel` throws for it.

S_ij is the product of the radial cutoff of r_ij, with width `delr`, and the
many-body screening of every third atom k.
The screening of k is the ellipse construction of the paper, between `Cmin` and
`Cmax` of the triple (i, j, k).

phi is not an input.
It is the pair term for which the energy of the reference structure of the pair
equals the Rose universal equation of state, so the model builds it from that
structure when it is constructed, for every pair of species.
`erose_form` 0, 1 and 2 select the three Rose forms, and `zbl` blends in the ZBL
repulsion at short range.
The pair terms are tabulated as LAMMPS does: 1000 points up to 1.1 rc, with a
cubic in each interval built from the five point slope.

### Second neighbours

A pair with `nn2` set to 1 counts the second neighbours of its reference
structure.
They are screened by the factor S of the Lee-Baskes construction and enter both
rho0 and the pair term, which becomes the series

```
phi(r) = phi_ref(r) - sum_n (-Z2 S / Z1)^n phi(a^n r)
```

The sum runs to n = 10 and stops at the first term smaller than 1e-20, as LAMMPS
does.
The B1, B2 and DIA reference pairs add the like-atom terms of both species, and
L12 uses the weights -3/4 and -1/4 for the two like-atom terms.
`nn2` for a C11 pair is not defined and the constructor throws.

### Files and species

`MEAMConfig` names a library file (`library`), an optional parameter file
(`parameters`, empty for none) and the library entries to use (`elements`).
The entries keep the order of `elements`, and an empty list takes the whole
library in file order.
The parameter file indexes elements from 1 in that order, as the element list of
`pair_coeff` does.
A parameter line separates its words with an equals sign, parentheses, commas,
single quotes, blanks and tabs, and either file may carry `#` comments.
A library entry may wrap over several lines, and the quotes around a name are
dropped.

An atom takes the element whose atomic number it has.
`atomic_numbers` gives one number per entry.
Without it each number is read from the leading chemical symbol of the entry
name, so `AlS` is aluminium and `FeS` is iron.
The `ielement` column of the library is not used, since the shipped 2NN library
sets it to 1 for every element.
An atom whose number no element has makes `forceImpl` throw
`std::invalid_argument`.

`z` in a library entry must equal the number of first neighbours of its lattice.
A lattice name that no element can have, `t0` other than 1, and `rho0` that is
not positive throw `std::invalid_argument` with the file and line number.

### Calls

`MEAMPot::forceImpl` writes the energy, the forces and, when `stress` is set and
the cell volume is positive, the Cauchy stress of `stress.hpp`.
The convention is that of `LJPot`: the stress is dE/d(epsilon) / V for the
strain that sends every position and every cell row r to r (I + epsilon), in
eV/Angstrom^3.
A compressed cell has negative diagonal entries, and the LAMMPS virial W is
-sigma V.

With `periodic` (the default) every image within reach is counted, also when the
reach exceeds half the cell, so a small cell is not a minimum-image
approximation.
The reach is the radial cutoff rc times the root of the largest ellipse bound of
the model.
`forceImpl` throws `std::invalid_argument` for a singular cell and for a cell so
thin that the image count would be unreasonable.
The bound is 1 for `Cmax` below 2, since the ellipse then never reaches past
r_ik = r_ij, and Cmax^2 / (4 (Cmax - 1)) from 2 up.
LAMMPS applies the second form to every `Cmax`, which agrees from 2 up, is
looser below 2, and diverges at `Cmax` = 1.
With `periodic` false the box is ignored and the atoms are a cluster.

The potential keeps nothing between calls.
`caps()` reports the periodic and stress flags and one instance serves
concurrent callers.
The cutoff is `MEAMPot::cutoff()`, which is rc.
`paramsKey()` hashes every number that decides the model, so two instances with
the same files and options share a key, and a changed parameter changes it.

The forces are the exact gradient of the energy, including the derivative of
every screening factor with respect to the three distances of a triple.
The kernel does not use the half-list or the staged interface of the
domain-decomposed kernels, and there is no `pot_spec` name, Python binding or C
ABI entry for it yet.

### Validation

The reference values in `CppCore/tests/data/meam/` come from LAMMPS 20260930
(`stable_30Sep2026_update1`) built with the MEAM package.
`make_lammps_ref.py` in that directory writes each `.ref` file from a LAMMPS
run, and every file records the version, the library and the parameter file.
The library and parameter files are those of LAMMPS, copied unchanged (see
`NOTICE` and `COPYING` there).

`MEAMPotTest` compares energy, forces, virial and stress with 11 such runs.
They are cubic and sheared triclinic cells of Ni, bcc Fe, and Si-C zincblende
with a mixed pair.
Three alloys of five species switch on `ialloy`,
`bkgd_dyn`, `mixture_ref_t`, `emb_lin_neg`, the Rose forms and the ZBL blend.
Four runs use second neighbours, among them a seven element alloy and the
Al-Si-Mg-Cu-Fe set.
They agree to better than 1e-11 eV in the energy and better than 1e-11
eV/Angstrom in the forces.
The test bounds are 1e-8 and 1e-7 for the alloys.

Without LAMMPS the tests still check that the forces are the central difference
gradient of the energy, that the stress is the strain derivative, that the
reference crystals follow the Rose equation of state, that the energy is
extensive when the cell is repeated, and that a cluster matches a periodic cell
far from its images.

---

# Fortran potentials: porting rules

Source: docs/orgmode/reference/fortran_potentials.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/fortran_potentials.html

Why kernels are ported and why they gather are explained in
[Fortran kernels: port, not wrap](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/explanation/fortran-kernels.html).

## Rules

1. *Module, `implicit none`, `private` by default.* Export the physics entry
   points
and the parameter type; nothing else.
2. *Kinds from `rgpot_kinds`* (`wp`, `ip`, `lp`).
No `real*8`, no `double precision`, no kind literals spelled out at use sites.
The module asserts `wp == c_double` at compile time.
3. *No COMMON, no `save` state in the physics.* Parameters live in a derived
   type
with defaults; scratch lives in local automatic arrays.
Saved state is allowed only in the `_capi` module (the parameter set and the
legacy workspace of the handle-free entry), never in a kernel.
Per-caller neighbour tables live in workspaces from `rgpot_workspace`.
`params_ready` is written once, under C++ `std::call_once`, and the parameter
block is read-only after that.
The handle-free entry's legacy workspace is process-serial and is not on the
Python path.
4. *Every dummy argument gets `intent`*, and arrays that cross into kernels are
`contiguous` where the caller can guarantee it.
5. *No `goto`, no arithmetic `if`, no labelled `do`.* Structured control flow
   only.
`cycle` and `exit` replace jump targets.
6. *Kernels are `pure`* (or `elemental`) wherever the algorithm allows, which is
also what `do concurrent` requires of anything it calls.
7. *Failures return a status.* No `stop`, no `write(6,*)` diagnostics from a
library kernel: set a message (in the workspace for a
`_ws` entry, through `rgpot_ferror` for the handle-free entry) and return
non-zero.
The C++ wrapper turns that into an exception.
8. *Neighbours come from rgpot's neighbour query* (`rgpot_nlist_fortran_build`
in `CppCore/rgpot/nlist/rgpot_nlist.h`) through `rgpot_neighbors`.
No pot builds its own list, and no pot repeats minimum-image arithmetic: the
table carries pair vectors and distances.

## Layout

Two modules per potential:

- `rgpot_<pot>.f90` :: parameters, pure kernels, the energy/force driver.
Pure Fortran, testable without the C++ stack.
- `rgpot_<pot>_capi.f90` :: the `bind(c)` entries, each returning a status:
`rgpot_<pot>_force_ws(handle, natoms, positions, cell, forces, energy)` on a workspace from `rgpot_fortran_workspace_new`,
and the handle-free `rgpot_<pot>_force(natoms, positions, cell, forces, energy)`
on the module's legacy workspace.
Potentials that take species (FeHe, CuH2, water-H) add
`atomic_numbers` after `positions` in both, and `rgpot_sw_force_ws` adds a
`strain` output.
`rgpot_<pot>_ensure_params` sets the saved parameter set once.
The C++ classes call the `_ws` entries.

The static library builds with hidden visibility.
Only the C++ wrapper inside `librgpot` calls the entry points, so no Fortran
symbol reaches the dynamic table and the old collision class (two potentials
exporting `force_`) cannot recur.

### Archive rules

The kernels are one of several PIC convenience archives that `link_whole` into a
single `librgpot`.
Three rules keep that arrangement sound; each was learned by breaking it.

- A convenience archive takes a *headers-only* dependency on anything another
archive also links.
Meson copies a static library's objects into every static library that links it,
so two archives that both `link_with` a third each carry its objects, and the
umbrella then sees every symbol twice.
Linking dependencies belong on the umbrella and on leaf binaries, where the
objects arrive once.
This is why `vesin_dep` has a `vesin_hdr_dep` counterpart, and `ptlrpc_dep` a
`ptlrpc_hdr_dep`.
- The *Fortran runtime is named explicitly*.
`librgpot` is a C++ target that takes the kernels through `link_whole`, so meson
has no Fortran source of its own to infer `-lgfortran` (or the flang equivalent)
from.
- *Generated sources propagate as headers.* A `declare_dependency` that lists a
generated `.cpp` in `sources:` compiles that translation unit again in every
consumer; list only the generated header.

The invariants are worth checking mechanically: no object appears in two whole-
linked archives, `librgpot` carries no `NEEDED` entry on a sibling rgpot object
(consumers that bundle the umbrella alone depend on this), and the Fortran
runtime appears when the kernels are enabled.

## Cell convention

C callers pass nine doubles, row-major, one cell vector per row.
Fortran reads the same memory column-major, so a `real(wp) :: cell(3, 3)` dummy
sees one cell vector per column, which is the layout `rgpot_neighbors` uses.
No transpose anywhere in the chain.

## Tests

Each port carries a Fortran-only test program alongside the Catch2 suite:
translation invariance, vanishing net force on a periodic cell, and analytic
forces against central differences of the energy.
The finite-difference check is what catches a mis-attributed gather term, since
such an error can leave the energy correct.

Pinned reference energies from the pre-port kernels live in the Catch2 tests, at
the tolerances the original suites used.
`eam_al` is the exception on the digits, not on the geometry.
EON r2549 `potinit.f` writes the aluminium parameters as default-real literals,
so a double-precision build stores the single-precision rounding.
The four-atom `al_fcc` cluster is pinned to that Fortran energy,
-5.217864006173226 eV, tighter than the historical relative 1e-4.
Keeping the extra printed digits moves the same geometry by 1.76e-6 eV.

### Compilers

CI builds the kernels with the conda-forge gfortran (13/14) and, on Windows,
with LLVM Flang.
The port was additionally built and tested under *gfortran 15.2.0*, which passes
all of it and reports diagnostics the older compilers stay quiet about, notably
`Unused parameter ... which has been explicitly imported` and `-Wcompare-reals`.
Both classes are worth reading rather than silencing: the first is dead code,
and the second is fair warning unless the comparison really is asking "are these
the same number I was handed before" -- cache validity or a switch parameter --
in which case say so in a comment at the site.

Flang on `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` cannot lower a by-value `BIND(C)` derived
type; it aborts rather than diagnosing.
Interfaces that must build there pass such structs by pointer, which is why the
vendored vesin interface binds `vesin_neighbors_byref`.

### Windows Flang + MSVC link

Flang emits COFF objects that MSVC `link.exe` can consume, but the flang-shipped
`llvm-ar` wraps them in a GNU archive.
`link.exe` then fails with `LNK1107` when it opens the static library.
Force MSVC's librarian (`lib.exe`) via `AR=lib` and the Meson native file
`ci/gha/machines/win-flang-msvc.ini` so the archives are COFF `.lib` and
`link_whole` into `librgpot` succeeds.
That is the supported Windows kernel path; do not disable Fortran to dodge the
archiver.

# Potential names and options

Source: docs/orgmode/reference/potential_names.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/potential_names.html

`pair_style rgpot` in LAMMPS (`pair_coeff * * Name [key value ...] El ...`), the
PLUMED action `RGPOT` (`POTENTIAL=Name OPTIONS`{key value ...}=) and the
`rgpot-eval` tool build a potential from the same name and options.
`engines/pot_spec.hpp` does the parsing for all three.

Names are matched without case.
Option values are Angstrom and eV, whatever units the host uses.
Options come as `key value` pairs separated by spaces.

| Name         | Options                                                                  | Stress |
|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------|
| `LJ`         | `u0`, `psi`, `cutoff`, `switch_width`                                    | yes    |
| `Morse`      | `de`, `a=, =re`, `cutoff`, `switch_width`                                | yes    |
| `SuttonChen` | `preset` (`platinum` or `gold`), `epsilon`, `c=, =a`, `n=, =m`, `cutoff` | yes    |
| `EAMTable`   | `file`, `format` (`funcfl`, `setfl` or `fs`), `skin`                     | yes    |
| `SWSi1985`   | none                                                                     | yes    |
| `TersoffSi`  | none                                                                     | yes    |
| `EMT`        | `parameters` (`asap` or `rasmussen`)                                     | no     |
| `EAMCell`    | none                                                                     | no     |
| `CPMD`       | `params`, a serialized `CPMDParams` file                                 | engine |

A build with the Fortran potentials also accepts `SWSi` (with a stress), and
`EDIP`, `LenoskySi`, `EAMAl`, `FeHe` and `CuH2` (without one).
`SWSi1985` is `StillingerWeberSi` and `SWSi` is the Fortran `SWPot`.
`TersoffSi` is `TersoffSiC`, which runs the 1989 kernel on every call, including
an all-silicon one.
`preset` also accepts `pt` and `au`.
`EAMTable` needs `-Dwith_eam_table=true`.
`CPMD` is present in RPC-enabled builds and loads `libcpmdc` from
`CPMDParams.enginePath` or `CPMDC_LIBRARY`.
Its `format` also accepts `eam`, `alloy`, `eam/alloy` and `eam/fs`.
Without `format`, the suffix decides: `.eam.alloy` or `.setfl` is `setfl`,
`.eam.fs` is `fs`, and `.eam` is `funcfl`.
`skin` is the Verlet skin of its own pair list in Angstrom, 1 by default (see
`eam_table`); it changes how often the list is rebuilt, not the result.
`SuttonChen` and `EAMTable` are built periodic and with the stress on.

`cutoff` defaults to the host's cutoff: the `pair_style` cutoff in LAMMPS.
PLUMED and `rgpot-eval` have none, so there the potential's own default is used
(15 Angstrom for `LJ`, 9.5 for `Morse`, 40 for `SuttonChen`).
An unknown name stops with a message that lists the names this build accepts.
An option the potential does not take, an option given twice, or a value that is
not a number (or not an integer, for `n= and =m`) stops with a message that
names the option.

The stress column is what a periodic cell needs for the virial.
LAMMPS takes a strain difference for a potential without one.
PLUMED stops instead, unless the action has `NOPBC`.

Species are element symbols (`Cu`, case as printed).
`RGPOT` also takes atomic numbers.

The table above is for named built-in potentials parsed by
`engines/pot_spec.hpp`.
The lammpc-backed LAMMPS path is configured through `PotentialConfig.lammps`
(`LammpsParams`) and is not selected by one of these name tokens.

# Developer Guide

Source: docs/orgmode/contributing/developer/index.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/contributing/developer/index.html

This section covers the day-to-day development workflow for `rgpot`.

### Environment Setup

All development is managed through [pixi](https://pixi.sh).
Install it first, then:

```bash
pixi install          # default environment (build + test)
pixi shell            # activate the environment
```

Environments declared in `pixi.toml`:

| Environment | Purpose |
|-------------|---------|
| /(default)/ | Compilers, Meson, CMake, Rust and cargo-nextest, clang-format, cppcheck, cpplint, ccache |
| `rpctest` | RPC integration tests: Cap'n Proto, pycapnp, numpy, ASE, pytest |
| `devbld` | Cap'n Proto and RocksDB (`rpc` and `cache` features) |
| `mpibld` | `devbld` plus Open MPI |
| `docs` | Documentation build (Sphinx, Doxygen, doxyrest, Emacs, pandoc) |
| `cigen` | CI workflow generation (Nickel) |
| `version` | cogapp for the version copies; no default feature |
| `xtbbld`, `tblitebld`, `tbbld` | xtb, tblite, or both |
| `tblite06bld` | tblite 0.6, to compile `TBLitePot` against that API |
| `metatomicbld` | torch, metatomic-torch, metatensor-torch and vesin from PyPI |
| `umaenginebld` | `rpc`, `metatomic` and `xtb` features together |
| `umaexport` | fairchem-core and torch for `scripts/export_uma_aoti.py`; no default feature |
| `xckernel`, `xckerneltest` | libxc and pylibxc; `xckerneltest` adds PySCF |
| `dftd3`, `dftd4`, `dftd` | s-dftd3, dftd4, or both |
| `engines` | LAMMPS, GROMACS, OpenMM, PLUMED and nanobind |
| `eonviz` | eOn and plotting packages; no default feature |

### Common Tasks

Tasks run with `pixi r <task>`.
A task that belongs to a feature needs that environment, as in
`pixi r -e docs docbld`.
`prek`, `lychee` and `snapper` are not pixi dependencies; install them before
running the tasks that call them.

| Task | Environment | Description |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| `rust-test` | default | Run Rust unit tests with nextest |
| `rust-test-all` | default | Run Rust tests with all features enabled (also rewrites the C header) |
| `gen-header` | default | Regenerate `rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h` from Rust source via cbindgen |
| `check-header-drift` | default | Fail when `rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h` differs from the cbindgen output |
| `gen-gha` | `cigen` | Export the Nickel workflows (`release.yml`, `release-prepare.yml`, `ci_docs.yml`, `cosmo-potctl.yml`, `ci_doc_commenter.yml`); `ci-orchestrator.yml` is hand-maintained |
| `gha-drift` | `cigen` | Fail when `.github/workflows` differs from a fresh `gen-gha` |
| `towncrier-draft` | default | Preview release notes (dry run) |
| `news-fragments-check` | default | Fail when a news fragment carries a copyright line, a comment block or a leading list marker (`--fix` rewrites) |
| `towncrier-build` | default | Write release notes into `CHANGELOG.md` |
| `release-potctl` | default | Project CLI (`cargo run -q -p potctl --`); for example `pixi r release-potctl -- release assert` |
| `release-sync-versions` | default | Write the version in `Cargo.toml` (`potctl release sync`; `pixi r release-sync-versions -- 1.2.3`), then run `release-cog` |
| `release-cog` / `version-drift` | `version` | Regenerate or check every version copy with cogapp |
| `release-assert-lockstep` | default | Assert every version copy matches `Cargo.toml` (`potctl release assert`) |
| `release-extract-changelog` | default | One `CHANGELOG.md` section (`potctl release notes`; optional `-o`) |
| `release-towncrier-check` | default | `towncrier check` vs base (CI: orchestrator `towncrier` job on PRs) |
| `ci-preflight` / `potctl-test` | default | `potctl ci preflight` / the `potctl` unit tests |
| Cut release | none | On `main`: `cog bump --auto` (cog 7+) then `git push --follow-tags`; see [release.org](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/contributing/developer/release.html) |
| Potentials CI | none | `ci-orchestrator.yml` jobs `potentials_metatomic` (`potctl ci metatomic-test`) / `potentials_uma_engine` (`potctl ci metatomic-test --rpc`) / `potentials_tight_binding` (`potctl ci xtb-tblite-test`) / `potentials_tblite_06` / `potentials_plugins` (`potctl ci plugin-test`) / `xckernel_goldens` (`potctl ci xckernel-test`); see [below](*One job and one ccache key per pixi environment) |
| `docbld` | `docs` | Build full documentation (org export + Doxygen + Sphinx) |
| `docdel` | `docs` | Clean all generated documentation artifacts |
| `gen-readme` | `docs` | Export `rgpot-core/README.org` to `rgpot-core/README.md` |
| `snapper-check` / `snapper-fix` | default | Semantic line breaks in `docs/orgmode` (TurtleTech snapper; GHA orchestrator `docs_snapper`) |
| `lychee-check` | default | Link audit with lychee (`.lychee.toml`; GHA orchestrator `docs_lychee`) |
| `prek` / `prek-install` / `prek-validate` | default | Run / install / validate `prek.toml` hooks (GHA orchestrator `prek` job) |

### One job and one ccache key per pixi environment

Each pixi environment that builds the project runs in its own CI job with its
own compiler-cache key (`ccache-pot-mta-`, `ccache-pot-engine-`, ...).
Two environments in one job share the step environment and the cache directory.
`potctl ci ensure-torch-metatomic` exports the torch and cmake paths of its
environment through `GITHUB_ENV`, so a later step in another environment
inherits them, and a cache entry written against one environment's headers can
satisfy a build against another's.
A `metatomicbld` build followed by an `umaenginebld` build in one job linked
objects compiled against Catch2 3.13 headers with the Catch2 3.16 library of the
second environment, and failed at the link of `plugin_test`.
Add a new environment leg as a new job, not as another step of an existing one.

### Regenerating the C Header

The C header `rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h` is auto-generated by `cbindgen` from
the Rust source.
It is committed to the repository so C/C++ consumers always have a working copy.
After changing the public Rust API:

```bash
pixi r gen-header
git diff rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h  # review changes
```

`gen-header` is an optional Cargo feature of `rgpot-core` and is not in its
default features, so neither a normal build nor `cargo publish` rewrites the
header.

cbindgen copies doc comments into the header, so editing the doc comment of an
`extern "C"` function changes it too.
The `rust_tests` CI job runs `tools/check_header_drift.sh`, which rebuilds the
header and fails when git sees a difference.
Commit the header with the change that caused it.

### Building Documentation

Documentation is built with Sphinx and served at
[rgpot.rgoswami.me](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me).
It combines:

- *Org-mode pages* (this guide, architecture, changelog) exported to RST
- *C++ API reference* generated by Doxygen + doxyrest
- *Rust API reference* generated by `sphinxcontrib-rust`

`pixi r -e docs doccheck` fails when a pinned citation is dropped, or when an
org page under `docs/orgmode` is not reachable from `docs/orgmode/index.org`.
The design notes copied into the manual are the markdown files under `docs/`
named from that index.

To build locally (`docbld` runs `cargo install sphinx-rustdocgen` on the way):

```bash
pixi r -e docs docbld
# Open docs/build/index.html
```

To clean generated artifacts:

```bash
pixi r -e docs docdel
```

### Git hooks (`prek`)

Hooks are configured in `prek.toml` and run with [prek](https://prek.j178.dev)
(Rust drop-in for pre-commit).
Prefer `prek` over `pre-commit` / `uvx pre-commit`.

```bash
# one-time: install shims into .git/hooks
pixi r prek-install   # or: prek install

# run all hooks on the whole tree (CI parity)
pixi r prek           # or: prek run -a --config prek.toml

# validate config only
pixi r prek-validate
```

The `prek` job of `CI (orchestrator)` runs `prek run -a --config prek.toml` on
pushes and pull requests (not on the weekly schedule).
Org docs also go through `snapper` (semantic line breaks) in the `docs_snapper`
job.
Links are audited separately by the orchestrator `docs_lychee` job, which also
runs on the weekly schedule.

# Testing

Source: docs/orgmode/contributing/developer/testing.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/contributing/developer/testing.html

### C/C++ Tests

```bash
meson setup bbdir -Dwith_tests=true -Dwith_rpc=true --buildtype=debug
meson compile -C bbdir
meson test -C bbdir --print-errorlogs
```

The `pixi` environments supply all build and test tools.
In a manual toolchain outside `pixi`, the top-level Meson configure tests need
`ninja`, `pkg-config`, `cmake`, the Python `venv` module, and a Fortran compiler
(`gfortran` or `flang`) for `fortran_sw_module_order`.
`eigen_subproject_fallback` also needs network access or a populated
`subprojects/packagecache` from `meson subprojects download eigen`.

`cmake` works as well.
CMake's `RGPOT_WITH_CACHE` defaults to `ON` and needs RocksDB, unlike Meson's
`with_cache=false`, so the command below turns it off.
[Build options](https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/reference/build_options.html) lists every Meson and
CMake option.

```bash
cmake -B build-cmake \
  -DRGPOT_BUILD_TESTS=ON \
  -DRGPOT_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON \
  -DRGPOT_WITH_RPC=ON \
  -DRGPOT_WITH_CACHE=OFF
cmake --build build-cmake
ctest --test-dir build-cmake --output-on-failure
```

Both register the same tests, except those only meson can run.

#### One test list for meson and CMake

`CppCore/tests/registry.txt` lists every test, one per line: its name, the
features that gate it, its kind, and its timeout, suite, working directory,
environment and flags.
Meson reads the file in `CppCore/meson.build`.
CMake reads it in `cmake/RgpotTestRegistry.cmake`.
`CppCore/tests/tests.cmake` uses that module to register the tests.
A test only meson can run, because it needs an engine, an external program or a
meson-only option, keeps its line with the reason CMake leaves it out.
The comments at the top of the file give the format and each feature.

A unit test, a Fortran program, a neighbour example, a Python script, or a rerun
of a test under other options needs nothing but its line, since both build
systems register those kinds in a loop.
A custom test is registered by hand in each build system, beside its fixtures,
and CMake stops the configuration when it registers a test whose gate does not
hold.

Each build has a `test_list_parity` test, which runs
`CppCore/tests/check_test_registry.py` against the configured build.
It fails when a registered test has no line, when a test whose gate holds is
missing, and when a test's options differ from its line.
`tools/check_test_parity.sh` configures the plain, the RPC and cache, and the
client-only builds with both build systems, without building them.
It runs both checks, then compares the features each build system found and the
tests each registered.
It then passes both `compile_commands.json` files to `tools/check_fp_parity.py`,
which fails when a source both build systems compile gets different contraction
or fast-math flags from each.
The `test_parity` CI job runs it, and `ci_gate` waits on that job.

```bash
python3 CppCore/tests/check_test_registry.py lint
pixi run -e mpibld bash tools/check_test_parity.sh
```

#### Floating-point contraction

`FastNlistTest`, `ReducedPairTest`, `EAMCellVerletTest`, `StreamParityTest`,
`NeighbourLayerTest` and `TersoffSiCTest` compare kernels bit for bit with plain
products and sums.
The kernels are built with contraction off.
The registry gives those six tests `fp_contract=off`, so both build systems
compile them with `-ffp-contract=off` too, neither side fuses, and the compare
stays exact.
A new test of that kind takes the same option.
Outside it, the test can pass on x86-64, where the baseline has no fused
multiply-add, and miss by an ulp on macOS arm64.
To exercise contraction on x86-64, build with Clang at the default debug
buildtype.
GCC does not fuse at `-O0`, and an optimized build folds the Morse test
expressions to constants.

```bash
CXX=clang++ meson setup bbfast -Dwith_tests=true \
  -Dcpp_args='-ffp-contract=fast -mfma'
meson compile -C bbfast
meson test -C bbfast --print-errorlogs
```

#### OpenMP teams

The OpenMP runtime may start fewer threads than a region asks for: under
`OMP_THREAD_LIMIT`, inside another parallel region, or with dynamic teams.
Every region in the library therefore opens in `CppCore/rgpot/Slices.hpp`.
A caller cuts its work into slices before the region and keeps one buffer per
slice.
`forEachSlice` and `forEachSlicePhase` run each slice once on the threads that
start, several to a thread on a short team, and the caller adds the buffers in
slice order, so the slice count fixes the bits and the team only the speed.
A potential takes its slice count from `teamSize(n, from, team)`, which is one
below the atoms the `kTeamFrom` of its class asks of the thread count.
The one-argument `teamSize(std::size_t)` overload is deprecated and remains
exported as a compatibility wrapper forwarding to
`teamSize(n, rgpot::kTeamMinAtoms, {})`.
From `kTeamMinAtoms`, the least of those counts, it adds its sums atom by atom
in index order on any thread count, so neither the slice count nor the team
changes its bits.
Ranks that wait for each other use `onFullTeam`, which runs them only when each
has its own thread; otherwise it returns false and the caller does the same work
through `forEachSlice`.
No other library file names a thread number or a team size.
The test suite fails when an OpenMP pragma, a runtime call, the OpenMP header or
the OpenMP macro appears anywhere else in the library sources.
That check is `CppCore/tests/test_openmp_confined.py`.

`ThreadTeamTest` requires the one-thread bits from every threaded potential at
1, 2, 3 and 8 threads and under `rgpot::TeamCap` short teams, dynamic teams and
nested regions, one atom below and at each atom count in each potential's
`kTeamFrom`, and on a system above `rgpot::kTeamMinAtoms` atoms, whose neighbour
build opens a team too.
Through `rgpot::teamsOpened` it checks that a call opens a region in the
potential's own sums exactly when it has at least the atoms `kTeamFrom` asks of
its thread count.
Neighbour tables must keep the bits of the full team under the same teams.
The test suite runs it again under `OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1` and
`OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=2`, and the `thread_limit` CI job runs the whole suite at both
limits:

```bash
OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1 meson test -C bbdir --print-errorlogs
OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=2 meson test -C bbdir --print-errorlogs
```

`BatchSpreadTest` requires the one-thread bits from a batch of 16 configurations
of 4 atoms, for `StillingerWeberSi`, `TersoffSiC` and `LJPot`, at 1, 2 and 4
threads.
The two and four thread calls each open one team.
A batch that contains `rgpot::kTeamMinAtoms` atoms opens none.
Systems between a class floor and `rgpot::kTeamMinAtoms`, for `LJPot` and
`StillingerWeberSi`, match serial single evaluations in energy and force bits at
4 threads with `OMP_MAX_ACTIVE_LEVELS` of 1 and of 2.
The batch opens one region per system, the same count as those evaluations, so a
spread worker does not walk each pair from both atoms.

`TersoffZblBuildTest` requires those bits from Tersoff and ZBL at 1, 2, 4 and 8
threads, below and above `rgpot::kTeamMinAtoms`, on a fresh list, a Verlet reuse
and a rebuild.

Under ThreadSanitizer, neither an uninstrumented `libgomp` nor a stock `libomp`
annotates OpenMP barriers, so both report false races across sequential regions;
an Archer-enabled `libomp` built with ThreadSanitizer support is needed instead
of adding suppressions.
Under AddressSanitizer and LeakSanitizer, `libomp` retains a known 128-byte
process-lifetime allocation in `___kmp_allocate_align`.
The OpenMP test binaries compile the suppression from
`CppCore/tests/lsan_libomp.hpp`, so only that runtime allocation is suppressed
and leak checks remain active for library and test code.
The suppression matches function names, so the frames must be symbolized.
Under pixi, Ubuntu's `llvm-symbolizer` can fail to start against the pixi
library path, which leaves libomp frames as bare `libomp.so` offsets and the 128
bytes unsuppressed.
Set `ASAN_SYMBOLIZER_PATH` to `tools/lsan/llvm-symbolizer`, which runs the
system symbolizer with `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` cleared.
`tools/check_lsan_libomp.sh` uses it by default, leaks 137 bytes from `main` and
53 bytes from inside an OpenMP region on purpose, and fails unless LeakSanitizer
reports those two and no libomp allocation.

### Rust Tests

`rust-test-all` enables every feature of `rgpot-core` (`schema`, `profile`,
`rpc`, `cache`, `gen-header`).
`gen-header` makes the build rewrite `rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h`.
A build rewrites the header without failing, so the
`rust_tests` job also runs `tools/check_header_drift.sh`, which fails when the
rewrite differs from the committed header.

```bash
pixi r rust-test          # default features only
pixi r rust-test-all      # all features
```

Or directly:

```bash
cargo nextest run --manifest-path rgpot-core/Cargo.toml
cargo test --doc --manifest-path rgpot-core/Cargo.toml  # doc tests
```

### RPC Integration Tests

The `rpctest` environment includes Python bindings via `pycapnp`.
`tests/rpc_integ.py` starts `potserv` with the `CuH2` backend, so the build needs the Fortran potentials (`with_fortran_pots`,
`auto` by default).

```bash
pixi shell -e rpctest
python tests/rpc_integ.py --server-bin ./bbdir/CppCore/potserv
python tests/rpc_integ.py \
  --server-bin ./bbdir/CppCore/potserv \
  --nwchem-smoke \
  --cpmd-smoke
python tests/test_cpmd_params.py
python tests/test_rpc_integ_cpmd.py
```

### NWChem suite (`--suite nwchem`)

The frontend and stub ABI tests build when
`with_tests=true` and `with_rpc=true`.
`meson test` points `RGPOT_NWCHEM_ENGINE` at the in-tree
`libnwchemc_fake_engine.so`.
Cases that need a real NWChem SCF `SKIP` unless
`NWCHEMC_LIBRARY` or `RGPOT_NWCHEMC_ENGINE` names a real `libnwchemc`.
The message ABI test uses a fake `nwchemc_*` shared library and verifies rgpot
passes serialized `NWChemParams` bytes through the `dlopen` boundary.

```bash
meson setup bbdir -Dwith_tests=true -Dwith_rpc=true
meson compile -C bbdir
meson test -C bbdir --suite nwchem --print-errorlogs
```

See
`CppCore/rgpot/NWChemPot/README.md`; the engine (`libnwchemc`) is built by the split [nwchemc](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/nwchemc)
project, not by rgpot.

### CPMD suite (`--suite cpmd`)

The frontend and stub ABI tests build when
`with_tests=true` and `with_rpc=true`.
The CPMD frontend loads a split `libcpmdc` engine at runtime via
`CPMDC_LIBRARY`, `RGPOT_CPMDC_ENGINE`, or `RGPOT_CPMD_ENGINE`.
Configure-only Python smokes use `PotentialConfig.cpmd` and do not require a
live engine.

```bash
meson setup bbdir -Dwith_tests=true -Dwith_rpc=true
meson compile -C bbdir
meson test -C bbdir --suite cpmd --print-errorlogs
pixi run -e rpctest python tests/rpc_integ.py --server-bin ./bbdir/CppCore/potserv --cpmd-smoke
```

See
`CppCore/rgpot/CPMDPot/README.md`; the engine (`libcpmdc`) is built by the split [cpmdc](https://github.com/OmniPotentRPC/cpmdc)
project, not by rgpot.

# Release Process

Source: docs/orgmode/contributing/developer/release.org
URL: https://rgpot.rgoswami.me/contributing/developer/release.html

rgpot has one release version, written by hand in one place: the
`[workspace.package] version` key of the root `Cargo.toml`.
`rgpot-core` and `rgpot-pair` inherit it with `version.workspace = true`, and
cargo writes it into `Cargo.lock`.
Every other copy sits between cogapp markers in a file listed in
`ci/version/files.txt`: `meson.build`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `pyproject.toml`,
`pixi.toml` (the workspace key only), `towncrier.toml`, `docs/source/conf.py`
(Sphinx `version` and `release`), the `RGPOT_VERSION` macros of
`rgpot-core/include/rgpot.h` and the dependency snippets of
`rgpot-core/README.md` and `rgpot-core/README.org`.
`ci/version/rgpot_version.py` reads the version from `Cargo.toml` for those
snippets.
Regenerate the copies, or check them, with the cogapp tasks of the `version`
pixi environment, which pins cogapp 3.6.0:

```bash
pixi r -e version release-cog
pixi r -e version version-drift
```

The tasks call `python -m cogapp`. cogapp also installs a `cog` script, which is
not cocogitto, so cogapp lives in its own environment and nothing calls it as
`cog`.
The `version-drift` prek hook runs the check on every pull request, and
`potctl release assert` compares each copy, the numeric `RGPOT_VERSION` macros
and the lock entries with `Cargo.toml`.
`RGPOT_VERSION` keeps a pre-release whole, as in `3.6.0-rc.1`, and `RGPOT_VERSION_PATCH`
is its numeric patch, `0`.
`rgpot-core/build.rs` (through `rgpot-core/version_macros.rs`) and `ci/version/rgpot_version.py`
both write that block, and a `potctl` test fails when they disagree.
Git tags are `vX.Y.Z` (see `cog.toml` `tag_prefix`).
Pre-release tags such as `v1.2.0-rc.1` are allowed; `release.yml` marks the
GitHub Release as prerelease and *skips* its own `cargo publish` step.
`publish.yml` also runs on every
`v*` tag and publishes `rgpot-core` without that check (see [[*Pre-release / RC
tags][Pre-release / RC tags]]).

Requires [cocogitto](https://docs.cocogitto.io) *7+* locally and in CI
(`setup-ci-tools` installs cocogitto 7.0.0 for `release-prepare.yml`), plus a
normal Rust toolchain so `potctl` (`potctl/` workspace crate;
`cargo run -p potctl -- …`) can run lockstep commands.
In `release.yml` and `release-prepare.yml`, the `setup-ci-tools` action builds a
portable `potctl` (an `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` binary on Linux, a universal
binary on macOS).
Do *not* hand-edit a `## [X.Y.Z]` section above the towncrier marker; fragments
under `docs/newsfragments/` are the only input for the next release notes block.

*Canonical changelog*: repository-root `CHANGELOG.md` (towncrier).
`docs/orgmode/changelog.org` only includes that file for Sphinx; do not maintain
a second prose changelog.

Tooling:

| Tool | Role |
|------|------|
| [cocogitto](https://docs.cocogitto.io) (`cog`) 7+ | Conventional-commit aware bump, version commit, annotated tag |
| [towncrier](https://towncrier.readthedocs.io) | Curated `CHANGELOG.md` from `docs/newsfragments/` |
| `potctl` (`potctl/`, `publish = false`) | Project CLI: `release sync` / `release assert` / `release notes` |
| `.github/actions/setup-ci-tools` | Build `potctl` (+ optional `cog`) once with `Swatinem/rust-cache`; optional artifact upload |
| `.github/actions/restore-ci-tools` | Later jobs/runners: download `ci-tools` artifact, put `bin/` on `PATH` (no second cargo build) |
| `.github/workflows/release.yml` | Staged on `v*`: `tools` → `gate` → (`cpp-smoke` ∥ `rust-test`) → `publish` (stable) or `publish-skip-rc` (pre-release) → `gh-release` |
| `.github/workflows/publish.yml` | On `v*` tags: `cargo publish --locked --no-verify -p rgpot-core` with a crates.io trusted-publishing token |
| `.github/workflows/release-prepare.yml` | Pull requests that touch release files, and `workflow_dispatch`: `tools` (`potctl`+`cog` artifact) → `prepare` (lockstep, towncrier draft, `cargo check`, cog dry-run, cog check) |
| `CI (orchestrator)` / `towncrier` | `towncrier check` on PRs (orchestrator job) |
| `CI (orchestrator)` / potentials | Feature-gated C++ backends (xtb+tblite, tblite 0.6, metatomic/vesin, engine plugins, plugins) on PRs |
| `SECURITY.md` | Supported versions + private report path |
| `.github/CODEOWNERS` | Release-surface review hints (enable on branch protection) |

*Secrets / protection (maintainer, once per repo)*:

- Repository secret `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` for the `release.yml` `cargo publish`
  step.
- `publish.yml` gets its token from `rust-lang/crates-io-auth-action` (crates.io
  trusted publishing, `id-token: write`); configure the trusted publisher on
  crates.io.
- Neither workflow names a GitHub Environment.
  To require reviewers, add an `environment:` key to the publishing jobs and
  create that environment under Settings > Environments.
- Prefer *signed tags* when cutting locally: `git tag -s vX.Y.Z` (or ensure
  `cog` produces signed tags if configured).
  GHA does not replace maintainer GPG.

*C++ distribution note*: the
tag/source is the C++ contract; `release.yml` runs a minimal `meson install` smoke (tests, examples, RPC and cache off, `pure_lib=true`). Optional backends (xtb/tblite/metatomic)
are validated on PRs via orchestrator potentials jobs, not re-run on every tag.
conda-forge / Spack / system packages are *out of band* (separate feedstock/PR
track), not part of `release.yml`.

### Changelog fragments

Add a fragment under `docs/newsfragments/` for each user-visible change (see
`docs/newsfragments/README.md`):

```bash
uvx towncrier create --content "Short user-facing note." 42.added.md
# or interactive:
uvx towncrier create
```

Types (see `towncrier.toml`): `breaking` (section Breaking, listed first),
`security`, `removed`, `deprecated`, `added`, `dev`, `changed`, `fixed`, `misc`.
`towncrier check` fails on a fragment of any other type, such as `style`.
`scripts/check_news_fragments.py` does not check the type.
Preview with `uvx towncrier build --draft` or `pixi r towncrier-draft`.

A fragment holds only the text of the entry.
The template `ci/release-notes.md` writes the bullet and the heading, so:

- Do not start a fragment with a list marker.
  Continuation lines need no indent.
- Do not put a copyright or SPDX line in a fragment.
- Do not put a comment block (`<!-- ... -->`) in a fragment.

The checker is `python scripts/check_news_fragments.py` (or
`pixi r news-fragments-check`).
It fails when a fragment starts with a dash or an asterisk and a space.
Leading whitespace before that marker does not change this.
It fails on a line starting with `copyright` or `(c)` and a space.
It fails on a line starting with `©=, =spdx-`, `[//]:` or `<!--`.
These prefixes match without regard to case.
It fails on a fragment with no text.
Add `--fix` to strip these from the files.
The template strips the same lines and a leading marker from the notes.

The `pull_request` trigger in `.github/workflows/ci-orchestrator.yml` reads:

```yaml
pull_request:
  branches: [main, develop]
  paths-ignore:
    - docs/**
    - '**/*.md'
    - newsfragments/**
    - LICENSE
```

The workflow skips a pull request whose files all match these patterns.
Such a pull request runs neither the `towncrier` job nor the `prek` job.
The `prek` job runs the fragment checker.
Any other pull request runs the `towncrier` job, so it needs a fragment.
This covers code, build files and CI files such as the workflows.
The job runs `potctl ci towncrier-check --compare-with <base sha>`.
That command runs `towncrier check`, which fails without a new fragment.
`towncrier check` passes without one when the pull request changes
`CHANGELOG.md`.
Use the `dev` type when library, CLI and crate behaviour stay the same.

### Commit check

`release-prepare.yml` runs `potctl ci cog-check` on the commits a pull request
adds.
Cocogitto 7 checks a positional range:

```bash
cog check --ignore-merge-commits <base>..HEAD
```

There is no `cog check --from`.
`--from-latest-tag` is a boolean, and it shares a group with that range.
`cog.toml` sets `ignore_merge_commits = true`, which skips a commit with more
than one parent (a `Merge branch` commit).
A develop sync whose subject is `merge:` has one parent, so cog still reports
`Commit type `merge` not allowed`.
The prepare check ignores that subject as well.

### Preparing a release (maintainer)

1. Ensure `main` is green (orchestrator `CI gate`, potentials if relevant).
2. Confirm fragments exist for everything since the last tag
   (`uvx towncrier build --draft`).
3. Local sanity:

   #+attr_rgpot: syntax compiles potctl and packages the crate
   #+begin_src bash
   cargo run -q -p potctl -- release assert
   cargo publish --manifest-path rgpot-core/Cargo.toml --locked --dry-run
   #+end_src

4. Dry-run bump (optional; also GHA `workflow_dispatch` on
   `release-prepare.yml`):

   #+attr_rgpot: syntax needs cocogitto
   #+begin_src bash
   cog bump --auto --dry-run
   # or: --patch / --minor / --major / --version 1.2.0
   #+end_src

5. Cut the release *locally* (needs push rights; does *not* publish to crates.io
   by itself; the tag workflows do).
   `cog bump` runs the `pre_bump_hooks` of `cog.toml` in this order:

   - `cargo run -q -p potctl --bin potctl -- release sync {{version}}` writes
     `[workspace.package] version` in `Cargo.toml` and nothing else
   - `pixi r -e version release-cog` regenerates the copies
   - `cargo update --workspace --offline` rewrites the `Cargo.lock` entries
   - `uvx towncrier build --yes --version {{version}}` updates `CHANGELOG.md`
     and clears the fragments
   - `cargo run -q -p potctl --bin potctl -- release assert --require-changelog {{version}}`
     is the gate

   #+attr_rgpot: syntax creates a commit and a tag and pushes them
   #+begin_src bash
   # Stable example:
   cog bump --version 1.2.0
   # or let cog compute from conventional commits since last tag:
   # cog bump --auto
   git push origin HEAD --follow-tags
   #+end_src

6. The tag push triggers `release.yml` (staged, not one fat job) and
   `publish.yml`:

   - `tools` job: `setup-ci-tools` builds `potctl` (rust-cache `shared-key`
     `potctl-ci-tools-<OS>`) and uploads artifact `ci-tools-<sha>-Linux`
   - `gate` job: `restore-ci-tools` only;
     `potctl release assert --require-changelog` and `potctl release notes`
     write artifact `release-notes-<sha>` (fail fast before the build jobs)
   - `cpp-smoke` ∥ `rust-test` (parallel; only need a green `gate`)
   - `publish` (stable tags only; skipped when the version is already on
     crates.io) or `publish-skip-rc` (pre-release tags), then `gh-release` (body
     from the gate artifact; `prerelease` for RC tags)
   - `publish.yml` runs `cargo publish --locked --no-verify -p rgpot-core` on
     the same tag

Within a single job, steps share the runner FS (no reinstall per step).
Across jobs, binaries travel via artifacts.
`rust-test` and `publish` share the `Swatinem/rust-cache` key
`rgpot-core-release`, so the next tag cut is cheap when sources are unchanged.

Do *not* run `cargo publish` by hand unless CI is unavailable; the workflows are
the source of truth.
Do *not* use `cargo publish` without `--locked` (lockfile drift must fail the
release).

### Pre-release / RC tags

```bash
cog bump --version 1.2.0-rc.1
git push origin HEAD --follow-tags
```

- Creates `v1.2.0-rc.1` and builds a towncrier section for `1.2.0-rc.1` if
  fragments exist.
- `release.yml` creates a *prerelease* GitHub Release and skips its own
  `cargo publish` step.
- `publish.yml` has no pre-release check, so it publishes `rgpot-core`
  `1.2.0-rc.1` to crates.io.
- Promote by a normal stable bump to `1.2.0` with a full fragment set if needed.

### Version policy

- *One source*: C++ (meson + CMake), the Rust crates (`rgpot-core`,
  `rgpot-pair`), the Python package, the towncrier stamp and the pixi workspace
  share the semver in `Cargo.toml` (optionally with a `-[a-z0-9.]+` suffix for
  RCs).
  `potctl` keeps its own version, because it does not publish.
- *One global tag*: `vX.Y.Z` or `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` (not `rgpot-core-v…`).
- *Crate publish* ships `rgpot-core` only; `release.yml` publishes it on stable
  tags and `publish.yml` on every `v*` tag.
  C++ consumers track the git tag / source tarball, not crates.io.

### Emergency / hotfixes

```bash
cog bump --patch
git push origin HEAD --follow-tags
```

For a named version:

```bash
cog bump --version 1.1.1
```

### Local checks before bump

```bash
pixi r rust-test-all
pixi r prek
uvx towncrier build --draft
cargo run -q -p potctl -- release assert
cargo run -q -p potctl -- release sync 9.9.9   # ok semver; use real target in dry tests
pixi r -e version version-drift   # must fail now
# refuse garbage:
cargo run -q -p potctl -- release sync not-a-version   # must error
# restore if you ran a fake version: git checkout -- Cargo.toml
cargo publish --manifest-path rgpot-core/Cargo.toml --locked --dry-run
pixi r lychee-check   # optional link hygiene
```

### After the tag

1. Confirm the `Release` workflow: lockstep gate, smoke install, rust tests,
   crates.io, GH Release body.
2. Confirm the `publish` workflow uploaded `rgpot-core`.
3. Optional: announce; open conda-forge/Spack bumps out of band if applicable.
